leaders.name: Ada Chen Rekhi
leaders.title: Executive Coach & Co-Founder
leaders.bio: Executive coach helping founders scale themselves, co-founder of Notejoy, former SVP of Marketing at SurveyMonkey, and former growth marketing lead at LinkedIn.

notableQuotes.quote: It's a terrible outcome to wake up one day and be late career and feel trapped because you have a certain lifestyle or certain expectations of the people around you that you have to go work this job, but then you look at yourself in the mirror and you're not happy going in there.
notableQuotes.context: On the danger of optimizing for external markers rather than personal values

notableQuotes.quote: A curiosity loop is essentially going to a whole bunch of people... asking them a specific question and getting back an incredible amount of information for about 20 minutes of work.
notableQuotes.context: Introducing her structured decision-making framework

notableQuotes.quote: Don't do what people tell you to do. Take it as an input and look for the hard feedback. Look for things that you strongly disagree with or are surprises to you.
notableQuotes.context: On how to process advice from curiosity loops

leaders.episodeSummary: Ada Chen Rekhi shares her curiosity loops framework for structured decision-making, her values-based approach to career navigation, and insights on executive coaching for founders. She discusses the explore-exploit model for early career growth, drawing from her path from Microsoft to LinkedIn to SVP of Marketing at SurveyMonkey, and offers candid advice on women navigating leadership in Silicon Valley.
leadershipPrinciples: Use structured feedback loops (curiosity loops) rather than ad-hoc advice to make better decisions
Optimize career choices around personal values, not external status markers
Early career should be about exploration with a thesis; exploitation comes later

leaders.name: Adam Fishman
leaders.title: Former CPO & Growth Leader
leaders.bio: Growth and product executive who was the first growth hire at Lyft, led product and growth at Patreon for four years, and served as CPO at Imperfect Foods; now an EIR at Reforge and growth advisor.

notableQuotes.quote: Onboarding is the only part of your product experience that a hundred percent of people are ever going to touch. Good luck getting a hundred percent feature adoption of anything else in your product.
notableQuotes.context: On why onboarding is the most powerful growth lever

notableQuotes.quote: Your brand is the promise that you're making and your product experience is your delivery of that promise. And those two things have to be in lockstep with each other.
notableQuotes.context: On the connection between brand promise and product onboarding

notableQuotes.quote: They didn't approach it that way. They didn't ask me those questions and I was too naive to recognize that they're not actually evaluating this with the competencies that you would expect for a growth leader.
notableQuotes.context: On his failed stint at Wyzant due to misaligned expectations around growth hiring

leaders.episodeSummary: Adam Fishman presents his Growth Competency Model — a four-part framework (growth execution, customer knowledge, growth strategy, communication and influence) for hiring and evaluating growth talent. He shares deep insights on onboarding as the highest-leverage growth investment, drawing from experiences at Lyft and Patreon where onboarding optimizations drove 25% revenue improvements, and advocates for internal hires and up-and-coming talent over senior external candidates.
leadershipPrinciples: Onboarding is the only part of your product 100% of users touch — don't mess it up
Hire growth people based on competency gaps, not pattern matching to senior leaders
Internal hires often outperform external ones for growth roles due to existing customer knowledge

leaders.name: Adam Grenier
leaders.title: Former Head of Growth Marketing & Innovation
leaders.bio: Growth marketing leader who built Uber's growth marketing infrastructure from the ground up, then led marketing at Lambda School and Masterclass; now advises companies on growth and marketing strategy.
keyThemes: burnout and mental health in tech

notableQuotes.quote: Start by assuming you no longer have product market fit, because you had product market fit in a different market. It's a different market now, so you have to start over.
notableQuotes.context: Advice on adjusting marketing strategy during economic shifts

notableQuotes.quote: If someone's like, 'Hey, you have a chicken on your head,' not saying, 'No, I don't' — versus saying, 'Yes, I do, and its name is Sally. What's your chicken's name?' builds on that and gives it more opportunity.
notableQuotes.context: On applying improv's 'Yes, and' principle to business collaboration

notableQuotes.quote: I don't need a Notion Clubhouse channel this week. Please just stop.
notableQuotes.context: On B2B companies blindly chasing consumer acquisition channels

leaders.episodeSummary: Adam Grenier shares his framework for evaluating emerging acquisition channels by mapping channel strengths against customer needs and company goals, drawing from experience at Uber, Lambda School, and Masterclass. He also discusses how improv skills translate to better cross-functional collaboration, the emerging growth CMO role, and opens up about burnout and mental health challenges in tech careers.
leadershipPrinciples: Start by assuming you no longer have product-market fit when markets change, because your entire customer base changed
Evaluate emerging channels by the overlap between channel strengths, customer needs, and company goals
Apply improv's 'Yes, and...' principle to cross-functional collaboration to build better rapport and solutions

leaders.name: Adriel Frederick
leaders.title: VP of Product
leaders.bio: VP of Product at Reddit leading new product incubation, former Director of Product at Lyft leading marketplace and pricing teams, and an early PM at Facebook where he was the first Black product manager and led user acquisition.

notableQuotes.quote: The algorithms don't understand long term effects often, nor do they understand how people might respond to it, nor do they understand your intent for the product. That is our job as product managers.
notableQuotes.context: On the PM role in algorithmic product design, pushing back on 'techno utopians'

notableQuotes.quote: I was the first Black product manager at Facebook... one phone number plus one device does not equal one person. Growing up in Trinidad, I just knew that wasn't true.
notableQuotes.context: On how diverse backgrounds directly improve product design for global users

notableQuotes.quote: The rest of the company needs to see what you're doing as being core and critical to the mission. It can't seem like these guys are just playing off in a corner.
notableQuotes.context: On preventing organ rejection of R&D teams within larger organizations

leaders.episodeSummary: Adriel Frederick discusses the PM's critical role in algorithmic product management, drawing from his experience building Facebook's growth team and Lyft's marketplace pricing. He shares powerful insights on how diversity drives better global product design, how to set up R&D teams that avoid organizational rejection, and how to lead product teams through company controversy by staying deeply connected to users.
leadershipPrinciples: When working on algorithmic products, the PM's job is deciding what the algorithm should own versus what people should own
Diverse teams build better global products because they reduce the need for external user research
As a PM leader, provide a buffering effect — pull the team down when overhyped, pull them up when demoralized

leaders.name: Aishwarya Naresh Reganti
leaders.title: AI Product Consultant & Educator
leaders.bio: Early AI researcher at Alexa and Microsoft with 35+ published research papers who has supported over 50 AI product deployments and teaches the top-rated AI product course on Maven.

notableQuotes.quote: Most people tend to ignore the non-determinism. You don't know how the user might behave with your product, and you also don't know how the LLM might respond to that.
notableQuotes.context: On the fundamental difference between building AI and traditional software products

notableQuotes.quote: Every time you hand over decision-making capabilities to agentic systems, you're kind of relinquishing some amount of control on your end.
notableQuotes.context: Introducing the agency-control tradeoff concept

notableQuotes.quote: It's not about being the first company to have an agent among your competitors. It's about have you built the right flywheels in place so that you can improve over time.
notableQuotes.context: On sustainable AI product strategy vs. rushing to ship agents

leaders.episodeSummary: Aishwarya Reganti explains why building AI products is fundamentally different from traditional software, centering on non-determinism and the agency-control tradeoff. She advocates for incremental autonomy deployment — starting with high human control and low AI agency, then progressively increasing autonomy as trust is built — and emphasizes that AI transformation requires leaders who are hands-on, cultures of empowerment, and obsessive understanding of workflows.
leadershipPrinciples: Building AI products requires understanding that non-determinism fundamentally changes the product development lifecycle
Start with high control and low agency, then incrementally increase autonomy as trust is earned
Leaders must rebuild their intuitions for AI — the CEO being hands-on with AI is the top predictor of success

leaders.name: Albert Cheng
leaders.title: Head of Growth & Monetization
leaders.bio: One of the top consumer growth minds in the world, having led growth and monetization at Duolingo, Grammarly, and Chess.com, with earlier experience at YouTube working on streaming and gaming features.
keyThemes: growth as connecting users to value

notableQuotes.quote: Growth as the job is to connect users to the value of your product. Growth sometimes gets this reputation that it's just pure metrics hacking.
notableQuotes.context: Reframing the purpose of growth work

notableQuotes.quote: User retention is gold for consumer subscription companies. If you don't retain your users, then a lot of the onus is on getting them to pay on day one.
notableQuotes.context: On the biggest missing piece in consumer subscription products

notableQuotes.quote: What if we actually sampled a number of different paid suggestions and interspersed them to free users across their writing? All of a sudden, people were seeing Grammarly as a much more powerful tool.
notableQuotes.context: On his biggest monetization win at Grammarly

leaders.episodeSummary: Albert Cheng shares his explore-exploit framework for finding growth opportunities, drawing from leading growth and monetization at Duolingo, Grammarly, and Chess.com. He reveals key monetization wins like sampling paid features for free Grammarly users, advocates for running 1,000 experiments per year, and discusses how AI is accelerating growth work while making experience-based intuitions less reliable.
leadershipPrinciples: Growth's job is to connect users to the value of your product, not pure metrics hacking
User retention is gold for consumer subscription companies — without it, you're forced to monetize on day one
High agency and clock speed matter more than deep experience, especially in fast-moving AI environments

leaders.name: Alex Hardiman
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: CPO at The New York Times leading teams across news, cooking, games, audio, and advertising products; previously CPO at The Atlantic and spent two years at Facebook leading news product.

notableQuotes.quote: Our impact and our business goals are in service of our mission, which is to seek the truth and help people understand the world, not the other way around.
notableQuotes.context: On how product work at the New York Times differs from big tech

notableQuotes.quote: When you're a product manager, you're driving specific metrics like engagement or subscribers, but you're also trying to help stories find their real audience in ways that trigger mission-driven impact. I didn't feel that when I was at Facebook.
notableQuotes.context: On the unique PM role at a mission-driven media company

notableQuotes.quote: We brought in consultants and they said, 'Maybe over the course of history it'll get to one million subscribers, if you're lucky.' It felt like a really big nervous moment.
notableQuotes.context: On the skepticism around the NYT's digital subscription paywall launch in 2011

leaders.episodeSummary: Alex Hardiman shares how product development at the New York Times is driven by mission rather than metrics alone, spanning the transformation from print to mobile-first and the bold bet on direct-to-consumer subscriptions. She draws on her experience across NYT, The Atlantic, and Facebook to discuss building product at non-tech companies, navigating controversial moments, and ensuring business goals serve journalistic mission.
leadershipPrinciples: Impact and business goals must serve the mission, not the other way around
Product managers at mission-driven companies drive metrics while also helping stories find their real audience
The shift from print-first to mobile-first requires leading with mobile in everything — formats, features, and revenue

leaders.name: Alex Komoroske
leaders.title: Founder & Former Head of Corporate Strategy
leaders.bio: One of the most original first-principles thinkers on product and tech, having spent 13 years at Google leading Chrome's Open Web Platform, AR in Maps, and company-wide strategy, then Head of Corporate Strategy at Stripe, now founding an AI-era startup.
keyThemes: adjacent possible and slime mold thinking

notableQuotes.quote: So much of the way that we build products is this builder mindset. What I look for instead are things that can be gardened, things that can grow on their own and that you can direct. If you do this properly, it looks like magic.
notableQuotes.context: On the gardener versus builder mindset for creating outsized value

notableQuotes.quote: LLMs are magical duct tape. So much of the industry presupposes that software is expensive to write and cheap to run, and LLMs undermine both of these.
notableQuotes.context: On how LLMs disrupt fundamental assumptions about software economics

notableQuotes.quote: We've seen a vast reduction in the cost of distribution of information, and now we're seeing a reduction in the cost of production. Most of it is slop. In this cacophony, you stand out by having good taste.
notableQuotes.context: On why taste becomes the most important skill in the AI era

leaders.episodeSummary: Alex Komoroske offers a deeply original perspective on how LLMs will reshape product development, arguing they're a disruptive 'magical duct tape' that changes the economics of software and makes taste the most critical competitive advantage. Drawing from 13 years at Google and his role at Stripe, he advocates for a gardener mindset over a builder mindset, organizational concepts inspired by slime mold, and disciplined reflection practices that generate his most impactful insights.
leadershipPrinciples: Think like a gardener, not a builder — garden things that grow on their own rather than manipulating to match a plan
LLMs are magical duct tape that undermines the assumption that software is expensive to write and cheap to run
Taste is the most important skill in the AI era — you must stand out from the background noise of AI-generated slop

leaders.name: Alexander Embiricos
leaders.title: Product Lead, Codex
leaders.bio: Product lead for Codex at OpenAI, the company's coding agent; previously founded a startup for five years and was a product manager at Dropbox, described by OpenAI's CPO as 'simply the best.'

notableQuotes.quote: Codex is a bit like this really smart intern that refuses to read Slack, doesn't check Datadog unless you ask it to.
notableQuotes.context: On the current state and limitations of AI coding agents

notableQuotes.quote: Even if we had no more progress with models today, we are way behind on product. There's so much more product to build.
notableQuotes.context: On the massive product opportunity ahead even with current AI capabilities

notableQuotes.quote: The current underappreciated limiting factor is literally human typing speed or human multitasking speed.
notableQuotes.context: On the bottleneck to AI progress and AGI

leaders.episodeSummary: Alexander Embiricos shares what it's like building Codex at OpenAI, where radical speed and bottoms-up autonomy are enabled by extraordinary talent density. He discusses Codex's explosive 20x growth, how it enabled the Sora Android app to ship in just 18 days, why his team is now focused on making code review easier rather than just code generation, and his belief that the biggest bottleneck to AI progress is human bandwidth, not model capability.
leadershipPrinciples: At AI companies, empirical learning matters more than planning — be ready, fire, aim rather than ready, aim, fire
Even with no more model progress, we're way behind on product — there's so much more to build
The bottoms-up approach only works with extraordinary talent caliber — you can't just deploy it anywhere

leaders.name: Alisa Cohn
leaders.title: Executive Coach
leaders.bio: Named the number one startup coach in the world by Global Gurus and top 50 coach by Thinkers50, having coached C-suite executives at Etsy, Venmo, DraftKings, Microsoft, Google, and the New York Times.

notableQuotes.quote: I know this is going to be challenging for you to hear — not going to promote you — but I want you to know this. It's really important to me that you're able to succeed in your career here.
notableQuotes.context: Specific language for handling promotion denials with compassion

notableQuotes.quote: They're trying to be the leader who everyone loves, but what really needs to happen is we need to drive towards results. This employee continuing to not do a great job... ultimately leads to the demise of your company.
notableQuotes.context: On why leaders must prioritize results over being liked

notableQuotes.quote: Hope for the future is so important.
notableQuotes.context: On the critical ingredient when delivering difficult feedback

leaders.episodeSummary: Alisa Cohn, the world's top-rated startup coach, provides extremely specific and actionable language for having difficult conversations, from denying promotions to addressing underperformance. She shares her three questions to end every meeting effectively, explains why a leader's job isn't to make people happy, and introduces the 'founder prenup' — a set of questions co-founders should discuss before committing to build together.
leadershipPrinciples: Your job as a leader isn't to make people happy — it's to drive results while treating people with respect
Always provide hope for the future when delivering difficult feedback like denied promotions
End every meeting with three specific questions to ensure maximum forward progress

leaders.name: Ami Vora
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: CPO at Faire, the largest B2B marketplace startup; was employee 150 at Facebook where she launched the developer platform, headed the $55B global ads business, oversaw Instagram ads, and led product and design at WhatsApp.

notableQuotes.quote: I really enjoy being right and then it turns out in the working world, that did not serve me so great. The hard part is sublimating your ego and saying it's more important to get to the outcome than to be right.
notableQuotes.context: On learning to disagree skillfully and let go of being right

notableQuotes.quote: If we all agree that the feeling of something should be, I'm sitting in Dolores Park with my friends on a sunny Saturday, then people will just naturally build something that feels more consistent.
notableQuotes.context: On using emotional metaphors to align product teams

notableQuotes.quote: The hill climb is all about the difference between a local optimum and a global optimum. The thing that gets me through the valley is remembering what the summit feels like.
notableQuotes.context: On persevering through difficult strategic transitions

leaders.episodeSummary: Ami Vora shares her approach to strategic leadership drawing from transformative roles at Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and now Faire. She emphasizes the power of emotional metaphors for team alignment, the art of skilled disagreement that prioritizes outcomes over being right, and navigating between local and global optima in product strategy, all while discussing the unique challenges of being a woman in tech leadership.
leadershipPrinciples: It's more important to get to the right outcome than to be right — sublimate your ego
Use metaphors and imagery to rally teams — 'what should users feel?' aligns teams better than specs
Distinguish between local optimum hill climbing and going through the valley toward the global optimum mountain

leaders.name: Amjad Masad
leaders.title: Co-Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Co-founder and CEO of Replit, an AI-powered software development and deployment platform with 34 million users globally, one of the fastest-growing developer communities and AI products in the world.

notableQuotes.quote: The idea behind Replit is that making software today is very difficult. We want to make it easier. People view this as a developer in their pocket.
notableQuotes.context: On Replit's core mission

notableQuotes.quote: Typically, you're bottlenecked where your ideas are not fitting in because they need to be made quickly. Now, you open up that bottleneck. You become limited by how fast you can generate ideas.
notableQuotes.context: On how AI changes the product development bottleneck

notableQuotes.quote: I could imagine five years from now, someone running a billion-dollar company with zero employees where the support is handled by AI, the development is handled by AI.
notableQuotes.context: On the future of AI-automated companies

leaders.episodeSummary: Amjad Masad demos Replit's AI-powered software creation capabilities and discusses the profound implications for product development, arguing that AI shifts the bottleneck from building to ideation. He envisions a future where billion-dollar companies could run with zero employees, and emphasizes that product builders should be playing with these tools now to understand the seismic shifts coming to how software is created and deployed.
leadershipPrinciples: Making software is too hard — the mission is to make it dramatically easier for everyone
AI shifts the bottleneck from building to ideation — you become limited by how fast you can generate ideas
The future may include billion-dollar companies with zero employees where AI handles development, support, and operations

leaders.name: Andrew 'Boz' Bosworth
leaders.title: Chief Technology Officer
leaders.bio: CTO of Meta and one of the first engineers at Facebook (joined 2006); created the Facebook News Feed, built the original mobile ads platform, helped build Groups, Messaging, and Timeline; created Meta's AR/VR organization (Reality Labs); leads Quest and Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.

notableQuotes.quote: Newsfeed was an easier case than people suspect. Everyone was outraged at the same time as they immediately doubled their usage of the product.
notableQuotes.context: On the famous backlash to the Facebook News Feed he helped create

notableQuotes.quote: I didn't sleep for more than four hours at a time. I'd wake up every four hours and check the report and see if anyone was attacking the site. They don't tell you about that stuff in the movies.
notableQuotes.context: On the reality of early Facebook engineering

notableQuotes.quote: I don't want to take away from the romanticism of it. It's just that most often, we hear those romantic stories from the successes. It's a healthy thing for people to want to throw themselves into something and take that risk, but it is not glamorous at the time.
notableQuotes.context: On survivorship bias in startup narratives

leaders.episodeSummary: Andrew 'Boz' Bosworth, Meta's CTO and one of Facebook's first engineers, shares stories and lessons from his 18-year tenure including creating the News Feed, building the mobile ads platform, and leading Reality Labs. He discusses why communication becomes the primary job of a leader, the truth behind the News Feed backlash (users doubled their usage while complaining), and lessons from Meta's recent turnaround.
leadershipPrinciples: Communication is the job — the higher you go, the more your impact comes from how well you communicate, not what you build
Newsfeed was easier than people suspect: everyone was outraged while simultaneously doubling their usage of the product — watch behavior, not complaints
Don't romanticize the startup grind — most romantic stories come from successes, but at the time it's not glamorous, just painful

leaders.name: Andrew Wilkinson
leaders.title: Co-Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Co-founder and CEO of Tiny, a holding company often called the 'Berkshire Hathaway of the internet' that owns 40+ businesses including Dribbble and AeroPress, bootstrapped from zero to hundreds of millions in value.

notableQuotes.quote: You don't want to walk into the gym on day one and try and deadlift 300 pounds. So when someone comes to me and they're a first time entrepreneur and they say, 'I'm going to make the next great AI company,' I think that is the equivalent.
notableQuotes.context: On why first-time founders should start with simpler, more achievable businesses

notableQuotes.quote: The biggest mistakes I've made have been going into business models where other people have repeatedly failed and thinking, I can do this better.
notableQuotes.context: On the importance of choosing markets with proven success patterns

notableQuotes.quote: It's like having the world's most reliable employee who costs $200 a month and works 24/7. So many knowledge work jobs are going to change massively.
notableQuotes.context: On AI's impact on knowledge work and business operations

leaders.episodeSummary: Andrew Wilkinson, who built Tiny into a 40+ business holding company worth hundreds of millions, shares strategies for selecting good business ideas, including 'fishing where the fish are' and starting simple. He discusses his AI obsession and how it's transforming knowledge work, the disconnect between money and happiness he discovered after becoming a billionaire, and how getting diagnosed with ADHD and taking SSRIs had more impact on his happiness than wealth.
leadershipPrinciples: Fish where the fish are — don't enter business models where others have repeatedly failed thinking you'll be different
Don't try to deadlift 300 pounds on day one — first-time founders should start with simpler businesses
AI is like having the world's most reliable employee who costs $200/month and works 24/7

leaders.name: Andy Johns
leaders.title: Former VP of Growth & Product
leaders.bio: Legendary growth leader at Facebook, Twitter, Quora, and Wealthfront (VP of Growth, VP of Product, then President), who transformed his career path to become a mental health advocate helping burned-out high achievers and veterans.
keyThemes: burnout and mental health in tech
signs of crisis in high achievers

notableQuotes.quote: When your sleep always sucks, when your relationships are constantly strained, when your physical health is failing... your body is telling you, 'Stop. Something needs to change.'
notableQuotes.context: On recognizing the warning signs of burnout

notableQuotes.quote: There are day-to-day stresses that are normal and we just have to put up with, but then there's the other stuff that's the flashing red alarm.
notableQuotes.context: On distinguishing normal work stress from genuine crisis

leaders.episodeSummary: Andy Johns, a legendary growth leader at Facebook, Twitter, Quora, and Wealthfront, shares his deeply personal story of burnout and transformation. Once in line to become CEO of Wealthfront, he came to realize the path wasn't right for him and completely changed his life to become a mental health advocate. He discusses the warning signs of burnout, the four-step process of deep personal change, and offers candid advice on mental health in the tech industry.
leadershipPrinciples: When core behaviors like sleep, relationships, and physical health are suffering, your body is telling you something needs to change
There are four steps to making lasting personal change — and most people skip the hard middle ones
Day-to-day stress is normal, but when fundamental functions get disrupted it's a flashing red alarm

leaders.name: Andy Raskin
leaders.title: Strategic Narrative Consultant
leaders.bio: Helps CEOs and company leaders align their teams around strategic narratives — stories that explain why people need their product — working with top companies on their pitches, positioning, and fundraising narratives.
keyThemes: old game to new game framework

notableQuotes.quote: Every movie starts with some kind of shift in the world. I call this the shift from the old game to a new game. This structure is about defining a movement, and that's very different from 'I'm going to solve your problem.'
notableQuotes.context: On the core structure of a strategic narrative

notableQuotes.quote: The way I learned how to pitch in business school was what I call the arrogant doctor: you have a problem, I have a solution. The structure that works is different.
notableQuotes.context: On why conventional pitching frameworks are inferior

leaders.episodeSummary: Andy Raskin teaches his strategic narrative framework that replaces the traditional 'problem-solution' pitch with a movement-based story structure. By framing a shift from an 'old game' to a 'new game,' companies can align sales, marketing, product, and fundraising around a single compelling narrative, as exemplified by Salesforce's 'software is over' positioning that created an entire market movement.
leadershipPrinciples: The best pitch isn't 'I solve your problem' — it's 'there's a new game and we help you win it'
Strategic narrative aligns sales, marketing, product, fundraising, and hiring around one compelling story
Every great company narrative starts with a shift from the old game to a new game — like Salesforce's 'software is over'

leaders.name: Anneka Gupta
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: CPO at Rubrik, Stanford GSB lecturer on product management, and board member at Tinuiti; previously was President, GM, and head of product at LiveRamp where she spent 11 years from early employee to executive.

notableQuotes.quote: When people say 'I want someone that's strategic,' what they're really saying is 'I want someone that can articulate a compelling and simple why' AND 'be a change agent to do things that are hard but best for the long-term.'
notableQuotes.context: Breaking down what it actually means to be 'strategic'

notableQuotes.quote: When I was able to switch my mindset and say, 'I'm actually going to figure out a way to have fun with this,' it actually changed my entire approach for dealing with super difficult situations.
notableQuotes.context: On her most important career mindset

leaders.episodeSummary: Anneka Gupta breaks down what it truly means to be 'strategic' — articulating a compelling why and being a change agent for hard decisions — drawing from 11 years growing LiveRamp from early employee to President and now leading product at Rubrik. She shares tactical advice on navigating difficult personalities, managing energy over time, giving hard feedback with humor and gratitude, and how to break into product management.
leadershipPrinciples: Being strategic means articulating a compelling 'why' AND championing hard changes for the long-term interest
Find how to have fun even in the most difficult situations — it opens your mind to more opportunities
You need both a compelling vision and the willingness to be a change agent, or people won't see you as strategic

leaders.name: Annie Duke
leaders.title: Author & Decision Strategist
leaders.bio: Bestselling author of 'Thinking in Bets' and 'Quit,' former professional poker player who won over $4M in tournaments including a World Series of Poker bracelet, now helps companies make better decisions as a special partner at First Round Capital.

notableQuotes.quote: It's so incredibly necessary in improving decision quality to take what's implicit and make it explicit. Your intuition is sometimes right. If you don't make it explicit, then you don't get to find out when it's wrong.
notableQuotes.context: On the fundamental principle of better decision-making

notableQuotes.quote: There is no such thing as a long feedback loop. The way you shorten it is to say, what are the things that are correlated with the outcome that I eventually desire?
notableQuotes.context: On using leading indicators to evaluate decisions before final outcomes

notableQuotes.quote: People generally think the purpose of a meeting is to discover, discuss, decide. The only thing that's supposed to happen in a meeting is the discussion part.
notableQuotes.context: On restructuring meetings for better decision-making

leaders.episodeSummary: Annie Duke, bestselling author and former World Series of Poker champion, shares frameworks for dramatically improving decision quality in product and business. She argues there's no such thing as a long feedback loop if you identify correlated leading indicators, explains why making implicit assumptions explicit is the single most impactful change companies can make, and reveals how she transformed decision-making at First Round Capital.
leadershipPrinciples: Take what's implicit and make it explicit — intuition is sometimes right, but if you don't make it explicit you can't find out when it's wrong
There is no such thing as a long feedback loop — shorten it by identifying correlated leading indicators
Pre-mortems are only useful if you set kill criteria and commit to actions when you see those signals

leaders.name: Annie Pearl
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: CPO at Calendly, previously CPO at Glassdoor and Director of Product at Fox; board member and member of Skip, a community for chief product officers.
keyThemes: where to play and how to win

notableQuotes.quote: Strategy is really just an integrated set of choices that outline how you're going to win in whatever marketplace you choose. A good product strategy answers: what's your winning aspiration, where are you going to play, what are the personas, and how are you going to win?
notableQuotes.context: On defining product strategy simply and clearly

leaders.episodeSummary: Annie Pearl shares her approach to product strategy as an integrated set of choices about where to play and how to win, drawing from her experience leading product at Calendly, Glassdoor, and Fox. She discusses the dynamics of building a product-led growth scheduling tool, the importance of reducing friction for all parties, and how product leaders should think about market segmentation and persona targeting.
leadershipPrinciples: Strategy is an integrated set of choices that outline how you're going to win in your chosen marketplace
A good product strategy answers: winning aspiration, where to play, segments, personas, and how to win
Product leaders must be willing to make hard choices about where NOT to play

leaders.name: Anton Osika
leaders.title: Co-Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Co-founder and CEO of Lovable, an AI software engineer that turns English prompts into working products; the fastest growing startup in Europe ever, hitting $4M ARR in four weeks and $10M ARR in two months with just 15 people.

notableQuotes.quote: The best word for a great product is that it's lovable. A lot of jargon I like to use is building a minimum lovable product, then a lovable product, then an absolutely lovable product.
notableQuotes.context: On the naming philosophy behind Lovable

notableQuotes.quote: Being a generalist, I think, is much more important than it used to be. If I'm putting together a product team today, I would really obsess about getting as many skill sets as possible for each person I hire.
notableQuotes.context: On how AI tools change the ideal team composition

notableQuotes.quote: People love the product. That's the driver of the growth.
notableQuotes.context: On what enabled $10M ARR in two months with 15 people

leaders.episodeSummary: Anton Osika shares how Lovable became Europe's fastest-growing startup ever by building an AI software engineer that turns English prompts into working products. With just 15 people, they hit $10M ARR in two months, driven entirely by product quality. He advocates for generalist hiring, minimum lovable products over MVPs, and discusses how AI tools are reshaping what product teams should look like going forward.
leadershipPrinciples: People love the product — that's the driver of growth, not marketing or hacks
Being a generalist is much more important than it used to be — obsess about getting many skill sets per person
Build a minimum lovable product, then a lovable product, then an absolutely lovable product

leaders.name: Anuj Rathi
leaders.title: Chief Product & Marketing Officer
leaders.bio: The most requested India-based product leader, currently CPMO at Jupiter Money; previously SVP of Revenue & Growth at Swiggy for seven years, VP of Product at Snapdeal, and the very first PM at Flipkart.

notableQuotes.quote: There are only three reasons why things do not happen the way you want: they can't do (capability), they won't do (motivation/alignment), or they were not set up to do (your problem as leader).
notableQuotes.context: On diagnosing leadership and execution failures

leaders.episodeSummary: Anuj Rathi, the most requested India-based product leader, shares his diagnostic framework for leadership — identifying whether execution gaps stem from capability, motivation, or system design failures. Drawing from being the first PM at Flipkart, seven years growing Swiggy's revenue, and now leading product and marketing at Jupiter Money, he discusses the unique dynamics of building products for the Indian market and how product management differs in India's high-growth tech ecosystem.
leadershipPrinciples: There are only three reasons things don't happen: can't do (capability), won't do (motivation), or not set up to do (your failure as leader)
Diagnose whether the issue is capability, alignment, or system design before jumping to solutions
Product building for India requires thinking about constrained environments, price sensitivity, and mobile-first design

leaders.name: Aparna Chennapragada
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: CPO at Microsoft overseeing AI product strategy for productivity tools and agents; previously CPO at Robinhood, VP at Google where she worked on Lens, Search, Shopping, AR, and AI Assistant, and board member at eBay and Capital One.

notableQuotes.quote: NLX is the new UX. Conversations also have grammars. They have structures. They have UI elements. They're invisible. What are the new principles, new constructs in natural language as an interface?
notableQuotes.context: On the emerging design discipline of natural language interfaces

notableQuotes.quote: If you're not prototyping and building to see what you want to build, I think you're doing it wrong. Taste-making becomes even more important because otherwise you just have a Frankenstein product.
notableQuotes.context: On how AI changes the product development process

notableQuotes.quote: I have a cheesy Chrome extension. Literally whenever I open a new tab, it just says, how can you use AI to do what you're going to do right now?
notableQuotes.context: On forcing herself to constantly think about AI-first approaches

leaders.episodeSummary: Aparna Chennapragada introduces the concept of NLX (natural language interface) as the new UX paradigm, arguing that even conversational AI products need deliberate design thinking around grammar, structure, and invisible UI elements. Drawing from her experience leading AI product strategy at Microsoft and previously Google Lens and Search, she emphasizes that prototyping-first development and taste-making become even more critical in the AI era to avoid Frankenstein products.
leadershipPrinciples: NLX (natural language interface) is the new UX — conversations also have grammars, structures, and invisible UI elements
If you're not prototyping and building to see what you want to build, you're doing it wrong in the AI era
Taste-making becomes even more important with AI because otherwise you just have a Frankenstein product

leaders.name: April Dunford
leaders.title: Positioning Expert & Author
leaders.bio: The world's foremost authority on product positioning, author of bestselling books 'Obviously Awesome' and 'Sales Pitch,' with a 25-year career as VP of marketing and advisor to companies like Google and Epic Games.

notableQuotes.quote: If your product isn't doing well, there's a chance that it may not be the product that's the problem, it may be your positioning.
notableQuotes.context: Lenny's framing of why positioning matters so much, which April builds on throughout

leaders.episodeSummary: April Dunford, the world's leading authority on product positioning, walks through her practical framework for nailing positioning — starting with competitive alternatives rather than features, selecting the right market category, and making your product's value obvious to the right customers. Drawing from work with over 200 companies and seven successful B2B startups, she demonstrates why positioning failures are often misdiagnosed as product failures.
leadershipPrinciples: If your product isn't doing well, the problem may not be the product — it may be your positioning
Positioning starts with competitive alternatives, not with your product features
The market category you choose frames everything customers expect from your product

leaders.name: Archie Abrams
leaders.title: VP of Product & Head of Growth
leaders.bio: VP of Product and Head of Growth at Shopify leading 600+ people across product, design, engineering, data ops, and growth marketing at one of the most uniquely operated companies in tech.
keyThemes: taste over metrics in core product
getting more people in the door

notableQuotes.quote: When teams break up the world into funnel stages, it gets very seductive to optimize for conversion rate. But it's almost always easier to just make it harder to do the thing right before your step in the funnel to increase your conversion rate.
notableQuotes.context: On the perverse incentives of funnel-stage metrics

notableQuotes.quote: The best way to get more people to get to a step is just get more people in the door in the first place. That will always hurt your conversion rate, but it may give you more people on the outside.
notableQuotes.context: On Shopify's counterintuitive approach to growth

leaders.episodeSummary: Archie Abrams reveals Shopify's unconventional approach to product and growth: core product teams have no KPIs and rely on taste and a 100-year vision from CEO Tobi, while the growth team uniquely optimizes for churn reduction rather than acquisition. He explains why funnel conversion rate optimization is often counterproductive and how Shopify maintains long-term experiment holdouts to check impact years after launch.
leadershipPrinciples: Optimizing for conversion rate at each funnel step is a trap — sometimes lower conversion but more volume is better
Core product teams shouldn't have KPIs — decisions should be based on taste, intuition, and long-term vision
Keep long-term holdouts for experiments and automatically check impact 1, 2, and 3 years later

leaders.name: Arielle Jackson
leaders.title: Marketer in Residence
leaders.bio: Former Google marketer who grew Gmail from a side project to hundreds of millions of users, one of the first marketers at Square, has worked with 100+ early-stage companies on brand strategy, and teaches a popular course on startup branding.

notableQuotes.quote: Disney means magic today. Volvo means safety. Those names are not good. No one would pick them from a spreadsheet. A bad name with a great company and great marketing is going to be great over time.
notableQuotes.context: On why startup founders shouldn't agonize over the perfect name

leaders.episodeSummary: Arielle Jackson, who grew Gmail from side project to hundreds of millions of users and was one of Square's first marketers, shares practical frameworks for startup brand strategy. She covers naming strategies (explaining that great names are filled with meaning over time), her three-pillar brand framework of purpose, positioning, and personality, and tactical advice for getting PR coverage as an early-stage startup.
leadershipPrinciples: A bad name won't kill a good company — Disney doesn't mean magic on its own, the company made it mean that
Brand framework has three pillars: purpose (why you exist), positioning (how you're different), personality (how you sound)
Great brand names are just vessels — the company's marketing and product fill them with meaning over time

leaders.name: Asha Sharma
leaders.title: CVP of Product, AI Platform
leaders.bio: Chief VP of Product for Microsoft's AI platform overseeing AI infrastructure, foundation models, and agent toolchains; previously COO at Instacart and VP of Product at Meta running Messenger and Instagram Direct; board member at Home Depot and Coupang.

notableQuotes.quote: We're approaching this world in which the marginal cost of the good output is approaching zero. We're going to see exponential demand for productivity and outputs. The way that you scale to that is with agents.
notableQuotes.context: On why agents are inevitable for scaling in the AI era

notableQuotes.quote: These are living organisms that just get better with more interactions. This is the new IP of every single company — products that think and live and learn.
notableQuotes.context: On the shift from product as artifact to product as organism

notableQuotes.quote: When all of that happens, the org chart starts to become the work chart. You just don't need as many layers.
notableQuotes.context: On how AI agents will reshape organizational structure

leaders.episodeSummary: Asha Sharma describes the paradigm shift from products as static artifacts to products as living organisms that think, learn, and improve with every interaction. Drawing from her roles leading Microsoft's AI platform, Instacart as COO, and Meta's messaging products, she argues that as marginal costs approach zero, agents will scale exponentially and fundamentally reshape org charts into work charts with fewer layers.
leadershipPrinciples: We're moving from product as artifact to product as organism — products that think, live, and learn are the new IP
When marginal cost of good output approaches zero, you'll see exponential demand and agents scaling to meet it
The org chart starts to become the work chart — you just don't need as many layers with agents

leaders.name: Austin Hay
leaders.title: Head of Marketing Technology
leaders.bio: One of the smartest people in MarTech, currently Head of Marketing Technology at Ramp; has advised Notion, Airbnb, Walmart, Robinhood on MarTech strategy; previously VP of Growth at mParticle and fourth employee at Branch Metrics.

notableQuotes.quote: From 2010 to 2020, we had the golden years of deterministic matching. You can't do that anymore. How can marketers make decisions with probabilistic data?
notableQuotes.context: On the fundamental shift in marketing attribution after privacy changes

leaders.episodeSummary: Austin Hay demystifies MarTech (Marketing Technology) and explains why it's a critical but overlooked function in growth organizations. He discusses the seismic shift from deterministic to probabilistic marketing data after IDFA changes, how to build models from partial data to make informed marketing decisions, and when and how to hire your first MarTech person, drawing from advising companies like Airbnb, Notion, and Walmart.
leadershipPrinciples: In the post-IDFA world, marketers must learn to make decisions with probabilistic data, not deterministic data
Build models from 30% of the population and extrapolate to 100% when you can't track individuals
MarTech is the infrastructure layer that makes all growth work possible — hire for it early

leaders.name: Ayo Omojola
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: CPO at Carbon Health, one of the biggest health tech companies; co-created and scaled Square's Cash Card and Cash App, former founder, angel investor in Mercury, Faire, and Modern Treasury.

notableQuotes.quote: Being different is not enough because it's easy to build something different. Being better is not enough because it's easy to just charge more. It has to be better in a way that matters to the end user.
notableQuotes.context: On Cash App's differentiation philosophy

notableQuotes.quote: When someone says, 'Why are you betting on Venmo?' I'd say, 'Try and send me a dollar that I can use now,' and there was only one app you could do it with.
notableQuotes.context: On Cash App's killer differentiator over Venmo

leaders.episodeSummary: Ayo Omojola shares lessons from co-creating Square's Cash Card and Cash App, centering on the principle that products must be both different AND better in ways that matter to users. He explains how Cash App's ability to let users send and instantly use money became their unchallengeable differentiator, and discusses applying these consumer product principles to his current role leading product at Carbon Health.
leadershipPrinciples: Being different is not enough and being better is not enough — it has to be better in a way that matters to the end user
The ultimate test: 'Try and send me a dollar that I can use now' — only Cash App could do it
Differentiation must be demonstrable, not just claimed — users should feel it in seconds

leaders.name: Bangaly Kaba
leaders.title: Director of Product Management
leaders.bio: Currently at YouTube, previously Head of Growth at Instagram, VP of Product at Instacart, and early growth PM at Facebook; known for his legendary blog post on choosing where to work.

notableQuotes.quote: What I call the anti-pattern: someone says 'this would be great to build' and you pull data to justify it. That's identify, justify, execute. Instead: understand, identify, execute. First understand from first principles what is actually going on.
notableQuotes.context: On replacing confirmation bias with genuine understanding

notableQuotes.quote: This framework has five components: vision, skills, incentives, resources, action plan. You need all of those to have change. Within those buckets you've got to figure out what's missing.
notableQuotes.context: On his change management framework used across Facebook, Instagram, Instacart, and YouTube

leaders.episodeSummary: Bangaly Kaba, with growth leadership experience spanning Facebook, Instagram, Instacart, and YouTube, shares his understand-identify-execute framework that replaces the common anti-pattern of building first and justifying later. He introduces his five-component change management framework (vision, skills, incentives, resources, action plan) and discusses how to build genuine growth culture through first-principles thinking rather than confirmation bias.
leadershipPrinciples: Replace 'identify, justify, execute' with 'understand, identify, execute' — understand from first principles before proposing solutions
Change requires five components: vision, skills, incentives, resources, and action plan — missing any one causes failure
Don't pull data to justify why something would be great to build — first understand what's actually going on

leaders.name: Barbra Gago
leaders.title: Former CMO
leaders.bio: Former CMO at Miro where she led the rebrand and created the 'visual collaboration' category; previously VP of Marketing at Greenhouse and Head of Marketing at CultureAmp; now building an employee progression platform startup.

notableQuotes.quote: When you're building a category, you need to make sure that there is a category that's validated by analysts and directory sites. But also, you want to have a lot of traction in terms of thought leadership — why is this the category? When you're generating a new category, you're also needing to educate buyers that there is a category that they can now budget for.
notableQuotes.context: On the mechanics of category creation from her Miro experience

notableQuotes.quote: There was this concept of an online whiteboard, which is a category, but it's a much smaller category. The biggest motivating factor of thinking about category creation at Miro was how do we become something really big and needed by every company and not just this little thing.
notableQuotes.context: On why Miro moved from 'online whiteboard' to 'visual collaboration'

leaders.episodeSummary: Barbra Gago, former CMO at Miro, Greenhouse, and CultureAmp, shares deep expertise on category creation strategy, including when to create a new category versus winning in an existing one. She details how she rebranded Miro from 'online whiteboard' to 'visual collaboration,' the mechanics of building buyer awareness for a new category, and the importance of building opinionated software that takes a clear stance on how work should be done.
leadershipPrinciples: When creating a category, you need analyst validation, thought leadership, and buyer education — you're teaching buyers to budget for something new
Category creation makes sense when your existing category is too small to capture the full potential of your product
Sometimes you should abandon category creation — at Greenhouse they tried and pulled back because it wasn't the right strategy

leaders.name: Ben Horowitz
leaders.title: Co-Founder & General Partner
leaders.bio: Co-founder of a16z, the world's largest venture capital firm with over $46B in committed capital; author of two NYT bestsellers including The Hard Thing About Hard Things; started his career as a PM and wrote the legendary 'Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager' piece.
keyThemes: Good Product Manager Bad Product Manager

notableQuotes.quote: The psychological muscle you have to build to be a great leader is to be able to click in the abyss and go, 'Okay, that way's slightly better. We're going to go that way.' If everybody agrees with the decision, then you didn't add any value because they would've done that without you. So the only value you ever add is when you make a decision that most people don't like.
notableQuotes.context: On what truly constitutes leadership value-add

notableQuotes.quote: The worst thing that you do as a leader is you hesitate on the next decision. We went public with $2 million in trailing 12 months revenue at 18 months old. That's obviously a bad idea. But the alternative was going bankrupt, and that's a worse idea.
notableQuotes.context: On choosing between two terrible options as CEO of Opsware

notableQuotes.quote: What I was trying to get out in Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager, was the job is fundamentally a leadership job. And it's a tricky leadership job because nobody is actually reporting to you.
notableQuotes.context: On the origin and core message of his famous PM essay

leaders.episodeSummary: Ben Horowitz, co-founder of a16z and author of The Hard Thing About Hard Things, shares hard-won lessons on leadership under extreme uncertainty, including his famous framework that a leader's only real value comes from making decisions most people disagree with. He discusses the origin of his legendary 'Good Product Manager, Bad Product Manager' essay, why the PM role is fundamentally about leadership without authority, and how success and failure both come from compounding series of decisions.
leadershipPrinciples: The only value you ever add as a leader is when you make a decision that most people don't like — if everybody agrees, they would have done it without you
The worst thing you do as a leader is hesitate on the next decision — both options are horrible but you must choose the slightly better one
The PM job is fundamentally a leadership job, and it's a tricky one because nobody actually reports to you

leaders.name: Ben Williams
leaders.title: VP of Product
leaders.bio: VP of Product at Snyk, one of the biggest developer security companies; led Snyk's evolution from product-led growth to product-led sales, community-driven growth, and developer-focused go-to-market strategy.

notableQuotes.quote: Being able to identify the various micro and macro loops, how they're all connected, being able to document them in a qualitative model to communicate a shared understanding of how you grow, it's really powerful. Augmenting that then with the quantitative side of things that helps guide quarter to quarter focus.
notableQuotes.context: On building a growth model that connects qualitative and quantitative understanding

notableQuotes.quote: You're never going to have a shortage of ideas in a high performing growth team. So, knowing where to focus amidst that kind of sea of ideas is a really important role of the strategy.
notableQuotes.context: On the real job of growth strategy

leaders.episodeSummary: Ben Williams, VP of Product at Snyk, provides a detailed look at how Snyk built and scaled its developer security business through product-led growth, community-driven adoption, and eventual evolution to product-led sales. He shares frameworks for identifying and documenting growth loops, structuring growth and product teams, making freemium decisions, and maintaining strategic focus when ideas are abundant.
leadershipPrinciples: Identify micro and macro growth loops, document them in a qualitative model, then augment with quantitative data to guide quarterly focus
In a high-performing growth team you'll never have a shortage of ideas — knowing where to focus amidst that sea of ideas is the critical role of strategy
Product-led growth and product-led sales are not mutually exclusive — PLG can evolve into PLS as the company scales

leaders.name: Benjamin Lauzier
leaders.title: Former VP of Product & Growth
leaders.bio: Former VP of Product and Growth at Thumbtack where he 3X'd growth in three years; employee #30 at Lyft where he led driver-side product and growth reaching 1% of US workers driving monthly; now advises marketplace founders and teaches marketplace growth at Reforge.

notableQuotes.quote: When you're running a marketplace, you tend to sit in your ivory tower looking at stats thinking, 'If only we could get people to do X, it'd be better for everyone.' That's missing the point that we're humans, and sometimes we act in ways that are non-deterministic or counterintuitive.
notableQuotes.context: On the danger of over-relying on data in marketplace management

notableQuotes.quote: Provide guardrails for what a good experience is in your marketplace, set a clear bar for quality, and provide the right coaching and tools for supply to be successful, and then take a step back and see where the gaps are.
notableQuotes.context: On his philosophy for managing marketplace supply

leaders.episodeSummary: Benjamin Lauzier draws from his experience as employee #30 at Lyft and VP of Product/Growth at Thumbtack to provide a comprehensive guide to building and scaling marketplace businesses. He covers pre-product-market-fit priorities, how to choose which marketplace side to focus on, tracking liquidity, supply-side growth strategies, and why most marketplaces fail, emphasizing the importance of market forces and empowerment over top-down control.
leadershipPrinciples: Provide guardrails for quality, coaching and tools for supply to succeed, then step back — believe in market forces over top-down control
When running a marketplace, resist the ivory tower of stats and remember you're dealing with humans who act non-deterministically
Pre-product-market-fit, focus relentlessly on one side of the marketplace — the one that's hardest to get

leaders.name: Benjamin Mann
leaders.title: Co-Founder
leaders.bio: Co-founder of Anthropic serving as tech lead for product engineering; one of the architects of GPT-3 at OpenAI before leaving over safety concerns; focused on aligning AI to be helpful, harmless, and honest.

notableQuotes.quote: I think 50th percentile chance of hitting some kind of superintelligence is now like 2028.
notableQuotes.context: On his timeline prediction for AGI

notableQuotes.quote: We felt like safety wasn't the top priority there. The case for safety has gotten a lot more concrete, so superintelligence is a lot about how do we keep God in a box and not let the God out.
notableQuotes.context: On why he left OpenAI to co-found Anthropic

notableQuotes.quote: Once we get to superintelligence, it will be too late to align the models. My best granularity forecast for could we have an X-risk or extremely bad outcome is somewhere between 0 and 10%.
notableQuotes.context: On the urgency of AI alignment work

leaders.episodeSummary: Benjamin Mann, co-founder of Anthropic and one of the architects of GPT-3, shares his deeply informed perspective on AGI timelines, AI safety, and why he left OpenAI to build a safety-first AI company. He discusses why scaling laws are accelerating rather than slowing, his economic Turing test for identifying AGI, the existential risks he estimates at 0-10%, and how these concerns shape both Anthropic's mission and his personal worldview.
leadershipPrinciples: Once we get to superintelligence, it will be too late to align the models — safety must be built in before, not after
Safety wasn't the top priority at OpenAI, which is why they left to start Anthropic — sometimes you must build the alternative
Superintelligence is about keeping God in a box — the stakes of alignment are existential, between 0 and 10% chance of extremely bad outcomes

leaders.name: Bill Carr
leaders.title: Former VP of Digital Media
leaders.bio: Spent 15 years at Amazon starting five years after founding, launched Amazon Music, Prime Video, and Amazon Studios as VP of Digital Media; co-author of the book Working Backwards which codifies Amazon's management practices.

notableQuotes.quote: Jeff would say, we took it as an article of faith. If we served customers well, if we prioritized customers and delivered for them, things like sales, revenue and active customers and the share price and free cash flow would follow. So when we're making a decision, we're going to start with what's best for the customer and come backward from there.
notableQuotes.context: On Amazon's customer obsession philosophy and the origin of 'Working Backwards'

notableQuotes.quote: Amazon was actually, to some degree, equally focused on process innovation. We stood on other people's shoulders. That's what all great companies should do. We would like to allow people to stand on Amazon's shoulders to learn what we learned.
notableQuotes.context: On why Amazon's process innovations matter as much as its product innovations

notableQuotes.quote: All of the products and all of the processes except for one were all developed in this one four year period from 2003 to 2007. This is where we were going from hypergrowth, zero to one, to one to infinity.
notableQuotes.context: On the concentrated period of innovation at Amazon

leaders.episodeSummary: Bill Carr, 15-year Amazon veteran and co-author of Working Backwards, provides a detailed inside look at Amazon's management operating system including the working backwards process, single-threaded leadership, input vs output metrics, the Bar Raiser hiring program, and disagree-and-commit culture. He reveals that nearly all of Amazon's iconic processes and products were created in a concentrated 2003-2007 window when the company needed systematic mechanisms to scale beyond founder involvement in every decision.
leadershipPrinciples: Start with what's best for the customer and come backward from there — if you serve customers well, revenue and growth will follow
Amazon's innovation came from process innovation as much as product innovation — both product and process were developed in the same 2003-2007 window
Leadership principles must be reinforced by specific processes to be real — without processes they're just posters on the wall

leaders.name: Bob Baxley
leaders.title: Design Executive & Advisor
leaders.bio: Designer, executive, and advisor who built and led design teams at Apple, Pinterest, Yahoo, and ThoughtSpot over three decades; played pivotal roles in designing the Apple Online Store, Apple App Store, Pinterest, and Yahoo Answers.

notableQuotes.quote: Design is trying to imagine the future you want to live in and then take the steps to make it real. Saying a company is design-led does not mean it's designer-led. I've never seen somebody graft it on after the fact. It's there at the beginning in the root DNA or doesn't exist.
notableQuotes.context: On what design truly means and why design culture can't be retrofitted

notableQuotes.quote: Almost everyone living in a modern economy now is going to have hundreds of interactions with a phone or with a computer. And unfortunately, a lot of those interactions are not going to be great. We have an obligation as product people to put that emotional energy back into people's lives.
notableQuotes.context: On the moral obligation of product builders

notableQuotes.quote: Steve listed the products he was most proud of: Apple II, the Mac, the iPod, the iPhone, Apple retail — and then he said Apple itself. The products are ephemeral, but there's something about the culture that's lasted a very long time.
notableQuotes.context: On Steve Jobs viewing Apple's culture as his greatest product

leaders.episodeSummary: Bob Baxley, a three-decade design leader at Apple, Pinterest, Yahoo, and ThoughtSpot, shares a deeply philosophical perspective on design as imagining and building the future, not just making things pretty. He distinguishes between design-led and designer-led companies, explains why Apple's design culture can't be replicated by hiring Apple alumni, and argues that product builders have a moral obligation to improve the hundreds of daily technology interactions people have.
leadershipPrinciples: Design is trying to imagine the future you want to live in and then take the steps to make it real
A company being design-led does not mean it's designer-led — design-led culture must be in the root DNA from the beginning, you can't graft it on later
We have an obligation as product people to put emotional energy back into people's lives through the hundreds of daily interactions they have with technology

leaders.name: Bob Moesta
leaders.title: Co-Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Co-creator of the Jobs-to-be-Done framework alongside Clay Christensen; serial entrepreneur who has started nine companies; author of Job Moves, a tactical guide to finding work you love based on interviewing and coaching thousands of job seekers.

notableQuotes.quote: One of the biggest misconceptions around Jobs to Be Done is this notion that it's pain and gain as opposed to context and outcome. When you hear somebody's story and it seems irrational, nine times out of 10, it's because you don't have the rest of the story.
notableQuotes.context: On the most common misunderstanding of JTBD

notableQuotes.quote: Snickers typically is a case where they missed the last meal, they're running out of energy. It competes with a protein drink, a Red Bull, a coffee. But a Milky Way is eaten after an emotional experience, usually alone. It competes with a glass of wine, a brownie, and a run.
notableQuotes.context: His classic Snickers vs Milky Way example of demand-side competitive analysis

notableQuotes.quote: Jobs helps you see the true competitive set from the demand side of the world as opposed to the competitive set from the supply side. It allows you to actually see what customers really want as opposed to trying to figure out how to sell things to people.
notableQuotes.context: On the fundamental shift JTBD brings to product thinking

leaders.episodeSummary: Bob Moesta, co-creator of the Jobs-to-be-Done framework with Clay Christensen, provides a definitive deep dive into JTBD, explaining that people hire products to make progress, not based on features. Using his famous Snickers vs Milky Way example, he demonstrates how JTBD reveals the true competitive set from the demand side, and explains why context and outcome — not pain and gain — are the real drivers of customer behavior.
leadershipPrinciples: People don't buy products, they hire them to make progress in their life — understand the job, not the product
Context and outcome, not pain and gain, are the true drivers — the context makes the irrational rational
Jobs-to-be-Done reveals the true competitive set from the demand side, not the supply side — Snickers competes with Red Bull, not Milky Way

leaders.name: Brandon Chu
leaders.title: VP of Product
leaders.bio: VP of Product at Shopify for seven years; known for his widely-read Medium posts on PM skills that have influenced a generation of product managers; previously bootstrapped a startup helping YouTube musicians monetize their fan bases.

notableQuotes.quote: I have a vision in my mind. One day, I'm going to see the whole earth in one view, and it's going to make me feel really small, which I think will make me feel connected. Since I was 16, I've been saving 2,000 dollars a year because I calculated it would cost half a million dollars by the time I was 55.
notableQuotes.context: On his lifelong dream to go to space and the PM-like approach of planning for it

leaders.episodeSummary: Brandon Chu, VP of Product at Shopify and author of some of the most widely-read essays on product management, shares insights on building product at Shopify, remote work effectiveness from a company that has done it since day one, the underrated value of platform PM work, and how writing publicly about your craft can dramatically accelerate your career. He also discusses the manager vs IC track debate and what Shopify has learned about organizational effectiveness.
leadershipPrinciples: Writing about your craft publicly forces you to synthesize your thinking and dramatically accelerates your career development
Platform PM work is underrated — building internal infrastructure that enables other teams creates enormous leverage
Remote work effectiveness requires deliberate systems, not just transplanting office practices — Shopify has done it from day one

leaders.name: Brendan Foody
leaders.title: CEO & Co-Founder
leaders.bio: CEO and co-founder of Mercor, the fastest-growing company in history to reach $500M in revenue (17 months); youngest unicorn founder ever; Mercor helps AI labs hire experts to train their models, with zero customer churn and 1,600%+ net retention.

notableQuotes.quote: The wealthiest companies in the world are willing to spend whatever it takes to improve model capabilities.
notableQuotes.context: On why the AI training market is so large

notableQuotes.quote: The lab's primary bottleneck to improve models is how they can effectively have some way of measuring what success looks like for the model.
notableQuotes.context: On the fundamental problem Mercor solves for AI labs

notableQuotes.quote: We grew from 1 to 400 million in revenue run rate in 16 months, fastest ascent in history.
notableQuotes.context: On Mercor's unprecedented growth trajectory

leaders.episodeSummary: Brendan Foody, the youngest unicorn founder ever, explains how Mercor became the fastest-growing company in history by identifying and filling a critical bottleneck for AI labs: finding expert humans who can measure and evaluate model capabilities. With zero customer churn and 1,600%+ net retention, Mercor's marketplace connects AI labs with the specialized talent they need to train models, capitalizing on the insight that the wealthiest companies will spend whatever it takes to improve AI capabilities.
leadershipPrinciples: The wealthiest companies in the world are willing to spend whatever it takes to improve model capabilities — follow the money to find the biggest opportunities
AI labs' primary bottleneck is measuring what success looks like for the model — humans who can do what models can't are the scarce resource
The market is bound by the amount of things where humans can do something that models can't — find and fill that gap

leaders.name: Bret Taylor
leaders.title: Co-Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Co-created Google Maps, co-founded FriendFeed (invented the Like button and real-time newsfeed), became CTO at Facebook, founded Quip (sold to Salesforce for $750M), became co-CEO of Salesforce, chairman of the board at OpenAI; now co-founder and CEO of Sierra, an AI agent company.

notableQuotes.quote: The whole market is going to go towards agents. The whole market is going to go towards outcomes-based pricing. It's just so obviously the correct way to build and sell software.
notableQuotes.context: On the future of software and AI agents

notableQuotes.quote: I was the product manager for Google Local. Had a pretty tough product review with Marissa and Larry. To not do that well with a link from the Google homepage is embarrassing. They gave me another shot to do the V2 that resulted in Google Maps. We got about 10 million people using it on the first day.
notableQuotes.context: On his biggest failure leading to his biggest success

notableQuotes.quote: Waking up every morning — what is the most impactful thing I could do today?
notableQuotes.context: On the mindset that enabled success across Google, Facebook, Salesforce, and Sierra

leaders.episodeSummary: Bret Taylor, one of tech's most prolific builders (Google Maps, Like button, FriendFeed, Quip, Salesforce co-CEO, Sierra), shares his conviction that the entire software market is moving toward AI agents with outcomes-based pricing. He discusses the mindset of daily impact prioritization that enabled his success across wildly different roles, why his biggest failure at Google led to Google Maps, and where the biggest remaining opportunities for startups lie in the AI era.
leadershipPrinciples: The whole market is going to go towards agents and outcomes-based pricing — it's so obviously the correct way to build and sell software
Wake up every morning asking 'what is the most impactful thing I could do today' — this mindset enables success across wildly different roles
Selling productivity software is extremely hard — learned this the hard way at Quip — which is why agents that deliver outcomes will win

leaders.name: Brian Balfour
leaders.title: Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Founder and CEO of Reforge, the leading professional education platform for product and growth; previously led growth at HubSpot; has witnessed the rise and fall of every major distribution channel and is predicting ChatGPT as the next major distribution platform.

notableQuotes.quote: Building a great product is one of those things that's necessary, but not sufficient. And actually the separation is between those that build really great distribution.
notableQuotes.context: On why distribution matters more than most founders think

notableQuotes.quote: All of the ingredients for new distribution platform are essentially happening. My prediction, the new distribution platform will be ChatGPT.
notableQuotes.context: On his prediction about the next major growth channel

notableQuotes.quote: It ends up being a prisoner's dilemma. Don't trick yourself into thinking that you can't play the game. The cycles seem to be getting shorter and shorter. If you don't do it, your competitors are going to go to the new platform. There is no opting out of the game.
notableQuotes.context: On why companies must adopt new distribution platforms

leaders.episodeSummary: Brian Balfour, founder of Reforge and former growth lead at HubSpot, makes a bold prediction that ChatGPT will become the next major distribution platform, comparable to the rise of Facebook's ad platform, Google Ads, and the App Store. He argues that product quality is necessary but insufficient — distribution is what separates winners from losers — and that platform cycles are shortening, creating a prisoner's dilemma where opting out is not an option.
leadershipPrinciples: Building a great product is necessary but not sufficient — the separation between winners and losers is distribution
New distribution platforms create prisoner's dilemmas — if you don't adopt, your competitors will and customer expectations change; there is no opting out
Platform distribution cycles are getting shorter — you have a smaller window to capitalize on each new one

leaders.name: Brian Chesky
leaders.title: CEO & Co-Founder
leaders.bio: CEO and co-founder of Airbnb, an $80 billion global business operating in 220 countries; known for his hands-on leadership style, functional org model, and controversial rethinking of the product management function.

notableQuotes.quote: Way too many founders apologize for how they want to run the company. They find some midpoint between how they want to run a company and how the people they lead want to run the company. That's a good way to make everyone miserable. Because what everyone really wants is clarity.
notableQuotes.context: On why founders should lead with conviction rather than consensus

notableQuotes.quote: There's a negative term called micromanagement. I think there's a difference between micromanagement, which is telling people exactly what to do, and being in the details. If you don't know the details, how do you know people are doing a good job?
notableQuotes.context: On his philosophy of hands-on leadership

notableQuotes.quote: If you build a great product and no one knows about it, did you even build a product? You can't be an expert in making the product unless you're also an expert in the market of it.
notableQuotes.context: On why Airbnb merged product management with product marketing

leaders.episodeSummary: Brian Chesky, CEO of Airbnb, provides a masterclass on founder-led product development, explaining his controversial decision to rethink the PM function by combining product management with product marketing, making the group smaller and more senior. He details his philosophy that leaders must be in the details, his fight against the organizational entropy cycle of division-to-advocacy-to-politics-to-bureaucracy, and why Airbnb's purely functional model enables managing by influence without politics.
leadershipPrinciples: Leaders are in the details — being in the details is not micromanagement; if you don't know the details, how do you know people are doing a good job?
Way too many founders apologize for how they want to run the company — finding a midpoint between your vision and everyone else's makes everyone miserable
You can't build a product unless you know how to talk about it — combine inbound product development with outbound marketing into one function

leaders.name: Brian Tolkin
leaders.title: Head of Product & Design
leaders.bio: Head of Product and Design at Opendoor; previously spent five years at Uber as employee #100 where he launched uberPOOL and took it global; started the product operations function at Uber before it was a recognized discipline.
