leaders.episodeSummary: Julie Zhuo, the first-ever guest on Lenny's Podcast, shares her journey from intern designer to VP of Design at Facebook, where she felt like an imposter for seven or eight years before realizing that discomfort and growth are inseparable. She offers career advice centered on embracing imposter syndrome, asking for help instead of faking confidence, and joining growing companies where opportunities to stretch yourself are abundant.
leadershipPrinciples: Feeling like an imposter coincides with the fastest and most intense periods of growth in your career — embrace it
Ask for help rather than faking it until you make it — vulnerability accelerates growth and builds camaraderie
Join a growing company if you want opportunities — growth creates more chances to raise your hand and try new things

leaders.name: Karina Nguyen
leaders.title: AI Researcher
leaders.bio: Karina Nguyen is an AI researcher at OpenAI where she helped build Canvas, Tasks, and the o1 chain-of-thought model. Prior to OpenAI, she was at Anthropic where she led post-training and evaluation for Claude 3 models and built the 100K context window document upload feature. She was also an engineer at the New York Times and a designer at Dropbox and Square.
keyThemes: building at the cutting edge of AI
creative thinking as a durable skill
how models are created and trained

notableQuotes.quote: When I first came to Anthropic I was like, 'Oh my God, I really love front-end engineering.' And then I realized Claude is getting better at front-end, better at coding. I think Claude can develop new apps. That's why I switched to research.
notableQuotes.context: On why she moved from engineering to AI research after seeing model capabilities improve

notableQuotes.quote: Creative thinking — you want to generate a bunch of ideas and filter through them. It's actually really, really hard to teach the model how to be aesthetic or really good visual design or how to be extremely creative in the way they write.
notableQuotes.context: On the skills that will be most valuable as AI improves at execution

leaders.episodeSummary: Karina Nguyen provides a rare inside look at building AI products at OpenAI, where she helped create Canvas, Tasks, and the o1 model. She explains why she switched from engineering to research after realizing models would become great at coding, and argues that creative thinking and aesthetic taste will be the most durable human skills as AI continues to improve at execution tasks.
leadershipPrinciples: Creative thinking will be the most valuable skill as AI gets better at execution — generate many ideas and filter through them
Switch to where the frontier is moving — she moved from engineering to research after realizing models would become great at coding
It is really hard to teach models aesthetics and visual design — human taste remains essential

leaders.name: Karri Saarinen
leaders.title: Co-Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Karri Saarinen is the co-founder and CEO of Linear, the fastest growing and most beloved issue tracking tool for software teams. He was previously the founding designer at Coinbase and a principal designer at Airbnb. Linear has been profitable for two years and has a net negative lifetime burn rate, meaning more cash in the bank than it has raised.
keyThemes: craft and quality as competitive advantage
no AB tests or metrics-based goals

notableQuotes.quote: The more it matters, the more design matters. The first iterations don't have to be super well designed because they are the first. But as you build the 100,000th email client, it has to be pretty good to be even considered.
notableQuotes.context: On why design quality becomes more important as product categories mature

notableQuotes.quote: We actually believe that when you start building the thing you actually start realizing more how it should work. Just put it into the app and ship it to production in the first week. It's only visible to us so we can test it out.
notableQuotes.context: On Linear's approach to rapid internal prototyping before polishing for release

leaders.episodeSummary: Karri Saarinen reveals how Linear built the most beloved issue tracking tool through an obsessive focus on craft, opinionated design, and a unique building method: ship rough prototypes internally in the first week, co-create with select customers, then polish before general release. With no AB tests, no metrics-based goals, paid work trials for hiring, and a net negative burn rate, Linear represents a counterculture approach to building SaaS products.
leadershipPrinciples: Ship early to yourself and select customers, but polish before general release — quality matters at the last mile
Hire people who care about craft — the quality of the product starts with the quality of the people
Design matters more as industries mature — the bar rises and you need high-level design to even be considered seriously

leaders.name: Katie Dill
leaders.title: Head of Design
leaders.bio: Katie Dill is Head of Design at Stripe, overseeing product design, brand, marketing creative, user research, content strategy, and design ops. She was previously Head of Design at Lyft and Head of Experience Design at Airbnb. She has built and led design teams at three hypergrowth companies, scaling them 10x each.

notableQuotes.quote: The use of the word beauty in books digitized by Google has decreased dramatically. As if people think about functionality and beauty as two opposite things. No, they're not. Beauty enhances functionality because it makes things easier to use, more approachable, more compelling.
notableQuotes.context: On why the tech industry undervalues beauty in product design

notableQuotes.quote: They went on taking turns quietly reading from the papers all the things that they saw that I was doing wrong. What was very clear was that I hadn't earned their trust. I wasn't bringing the team along with me.
notableQuotes.context: On the design team intervention at Airbnb that became her biggest leadership lesson

leaders.episodeSummary: Katie Dill shares the design team intervention story from her early days at Airbnb that became the biggest learning experience of her leadership career: she came in swinging with changes but hadn't earned trust first. She argues that beauty and functionality are not opposites — beauty enhances functionality by making products easier and more compelling to use, and painstaking detail signals to customers that you care about things they can't see.
leadershipPrinciples: Beauty and functionality are not opposites — beauty enhances functionality by making things easier to use, more approachable, and more compelling
Before making changes as a new leader, earn your team's trust first — bring them along with you
Painstaking design detail signals to customers that you care about the things they can't see too

leaders.name: Kayvon Beykpour
leaders.title: Former Head of Product & GM Consumer
leaders.bio: Kayvon Beykpour was the longest-tenured head of product at Twitter and GM of the consumer business until Elon Musk's acquisition. He arrived at Twitter through the acquisition of Periscope, the world's largest live-streaming platform that inspired Instagram Live, TikTok Live, and Facebook Live. He transformed Twitter's product culture from stagnant to regularly shipping major features.

notableQuotes.quote: The sacred cows are like their own roadmap. What are all the things that you think we're not allowed to change? Let's start there.
notableQuotes.context: On how he identified what to work on when transforming Twitter's product culture

notableQuotes.quote: We wanted to change the lack of ambition, the lack of creativity, the lack of customers feeling that the product had changed at all. I was like, 'I might flame out completely, but Hell if I don't try.'
notableQuotes.context: On the mindset behind transforming Twitter from a stagnant product org to one shipping regularly

leaders.episodeSummary: Kayvon Beykpour shares how he transformed Twitter's product culture from risk-averse and stagnant to one that shipped Super Follows, Spaces, Communities, Twitter Blue, and many more features. His approach: treat sacred cows as the roadmap, use acquihires and hungry leaders to inject ambition, and accept you might flame out while trying. He also shares the surreal story of meeting Elon Musk for the first time over FaceTime and returning to Twitter HQ after being fired during paternity leave.
leadershipPrinciples: The sacred cows are their own roadmap — start with all the things people think you're not allowed to change
Use acquihires and hungry up-and-coming product leaders to break through organizational inertia
Change the lack of ambition, the lack of creativity, and the lack of customer perception that the product has changed

leaders.name: Keith Coleman
leaders.title: Product Lead, Community Notes
leaders.bio: Keith Coleman is the Product Lead for Community Notes at X (formerly Twitter). He has led the product through four different company leaders, including Jack Dorsey and Elon Musk, and helped it become the primary fact-checking tool now adopted by Meta. He advocates for small, lean teams that can accomplish outsized results.

notableQuotes.quote: We want all of humanity to participate and sometimes people are surprised by that. Every post is eligible for notes. We shouldn't exempt Elon. We shouldn't exempt government figures. Even advertisers can get notes.
notableQuotes.context: On the philosophy that no one should be exempt from Community Notes

notableQuotes.quote: If I were to start a company in that company, it would be even leaner than I would've made it before. I've been amazed with just how much the team is able to accomplish with a small group.
notableQuotes.context: On the surprising effectiveness of small teams at X

leaders.episodeSummary: Keith Coleman shares the inside story of building Community Notes from its surprising origins through surviving four different leaders at Twitter/X. He explains why the product's core principle — that all of humanity should participate and no one should be exempt — has been key to its success, and why working with an extremely lean team has proven far more effective than he expected. Community Notes has since been adopted by Meta as their main fact-checking approach.
leadershipPrinciples: Every post is eligible for notes — don't exempt anyone, including leadership, government figures, and advertisers
All of humanity should participate in content moderation — the more people contribute, the better the data
Small teams accomplish more than you'd expect — lean execution leads to outsized impact

leaders.name: Keith Yandell
leaders.title: BD & Corporate Development Leader
leaders.bio: Keith Yandell has been at DoorDash for about seven years, leading the legal, HR, marketing, customer support, and currently the BD and corporate development teams. Before DoorDash, he led litigation at Uber. He is known for the company's no-politics, no-asshole culture and radical directness in hiring.

notableQuotes.quote: After interviewing him, I went to Tony Xu and said, 'Tony, I think this guy's a jerk.' Tony said, 'Keith, have dinner with him. If you still think he's a jerk, we won't hire.' At dinner I asked, 'Are you an asshole?' His response completely changed my perspective.
notableQuotes.context: On the story of how radical directness in culture interviews led to hiring their VP of engineering

notableQuotes.quote: We were weeks of runway situation and had been told no by everyone. It's just the difference between a founder and a non-founder. If you're really a founder, you just have to find a way. It only takes one yes.
notableQuotes.context: On DoorDash's near-death experience and founder persistence

leaders.episodeSummary: Keith Yandell shares how DoorDash built its no-politics, no-asshole culture through radical directness — including the time he asked a VP of engineering candidate 'Are you an asshole?' in a dinner meeting, which paradoxically convinced the candidate to join because DoorDash was willing to walk away from a qualified hire over culture fit. He also reveals DoorDash's near-death survival story, with weeks of runway and every investor saying no, saved only by founder Tony Xu's relentless drive.
leadershipPrinciples: If you really enjoy a candidate except for a culture concern, give them direct feedback and see how they engage — that tells you everything
It only takes one yes — keep going even when everyone says no and you have weeks of runway left
Willingness to walk away from a qualified hire who doesn't meet the culture bar is what convinces great people to join

leaders.name: Ken Norton
leaders.title: Executive Coach & Former Google PM Leader
leaders.bio: Ken Norton spent 14 years at Google leading product teams that built Google Docs, Google Calendar, and Google Maps, and did a stint at Google Ventures. He is now a full-time executive coach specializing in working with product leaders. His famous 'bring the donuts' essay has influenced a generation of product managers.
keyThemes: art of product management over science
servant leadership and bringing the donuts

notableQuotes.quote: Part of what's pretty exciting about product management is you are a leader from day one. There's leadership all over the place, but that's your job. You're a leader. You don't have any formal authority, but you're a leader. You're expected to lead.
notableQuotes.context: On what makes product management unique as a leadership role

notableQuotes.quote: Bringing the donuts was really a metaphor around being a servant leader, bringing whatever needs to be done, filling the white space, filling the gaps, whatever needed to happen. It doesn't always have to be donuts.
notableQuotes.context: On the enduring meaning behind his famous essay about PM servant leadership

leaders.episodeSummary: Ken Norton, who led product teams behind Google Docs, Calendar, and Maps over 14 years at Google, shares his philosophy that the art of product management matters far more than the science. Now a full-time executive coach, he covers the creative versus reactive mindset, why PMs are leaders from day one despite having no formal authority, and how his famous 'bring the donuts' essay was always about servant leadership — doing whatever needs to be done to help your team succeed.
leadershipPrinciples: You are a leader from day one in product management — you have no formal authority, but leadership is your job
The art of product management is much more important than the science of product management
Bringing the donuts is a metaphor for servant leadership — fill the white space, do whatever needs to be done

leaders.name: Kenneth Berger
leaders.title: Executive Coach & Former First PM at Slack
leaders.bio: Kenneth Berger was the first product manager at Slack and spent over 10 years in tech before transitioning into coaching startup leaders. His core focus is helping leaders learn how to ask for what they want, a deceptively simple skill that he argues is at the core of most career and life struggles.

notableQuotes.quote: The core idea is ask for what you want. Turns out when you actually ask for what you want out loud, you're much more likely to get it.
notableQuotes.context: On the deceptively simple skill at the core of most career struggles

notableQuotes.quote: Complaints are great inspiration. Every complaint implies a dream. Let me envision a better future. Let me think about what's an effective way to actually move towards that.
notableQuotes.context: On how to figure out what you actually want by paying attention to your complaints

leaders.episodeSummary: Kenneth Berger, the first PM at Slack turned executive coach, presents his magnum opus: the transformative power of simply asking for what you want. He explains why people pleasers avoid asking while control freaks order people around, and how finding the middle ground of authentic asking is the key to integrity, fulfillment, and career success. His practical framework includes using complaints as inspiration to uncover dreams and learning to hear the world's response without fear.
leadershipPrinciples: Ask for what you want out loud — you're much more likely to get it, and the alternative is fooling yourself about what you're pursuing
Every complaint implies a dream — use complaints as inspiration to envision a better future
People pleasers avoid asking; control freaks order people around — the skill is finding the middle ground of authentic asking

leaders.name: Kevin Aluwi
leaders.title: Co-Founder & Former CEO
leaders.bio: Kevin Aluwi is the co-founder and former CEO of Gojek, one of the first and most successful super apps in the world and the biggest startup in Indonesia and Southeast Asia. Gojek grew to 2.7 million drivers, 3 billion orders per year, and 15 million merchants, culminating in Indonesia's largest IPO of all time at a $27-28 billion valuation.

notableQuotes.quote: The most common form of resistance was by motorcycle taxi mafia. They would physically assault our drivers with bricks, knives, and machetes. It would've been easy to say they're contractors, let them sort it out. Instead, we hired private security to help extract our drivers from sticky situations.
notableQuotes.context: On the extreme physical challenges of building a ride-hailing service in Indonesia

notableQuotes.quote: We started with a very local problem — millions of motorcycle taxi drivers in Indonesian urban centers — and evolved into a general on-demand consumer super app with car drivers, grocery deliveries, payments, and financial services.
notableQuotes.context: On how Gojek grew from a local solution into one of the world's first super apps

leaders.episodeSummary: Kevin Aluwi shares the extraordinary story of building Gojek from a motorcycle taxi service into Southeast Asia's largest super app, facing challenges most founders never encounter — including motorcycle taxi mafias physically assaulting drivers. He reveals how Gojek's scrappy operations, willingness to take responsibility for driver safety, and focus on a uniquely local problem grew into 2.7 million drivers, 3 billion annual orders, and Indonesia's largest IPO.
leadershipPrinciples: When third-party contractors face physical violence, take responsibility rather than saying they should sort it out themselves
Start with a uniquely local problem — motorcycle taxis in Indonesia — then expand into a general on-demand super app
The scale of emerging markets is consistently underappreciated — 3 billion orders per year from a region most people overlook

leaders.name: Kevin Weil
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Kevin Weil is Chief Product Officer at OpenAI. He was previously head of product at Instagram and Twitter, and co-creator of the Libra cryptocurrency at Facebook. He serves on the boards of Planet, Strava, and the Black Product Managers Network.
keyThemes: building on a shifting technology foundation
writing evals as core PM skill
which AI markets startups should own

notableQuotes.quote: The AI model that you're using today is the worst AI model you will ever use for the rest of your life. Every two months, computers can do something they've never been able to do before and you need to completely think differently about what you're doing.
notableQuotes.context: On the fundamental difference between building on AI versus any other technology foundation

notableQuotes.quote: If you're building and the product is right on the edge of the capabilities of the models, keep going because you're doing something right. Give it another couple months and the models are going to be great, and suddenly your product will really sing.
notableQuotes.context: On advice to developers building products at the frontier of model capabilities

leaders.episodeSummary: Kevin Weil, CPO of OpenAI, shares how building products on AI is fundamentally different from any other technology because the foundation keeps improving — the model you use today is the worst you'll ever use. He explains why internal usage explosion (like with ImageGen and Instagram Stories) is the strongest signal a product will work, advises developers to keep building on the edge of model capabilities, and argues that writing evals is becoming a core PM skill.
leadershipPrinciples: The AI model you're using today is the worst AI model you will ever use for the rest of your life — plan accordingly
If your product is right on the edge of model capabilities, keep going — in two months the models will be great and your product will sing
Internal usage explosion is the strongest signal that a product will work — if your team can't stop using it, users won't be able to either

leaders.name: Kevin Yien
leaders.title: Product Lead, Merchant Experiences
leaders.bio: Kevin Yien leads product for merchant experiences at Stripe. He previously built the restaurant business and ecosystem teams at Square, and was head of product and design at Mutiny. He is known for his unique hiring practices including the 'unsell email' and his emphasis on decision logs for building product sense.
keyThemes: PMs must sell and support their own product

notableQuotes.quote: If you can't sell or support your own product, I don't trust you to build the product. The PM job can become a little too internal, influencing stakeholders and getting alignment. But you need to be close to customers.
notableQuotes.context: On why PMs must be able to sell and support the product they build

notableQuotes.quote: Product sense is just a fancy way of saying you can make good decisions with insufficient data. PMs need as many reps as possible in making decisions, documenting the rationale, and then crucially seeing the outcome of them.
notableQuotes.context: On why every PM should keep a decision log to build product sense

leaders.episodeSummary: Kevin Yien shares a toolkit of unique PM practices: keep a decision log to build product sense through reps, send an 'unsell email' to candidates listing everything terrible about the role to find A+ hires, and always be able to sell and support your own product. Drawing on experience at Stripe, Square, and Mutiny, he argues that the PM job has become too internal and that staying close to customers through direct selling and support is essential.
leadershipPrinciples: If you can't sell or support your own product, I don't trust you to build the product — PMs must stay close to customers
Product sense is just making good decisions with insufficient data — keep a decision log to build that muscle
Send an unsell email at offer stage listing all the terrible things about the role — candidates who are still excited are A+ hires

leaders.name: Kim Scott
leaders.title: Author & Executive Coach
leaders.company: Radical Candor / Former Google, Apple University
leaders.bio: Kim Scott is the author of Radical Candor, the single most referenced book on Lenny's Podcast, which has sold over 1 million copies and been translated into 23 languages. She was a CEO coach at Dropbox, Qualtrics, and Twitter, a faculty member at Apple University, and led AdSense, YouTube, and DoubleClick teams at Google.
keyThemes: ruinous empathy as most common mistake

notableQuotes.quote: Don't ask 'Do you have any feedback for me?' You're wasting your breath. Ask 'What could I do or stop doing that would make it easier to work with me?' Do not write down my question — it needs to sound authentic to you.
notableQuotes.context: On the specific language to use when soliciting feedback from your team

notableQuotes.quote: 90% of us make 90% of our mistakes in the ruinous empathy bucket. We care personally but we're so worried about hurting someone's feelings that we fail to tell them something they'd be better off knowing in the long run.
notableQuotes.context: On why ruinous empathy — not obnoxious aggression — is the most pervasive problem

leaders.episodeSummary: Kim Scott, author of the million-copy bestseller Radical Candor, gets deeply practical and tactical about how to practice the framework. She reveals that 90% of feedback failures are ruinous empathy — caring too much about feelings to be honest — not obnoxious aggression. Her key advice: ask 'What could I do or stop doing that would make it easier to work with me?' in your own authentic voice, and use the framework as a compass rather than a judgment tool.
leadershipPrinciples: Radical Candor is caring personally and challenging directly at the same time — most people fail on one dimension or both daily
90% of mistakes fall into ruinous empathy — caring but not being honest — which is far more common than obnoxious aggression
Don't ask 'Do you have any feedback for me?' — ask 'What could I do or stop doing that would make it easier to work with me?'

leaders.name: Kiriti Badam
leaders.title: AI/ML Infrastructure Engineer
leaders.bio: Works on Codex at OpenAI with a decade of experience building AI and ML infrastructure at Google and Kumo, and has supported over 50 AI product deployments across startups and enterprises.

notableQuotes.quote: When you start small, it forces you to think about what is the problem that I'm going to solve. One easy, slippery slope is to keep thinking about complexities of the solution and forget the problem.
notableQuotes.context: On why incremental AI agent deployment leads to better products

notableQuotes.quote: Persistence is extremely valuable. Successful companies right now building in any new area, they are going through the pain of learning this. Pain is the new moat.
notableQuotes.context: On what separates companies that succeed with AI from those that fail

notableQuotes.quote: You don't start hiking Half Dome every day, but you start training yourself in minor parts and then you slowly improve. That's extremely similar to building AI products.
notableQuotes.context: Analogy for why you should start with minimal AI autonomy and build up

leaders.episodeSummary: Kiriti Badam, working on Codex at OpenAI, shares practical frameworks for building AI products successfully, emphasizing incremental deployment that starts with high human control and progressively grants more agency to AI systems. He illustrates through customer support automation examples how companies should start with AI suggestions to humans, then gradually let AI act autonomously as confidence builds, and argues that persistence through the pain of AI adoption is the new competitive moat.
leadershipPrinciples: Start small and build step-by-step — it forces you to think about the actual problem you're solving
Pain is the new moat: companies that persist through the difficulty of learning AI implementation win
Don't start with full autonomy agents on day one; begin with high human control and graduate complexity

leaders.name: Kristen Berman
leaders.title: CEO & Co-Founder
leaders.bio: Kristen Berman is the CEO and co-founder of Irrational Labs, a behavioral science consulting firm she co-founded with Dan Ariely in 2013. Her team of 20 behavioral scientists helps companies like Google, Airbnb, PayPal, Microsoft, TikTok, and Credit Karma use behavioral design to drive engagement and behavior change.

notableQuotes.quote: Economics says people are rational. That's just not true. In behavioral economics, people make decisions with lots of emotion, present bias, social norms. But the good news is we do these things in predictable ways. Once you understand how people behave, you can start to change it.
notableQuotes.context: On what behavioral economics is and why it matters for product design

notableQuotes.quote: A popular FinTech app's most requested feature was budgeting. It came through all the support forums and interviews. We convinced them to test it rather than just build it. The result was surprising — the budgeting variations didn't outperform simply telling people how much they spend.
notableQuotes.context: On why the most-requested feature isn't always the right thing to build

leaders.episodeSummary: Kristen Berman brings behavioral science to product design, sharing how her firm Irrational Labs helped TikTok reduce misinformation sharing by 24%, increased doctor appointment setup by 20% for One Medical, and helped Credit Karma boost recurring deposits by 18%. Her core insight: people behave irrationally but predictably, so always test before building the most-requested feature — what users say they want often doesn't match what actually drives behavior change.
leadershipPrinciples: People make decisions with lots of emotion in predictable ways — once you understand the patterns, you can design to change behavior
Always test before building the most-requested feature — what users say they want is not always what drives the behavior you need
Combine the field of psychology and economics to understand why users behave the way they do

leaders.name: Krithika Shankarraman
leaders.title: Executive in Residence
leaders.company: Thrive Capital / Former VP Marketing at OpenAI, First Marketing Hire at Stripe
leaders.bio: Krithika Shankarraman was the first marketing hire and VP of Marketing at OpenAI, the first marketing hire at Stripe (the only marketer for three years), and an early marketing leader at Retool and Dropbox. She also did marketing for Android at Google. She is now executive in residence at Thrive Capital, supporting portfolio founders on marketing.
keyThemes: B2B companies learning from consumer marketing

notableQuotes.quote: Everyone knew of ChatGPT, but when you clicked one zoom level further, the thing that came up was, 'I don't know what to use it for.' The work of marketing became creating this use case epiphany where people say, 'I had no idea ChatGPT can do that.'
notableQuotes.context: On why the fastest-growing product in history still needed marketing

notableQuotes.quote: A lot of marketing metrics tend to be vanity metrics about clicks, views, impressions. I think those are all bullshit numbers. What is that experience that you want your customers to come away with when they interact with your brand?
notableQuotes.context: On rejecting vanity metrics in favor of customer experience outcomes

leaders.episodeSummary: Krithika Shankarraman, the first marketing hire at both OpenAI and Stripe, reveals that even the fastest-growing product in history needed marketing — because everyone knew ChatGPT but didn't know what to use it for. She advocates an anti-playbook approach to marketing, arguing that vanity metrics like clicks and impressions are bullshit and that the real work is deeply understanding your customer and creating use case epiphanies.
leadershipPrinciples: Clicks, views, and impressions are bullshit numbers — focus on what experience you want customers to come away with
Everyone knew ChatGPT but didn't know what to use it for — marketing's job was creating use case epiphanies
There's no playbook for marketing — you have to spend hours understanding your customer rather than copying other companies

leaders.name: Kunal Shah
leaders.title: CEO & Founder
leaders.bio: Kunal Shah is the CEO and founder of CRED, a FinTech startup based in India valued at over $6 billion that processes over 20% of all credit card bill payments in India. He previously founded Freecharge, which he sold for over $400 million to Snapdeal. With a background in philosophy and over 1 million followers on social media, he is one of the most respected entrepreneurs in India.
keyThemes: trust as essential in Indian markets

notableQuotes.quote: A lot of CEOs have done well because they follow the dharma of the founders quite well. 'These are the principles that were given to me and I'm going to sustain this and make it even bigger.'
notableQuotes.context: On why so many Indian immigrants become successful CEOs at major tech companies

notableQuotes.quote: No Indian has ever been paid an hourly salary in their entire life. The concept of time is not the same.
notableQuotes.context: On the fundamental cultural differences that affect how products are built and used in India

leaders.episodeSummary: Kunal Shah, one of India's most respected entrepreneurs, explains what makes building products in India fundamentally different from the US — from the cultural relationship with time and trust, to why companies can grow DAUs quickly but struggle with ARPUs. He shares why so many Indian immigrants become successful tech CEOs through following the 'dharma of the founders,' and argues that India is entering a new era where founders are finally being celebrated and the startup ecosystem is thriving.
leadershipPrinciples: Many successful immigrant CEOs follow the dharma of the founders — sustaining the original principles while making the company bigger
India can grow DAUs quickly but not ARPUs — understanding this gap is critical for building products there
Trust is the essential ingredient for building in India — in a low-trust society, building trust is your competitive advantage

leaders.name: Lane Shackleton
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Lane Shackleton is CPO at Coda, where he has led the product team for over eight years, previously serving as Group PM at YouTube and starting his career as an Alaskan mountain guide.

notableQuotes.quote: Moments that stretch you or moments that you feel uncomfortable in or you find yourself saying, 'Oh shit. I shouldn't be here,' those are the moments you should be seeking out.
notableQuotes.context: On how to measure career growth by counting stretch moments rather than asking vague questions about development

notableQuotes.quote: The core job of a product person in general is to turn ambiguity into clarity.
notableQuotes.context: Describing his unifying thesis for what makes great product managers

notableQuotes.quote: Goals with good intentions don't work. Instead of being obsessed with the goal, be obsessed with the system that gets you there.
notableQuotes.context: Explaining his 'systems not goals' principle, inspired by Jerry Seinfeld's practice of writing daily

leaders.episodeSummary: Lane Shackleton shares his principles for great product management, centered on the idea that a PM's core job is turning ambiguity into clarity. He discusses Coda's unique approach to career levels, the importance of systems over goals, and how default-on customer engagement builds better product instincts than one-off research sprints.
leadershipPrinciples: The core job of a product person is to turn ambiguity into clarity
Be obsessed with the system that gets you to the goal, not the goal itself
Default-on customer engagement beats one-off research goals

leaders.name: Laura Modi
leaders.title: Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Laura Modi is the founder and CEO of Bobbie, the first female-founded organic infant formula company in the US, and former Director of Hospitality at Airbnb.

notableQuotes.quote: We need to turn off our site and stop growing the business.
notableQuotes.context: Her head of growth's recommendation during the formula shortage crisis to protect existing subscribers

notableQuotes.quote: I feel like we have failed to breastfeed. And the alternative is that I need to give her a medical solution to survive, which it's milk.
notableQuotes.context: Describing the personal experience that led her to found Bobbie and challenge the stigma around formula

notableQuotes.quote: Energy at Airbnb was the currency. Unless you had that energy, nothing was happening.
notableQuotes.context: Reflecting on what she learned about culture-building at Airbnb and brought to Bobbie

leaders.episodeSummary: Laura Modi shares the story of founding Bobbie, an organic infant formula company disrupting a 40-year-old duopoly, and the gut-wrenching decision to shut down her website during the formula shortage to protect existing customers. She draws on lessons from Airbnb about culture-building, storytelling, and putting users first.
leadershipPrinciples: Put existing customers first, even if it means turning off growth
Personal connections within teams are imperative for building a lasting business
You can't take a big leap without first taking a major risk

leaders.name: Laura Schaffer
leaders.title: Head of Growth
leaders.bio: Laura Schaffer is Head of Growth at Amplitude, previously VP of Product and Growth at Rapid and Head of Growth at Twilio where she built the growth engineering team from scratch.
keyThemes: voice of customer as career accelerator

notableQuotes.quote: We just asked for forgiveness and put these questions into the signup flow and ran as an A/B test with a small group... an improved conversion by like 5%, just improved signups.
notableQuotes.context: Describing a bold experiment at Twilio that unexpectedly improved conversion

notableQuotes.quote: Your executive team and executive teams at companies are often very sharp, but the nature of their day-to-day just does not link them with customers.
notableQuotes.context: Explaining why staying close to customers is the most powerful career growth strategy

notableQuotes.quote: There's not a single leader or executive that isn't going to be stoked to hear about valuable customer insights that highlight problems they might not be seeing.
notableQuotes.context: Advising on how to build influence by sharing customer insights upward

leaders.episodeSummary: Laura Schaffer shares her career growth framework of proactively surfacing customer insights to create your own opportunities, drawing on her experience building the growth team at Twilio from scratch. She offers contrarian advice on experimentation, arguing teams should sometimes just ship rather than A/B test everything, and explains how she grew her career by staying closer to customers than anyone else.
leadershipPrinciples: Carve your own path rather than waiting for one to be given to you
Your superpower is staying close to the customer and surfacing insights executives can't see
Sometimes you should just ship it rather than running an experiment

leaders.name: Lauren Ipsen
leaders.title: Talent Partner
leaders.bio: Lauren Ipsen is a Talent Partner at General Catalyst and one of the most experienced product leadership recruiters in tech, having placed over 80 senior product leaders across major companies.

notableQuotes.quote: Who is going to be best for this specific role at this specific time, not necessarily who is the best talent in the world or in the market. Those are two very, very different questions to ask.
notableQuotes.context: Advising founders on the most common mistake in hiring senior product leaders

notableQuotes.quote: Regardless of whether or not you're hiring, you should always be keeping a pulse on the market. That is the most important thing.
notableQuotes.context: On the importance of continuous talent awareness for both hiring managers and candidates

notableQuotes.quote: Product leaders can come in a lot of different flavors, and so I think it's trying to determine where this person should major and minor, where they should spike.
notableQuotes.context: Explaining how to define the right product leader archetype for a given company stage

leaders.episodeSummary: Lauren Ipsen, one of tech's most accomplished product leadership recruiters, shares tactical advice on hiring senior product leaders, including why chasing big names often backfires, the three main archetypes of product leaders, and why founders must define specific mandates before starting a search. She also advises PMs on how to position themselves for the best opportunities.
leadershipPrinciples: Hire for what the company needs today, not the biggest name in the market
Always keep a pulse on the market regardless of whether you're actively hiring
Define the specific mandate and success criteria before starting any search

leaders.name: Lauryn Isford
leaders.title: Head of Growth
leaders.bio: Lauryn Isford was Head of Growth at Airtable and previously led growth initiatives at Facebook/Meta, specializing in onboarding optimization and activation strategy.

notableQuotes.quote: An activation rate that falls in a lower percentage range, maybe for most companies five to 15%, is better than one that falls in a higher percentage range because it means that there's likely much higher correlation with long-term retention.
notableQuotes.context: On how to properly define an activation metric

notableQuotes.quote: The investments we made in onboarding over about a six to eight month period together drove a 20% lift in activation rate for Airtable.
notableQuotes.context: Quantifying the impact of Airtable's onboarding redesign

notableQuotes.quote: There's generally two reasons why a growth team wants to experiment: to understand metric impact precisely, and risk mitigation. Sometimes you don't need either.
notableQuotes.context: Her contrarian take on why growth teams over-index on A/B testing

leaders.episodeSummary: Lauryn Isford dives deep into onboarding as the most undervalued growth lever, sharing how she led a redesign of Airtable's onboarding that drove a 20% lift in activation. She offers a contrarian perspective on experimentation culture, arguing growth teams should use A/B tests primarily for risk mitigation rather than as a default practice, and shares tactical advice on defining activation metrics.
leadershipPrinciples: Onboarding is the single biggest undervalued growth lever for self-serve products
Experiment when you need to, not by default — see it primarily as risk mitigation
A lower activation rate threshold with higher retention correlation is better than a high-percentage vanity metric

leaders.name: Logan Kilpatrick
leaders.title: Head of Developer Relations
leaders.bio: Logan Kilpatrick leads developer relations at OpenAI, supporting developers building on OpenAI APIs and ChatGPT, previously a machine learning engineer at Apple and NASA open source policy advisor.

notableQuotes.quote: Finding people who are high agency and work with urgency, if I was hiring five people today, those are the top two characteristics I would look for.
notableQuotes.context: On what OpenAI looks for when hiring

notableQuotes.quote: We're not going to launch an AI sales agent. That's just not what we're building towards. Companies who have domain specific knowledge can leverage our models.
notableQuotes.context: Advising startups on where to build products without competing with OpenAI

notableQuotes.quote: 2024 is the year of multimodal AI, but it's also the year that people really push the boundaries of some of these new UX paradigms around AI.
notableQuotes.context: On the future of AI interfaces beyond chat

leaders.episodeSummary: Logan Kilpatrick shares an inside view of OpenAI's culture and shipping velocity, discusses where the biggest opportunities lie for startups building on AI APIs, and explains why vertical, domain-specific applications will thrive while general-purpose assistants will struggle to compete with ChatGPT. He emphasizes hiring for high agency and urgency as the keys to building great teams.
leadershipPrinciples: Hire for high agency and urgency above all other traits
Build vertical and domain-specific AI applications rather than competing with general-purpose assistants
The best AI products will push beyond the chat paradigm into new interfaces

leaders.name: Luc Levesque
leaders.title: Chief Growth Officer
leaders.bio: Luc Levesque is Chief Growth Officer at Shopify, previously recruited by Mark Zuckerberg to grow Facebook Messenger, Instagram and WhatsApp, and has been a growth advisor to Twitter, Pinterest, Canva and others.

notableQuotes.quote: The right growth advisor can have literally company changing impact. The right person at the right time can literally say a sentence that changes the trajectory of your company.
notableQuotes.context: On the outsized impact of great growth advisors

notableQuotes.quote: I don't care how hard you've worked. I don't care what you're working on, what the activities are. What are the outcomes? What is the impact you're having?
notableQuotes.context: Describing Facebook's impact-obsessed culture learned from working with Zuckerberg

notableQuotes.quote: When somebody's boss leaves the company and then comes back to poach them, that is such a strong signal because they would never do that unless this person was really, really good.
notableQuotes.context: On his framework for identifying signs of excellence in hiring

leaders.episodeSummary: Luc Levesque shares lessons from being recruited by Zuckerberg to join Facebook and his experience as Shopify's Chief Growth Officer. He reveals his detailed hiring playbook built around 'signs of excellence,' explains why impact must be the singular metric that drives company culture, and offers tactical advice on finding, assessing, and closing top growth talent.
leadershipPrinciples: Focus exclusively on impact, not activity — reward outcomes, not effort
The best predictor of future performance is past performance: look for signs of excellence
Hiring is the skill you need to become world-class at as you scale as a leader

leaders.name: Lulu Cheng Meservey
leaders.title: Head of Communications
leaders.bio: Lulu Cheng Meservey is the former Head of Communications at Substack, known for taking bold, risk-forward approaches to PR that generated outsized attention and brand awareness.

notableQuotes.quote: Find your audience's cultural erogenous zones. It's a huge lift to try to change someone's worldview. It's a light lift to shape what you want to say to fit into their worldview.
notableQuotes.context: Her framework for crafting messages that spread

notableQuotes.quote: If you're a startup your enemy is the status quo. When you minimize risk by doing nothing, you're letting your greatest enemy win by default.
notableQuotes.context: On why comms teams should take more risks

notableQuotes.quote: Put the pill in some cheese — take the message you need to deliver and wrap it in something people actually want to consume.
notableQuotes.context: Her memorable metaphor for crafting sticky stories

leaders.episodeSummary: Lulu Cheng Meservey shares her unconventional approach to startup communications, arguing that the biggest risk is doing nothing and that comms teams should make mistakes of commission rather than omission. She provides tactical frameworks for making ideas spread, including finding audience 'cultural erogenous zones' and minimizing cognitive burden in messaging.
leadershipPrinciples: Your enemy as a startup is the status quo — doing nothing is the biggest risk
Make mistakes of commission rather than omission so you can learn and adapt
Find your audience's cultural erogenous zones and bridge your message to their passions

leaders.name: Madhavan Ramanujam
leaders.title: Managing Partner & Investor
leaders.bio: Madhavan Ramanujam is the author of Monetizing Innovation and Scaling Innovation, former managing partner at Simon-Kucher, now investing full-time in early-stage AI companies through his fund 49 Palms Ventures.

notableQuotes.quote: When we think about price, we think about it as a measure. Like liter is a measure of volume, price is a measure of value.
notableQuotes.context: Reframing pricing from a dollar figure to a measure of customer value

notableQuotes.quote: You cannot prioritize a product roadmap without having a willingness to pay conversation. If you're just prioritizing based on what you think or feel, you're getting it wrong.
notableQuotes.context: His core argument for why pricing research should inform product prioritization

notableQuotes.quote: 20% of what you build drives 80% of the willingness to pay. If you don't know this, you're probably over-indexing on the wrong things.
notableQuotes.context: On the Pareto principle applied to feature prioritization and willingness to pay

leaders.episodeSummary: Madhavan Ramanujam makes the case that pricing should be a core part of product development from day one, not an afterthought. Drawing on his work with 250+ companies, he explains why willingness-to-pay conversations should drive roadmap prioritization, how 72% of innovations fail because companies skip these conversations, and why pricing belongs in the product function.
leadershipPrinciples: You cannot prioritize a product roadmap without having willingness to pay conversations
Price before product — have the monetization conversation much earlier than you think
Pricing should sit in the product function, not finance or sales

leaders.name: Maggie Crowley
leaders.title: Vice President of Product
leaders.bio: Maggie Crowley is VP of Product at Toast, previously VP at Charlie Health and Drift, with an MBA from Harvard and a background as an Olympic speed skater.

notableQuotes.quote: If you ever find yourself saying, 'that's not my job,' that's probably a thing you should do.
notableQuotes.context: On the mindset that separates the best PMs from average ones

notableQuotes.quote: The best PMs not only can find the one thing to work on, but they can stay with that one thing long enough to actually finish it.
notableQuotes.context: Describing simplification as the core PM skill

notableQuotes.quote: So many people will say here's the metric I care about, but the really good PMs remember to follow up. I can't tell you how rare that is.
notableQuotes.context: On why proactive follow-up on shipped features distinguishes great PMs

leaders.episodeSummary: Maggie Crowley identifies the three common threads of the best PMs she's worked with: simplifying relentlessly, following up on results proactively, and being willing to do whatever it takes. She shares tactical advice on writing product strategy, warns that being 'data-driven' can be a red flag for lack of product conviction, and discusses how content creation accelerated her career.
leadershipPrinciples: The best PMs simplify relentlessly and stick with priorities long enough to finish
If you find yourself saying 'that's not my job,' that's probably a thing you should do
Being 'data-driven' is a red flag — great PMs are data-informed but conviction-led

leaders.name: Manik Gupta
leaders.title: Corporate Vice President, Consumer
leaders.bio: Manik Gupta is CVP at Microsoft leading consumer efforts, formerly CPO at Uber and Director of Product for Google Maps, with deep experience building category-defining consumer products.

notableQuotes.quote: What's the secret? Well just hang around superstars. That's what Steve Kerr said, and that's exactly what it is.
notableQuotes.context: On the most important career advice — surround yourself with great people

notableQuotes.quote: When you look at individuals and think about what made them successful, we tend to put greater emphasis on effort and less on luck and risk.
notableQuotes.context: Referencing Morgan Housel's Psychology of Money on career humility

leaders.episodeSummary: Manik Gupta draws on his experience leading Google Maps and serving as CPO at Uber to discuss building successful consumer products and the path to becoming a CPO. He introduces the concept of the 'consumer stack,' distinguishes company-market fit from product-market fit, and emphasizes that surrounding yourself with excellent people is the most reliable career strategy.
leadershipPrinciples: Surround yourself with the best people you can find — just hang around superstars
Company-market fit matters as much as product-market fit
The most important career skill is creating opportunities through great people

leaders.name: Marc Andreessen
leaders.title: Co-founder & General Partner
leaders.bio: Marc Andreessen invented the web browser, co-founded Netscape and Andreessen Horowitz, and is one of the most influential technology investors and thinkers of the modern era.

notableQuotes.quote: AI is the philosopher's stone. We have a technology that transfers the most common thing in the world, which is sand, converted into the most rare thing in the world which is thought.
notableQuotes.context: On the historic significance of the current AI moment

notableQuotes.quote: There's like a Mexican standoff happening between PM, engineer, and designer roles. Every coder now believes they can be a PM and designer. They're actually all kind of correct.
notableQuotes.context: On how AI is collapsing the boundaries between product roles

notableQuotes.quote: If we didn't have AI, we'd be in a panic right now about what's going to happen to the economy. The timing has worked out miraculously well.
notableQuotes.context: On the convergence of demographic decline and AI capabilities

leaders.episodeSummary: Marc Andreessen argues we are living through a once-in-a-century moment where AI, demographic decline, and institutional upheaval converge. He explains why AI will create super-empowered individuals rather than mass unemployment, predicts the convergence of PM, designer, and engineering roles, and urges everyone to develop deep agency to fully leverage AI's transformative potential.
leadershipPrinciples: AI is the philosopher's stone — it transforms sand into thought, and this is a once-in-a-century moment
The additive effect of being good at two or three domains is multiplicative, not additive
Focus on building agency in people — the ability to be a primary participant in events

leaders.name: Marc Benioff
leaders.title: Co-founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Marc Benioff is the co-founder and CEO of Salesforce, the second largest B2B SaaS company in the world, a pioneer of cloud computing and SaaS business models.
keyThemes: domain name investing as vision proxy

notableQuotes.quote: I'm throwing everything against the wall. I'm looking at what's going to stick. I am looking to try to find the winning tactic and turn it into a winning strategy.
notableQuotes.context: On his approach to Salesforce's legendary launch strategy

notableQuotes.quote: I actually never look at the stock. I find the stock to be very distracting. The stock isn't the goal. That's not why we're doing this.
notableQuotes.context: On maintaining focus on mission rather than market cap

notableQuotes.quote: You want the mindset of, 'Oh, the next thing is coming. I can't wait for the next thing.'
notableQuotes.context: On approaching AI and agents with excitement rather than resistance

leaders.episodeSummary: Marc Benioff shares stories from 25 years of building Salesforce, including his mentorship under Steve Jobs, the story behind gifting the appstore.com domain, and his approach to staying ahead of technology waves from cloud to AI agents. He emphasizes beginner's mind, relentless experimentation, and the power of generosity in founder relationships.
leadershipPrinciples: The mindset should be 'I can't wait for the next thing' — never resist the next wave
Throw everything against the wall, see what sticks, then turn winning tactics into winning strategies
Don't look at the stock price — the stock isn't the goal

leaders.name: Marily Nika
leaders.title: Product Lead
leaders.bio: Marily Nika is a Product Lead at Meta focusing on Metaverse and identity, formerly at Google for 8+ years on Glass and ML, and teaches the most popular AI/PM course on Maven.

notableQuotes.quote: There is something called the shiny object trap. Don't do AI for the sake of doing AI. Make sure there is a problem there, a pain point that needs to be solved in a smart way.
notableQuotes.context: Warning PMs about implementing AI without clear problem definition

notableQuotes.quote: ChatGPT and technology is enhancing our work. It does not steal from us.
notableQuotes.context: Addressing fears about AI replacing creative workers

leaders.episodeSummary: Marily Nika helps product managers navigate the rapidly evolving AI landscape, warning against the 'shiny object trap' of implementing AI without clear problem definition. She shares resources for staying current with AI developments, discusses how AI tools can already boost PM productivity, and emphasizes that AI should enhance rather than replace human work.
leadershipPrinciples: Don't do AI for the sake of doing AI — make sure there's a real problem to solve first
AI enhances our work, it doesn't steal from us — reframe the narrative
Stay current by reading broadly about technology, not just AI-specific content

leaders.name: Marty Cagan
leaders.title: Founder
leaders.bio: Marty Cagan is the founder of SVPG and author of INSPIRED, EMPOWERED, and TRANSFORMED, having worked with more product teams than arguably anyone alive over his 20+ year career.

notableQuotes.quote: People don't buy the problem, they buy your solution. The real question is, do you solve it better than everybody else?
notableQuotes.context: Challenging the overemphasis on problem discovery versus solution quality

notableQuotes.quote: Be careful. If you need to spend a little time on the problem, fine, but save as much time as possible to come up with the winning solution.
notableQuotes.context: Coaching teams on how to allocate time between problem and solution space

leaders.episodeSummary: Marty Cagan explores the fundamental nature of product work, arguing that the gap between companies with strong product cultures and everyone else is vastly underestimated. He challenges conventional wisdom about problem discovery, emphasizing that winning solutions matter more than problem definition, and explains what truly empowered product teams look like in practice.
leadershipPrinciples: People don't buy the problem, they buy your solution — spend most of your time on winning solutions
The gap between great product companies and everyone else is like trying to explain the Grand Canyon with pictures
Empowered teams are given problems to solve, not features to build

leaders.name: Matt Abrahams
leaders.title: Professor of Communication
leaders.bio: Matt Abrahams is a Stanford professor teaching communication and public speaking, host of the Think Fast, Talk Smart podcast, and author of Think Faster and Talk Smarter.

notableQuotes.quote: Strive for connection over perfection by daring to be dull. Just answer the question. Just give the feedback. By doing that, you dial down the volume of self-evaluation.
notableQuotes.context: His core framework for reducing speaking anxiety

notableQuotes.quote: You actually have to prepare to be spontaneous. That's counterintuitive, but when you think about it in athletics or jazz music, of course you would prepare and practice.
notableQuotes.context: On why spontaneous communication requires deliberate preparation

leaders.episodeSummary: Matt Abrahams shares research-backed techniques for reducing public speaking anxiety and improving spontaneous communication. His core advice centers on striving for connection over perfection, preparing to be spontaneous through practice, and using visualization to desensitize anxiety — skills that become increasingly important as leaders advance in their careers.
leadershipPrinciples: Strive for connection over perfection — dare to be dull to dial down self-evaluation
You actually have to prepare to be spontaneous, just like athletes and jazz musicians
Visualization desensitizes anxiety — see yourself succeeding before you speak

leaders.name: Matt Dixon
leaders.title: Author & Sales Researcher
leaders.bio: Matt Dixon is author of The Challenger Sale and The JOLT Effect, known for his groundbreaking research into what makes the best salespeople different, based on analysis of millions of sales conversations.
keyThemes: fear of messing up vs fear of missing out

notableQuotes.quote: Dialing up the FOMO backfires 87% of the time. They're not afraid of missing out, they're afraid of messing up.
notableQuotes.context: Research finding on why traditional urgency-based sales tactics fail

notableQuotes.quote: Most salespeople are trying to figure out what's keeping the customer up at night. The challenger approach is about showing the customer what should be keeping them up at night.
notableQuotes.context: Defining the challenger selling methodology

notableQuotes.quote: We collected two and a half million sales calls and studied them with a machine learning platform at scale.
notableQuotes.context: On the research methodology behind The JOLT Effect

leaders.episodeSummary: Matt Dixon shares findings from analyzing 2.5 million sales calls, revealing that indecision (not competition) is the primary reason deals are lost. He introduces the JOLT method for overcoming buyer indecision and explains the Challenger Sale approach of teaching customers about risks they don't yet recognize, all backed by large-scale data analysis.
leadershipPrinciples: You lose most deals not to competition but to customer indecision driven by fear of failure
Dialing up FOMO backfires 87% of the time — customers fear messing up, not missing out
The challenger approach shows customers what should keep them up at night, not what already does

leaders.name: Matt LeMay
leaders.title: Product Leadership Consultant & Author
leaders.bio: Matt LeMay is a product leadership consultant and author of Product Management in Practice, known for his practical frameworks on avoiding low-impact PM work and staying connected to company goals.

notableQuotes.quote: If you were the CEO of this company, would you fully fund your own team? Frankly, most people I ask that question don't know the answer right away.
notableQuotes.context: His litmus test for whether a PM team is doing impactful work

notableQuotes.quote: The low-impact PM death spiral starts with adding little features here and there, making little cosmetic improvements until the next round of layoffs.
notableQuotes.context: Describing the pattern that leads to PM teams being cut

notableQuotes.quote: We still have too many teams doing work around the work.
notableQuotes.context: Quoting Daniel Ek's Spotify layoff message about the PM overhead problem

leaders.episodeSummary: Matt LeMay tackles the uncomfortable reality that many PM teams are caught in a 'low-impact death spiral' of small feature work disconnected from company goals. He provides a three-step framework for becoming impact-first, warns that even following best practices won't protect PMs who aren't driving real business outcomes, and challenges PMs to ask whether the CEO would fund their team.
leadershipPrinciples: Set team goals no more than one step away from company goals — don't let them cascade into oblivion
If you were the CEO, would you fully fund your own team? If not, you have a problem
You can follow all the best practices but if your company goes out of business, perfect OKRs won't save you

leaders.name: Matt MacInnis
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Matt MacInnis is CPO and former longtime COO at Rippling, a $16B+ company, known for his brutally honest leadership philosophy and building complex, high-growth businesses.

notableQuotes.quote: It is really important to me that we've deliberately understaffed every project at the company. If you overstaff, you get politics.
notableQuotes.context: On his contrarian approach to team sizing

notableQuotes.quote: The most selfish thing you can do is withhold feedback from someone. You're optimizing for your own comfort.
notableQuotes.context: On why radical candor is a moral obligation for leaders

notableQuotes.quote: The purest form of ambition and most intense source of energy in the business is the founder CEO. Every next circle of management can be an order of magnitude drop off in intensity.
notableQuotes.context: On the biggest danger in scaling companies

leaders.episodeSummary: Matt MacInnis shares his intense leadership philosophy from building Rippling into a $16B company, arguing that deliberate understaffing prevents politics, radical feedback is a moral obligation, and every management layer risks diluting founder intensity. His approach demands extraordinary effort for extraordinary results and treats comfort zones as danger signals.
leadershipPrinciples: Deliberately understaff every project — overstaffing creates politics, waste, and cruft
If you're in the comfort zone at work, you're making a mistake — 99th percentile outcomes require extraordinary effort
Withholding feedback is the most selfish thing you can do — it optimizes for your comfort over their growth

leaders.name: Matt Mochary
leaders.title: Executive Coach
leaders.bio: Matt Mochary is Silicon Valley's most sought-after executive coach, working with CEOs of OpenAI, Coinbase, Reddit, Rippling, Notion, and partners at Sequoia and YC, and author of The Great CEO Within.

notableQuotes.quote: The biggest marker between a botched layoff and a successful layoff is: did they hear it from their manager in a one-on-one?
notableQuotes.context: On the single most important factor in layoff execution

notableQuotes.quote: If they heard it in an email, in a group chat, that's when people start going on Twitter and newspapers, because it feels dehumanizing.
notableQuotes.context: On why impersonal layoffs create lasting damage

leaders.episodeSummary: Matt Mochary, coach to the CEOs of OpenAI, Coinbase, and Reddit, shares his most practical leadership advice including why learning to fire people well is a critical skill, how anger and fear mislead leaders, and the single most important factor that determines whether a layoff goes well or creates lasting damage to a company's reputation.
leadershipPrinciples: Learning to fire people well is one of the most important leadership skills
Anger and fear often point you in the exact opposite direction you should be going
The biggest marker of a botched layoff is whether people heard it from their manager one-on-one or not

leaders.name: Matt Mullenweg
leaders.title: Co-creator & CEO
leaders.bio: Matt Mullenweg is the co-creator of WordPress, which powers 40% of the web, and CEO of Automattic, a $7B+ company that owns WordPress.com, Tumblr, WooCommerce, and other web products.

notableQuotes.quote: If you're really open and open source, sometimes you have to stand up to bullies and fight to protect your open source ideals.
notableQuotes.context: On the WP Engine controversy and defending WordPress

notableQuotes.quote: Previously, 1% of the world thought I was terrible and now I feel like it's up to four or 5%.
notableQuotes.context: Self-aware humor about the backlash from his public stances

leaders.episodeSummary: Matt Mullenweg addresses the WP Engine controversy head-on, sharing his perspective on defending the WordPress open source ecosystem from what he sees as trademark abuse by private equity-backed companies. He also discusses his views on AI and open source, why he considers Meta's Llama 'fake open source,' and Automattic's acquisition philosophy.
leadershipPrinciples: If you're truly open source, sometimes you have to stand up to bullies to protect your ideals
Open source creates the most durable competitive moats through community and ecosystem
Products like Llama that restrict commercial use are 'fake open source'

leaders.name: Matthew Dicks
leaders.title: Author & Storytelling Coach
leaders.bio: Matthew Dicks is a 59-time Moth Story Slam winner, author of Storyworthy, and one of the most acclaimed storytelling coaches in the world who teaches leaders to communicate through narrative.

notableQuotes.quote: Everyone loves the word storytelling in business. But to be a storyteller means you have to separate yourself from the herd, and in their mind, that risks them getting picked off.
notableQuotes.context: On why business leaders struggle with real storytelling

notableQuotes.quote: How many times have you gone to a conference, listened to someone speak, and by the time you're pulling into the driveway, you can't remember anything? That's what happens if we don't speak in story.
notableQuotes.context: On why storytelling is essential for being remembered

leaders.episodeSummary: Matthew Dicks, the winningest Moth Story Slam competitor in history, shares his framework for telling stories that stick. His core insight is that all great stories are rooted in a 'five-second moment' of transformation, and he argues that without story, business communication is forgettable 100% of the time. He provides actionable techniques for finding and telling personal stories in professional contexts.
leadershipPrinciples: All great stories are rooted in a five-second moment of transformation in someone's life
If you're not telling stories, you will be forgotten 100% of the time
Our minds are not designed to remember pie charts or statistics — they remember stories with imagery

leaders.name: Maya Prohovnik
leaders.title: Head of Product, Podcasting
leaders.bio: Maya Prohovnik leads product for Spotify's podcasting platform, was employee #1 at Anchor (acquired by Spotify), which now powers over 75% of all new podcasts globally.

notableQuotes.quote: We hired college interns to manually submit hundreds of thousands of podcasts through Apple accounts. People think we had some secret backdoor deal, but we just had college students doing it manually.
notableQuotes.context: On the scrappy growth hack that gave Anchor massive hosting market share

notableQuotes.quote: We were obsessed with reducing friction, this was our constant battle.
notableQuotes.context: Describing Anchor's core product philosophy that drove their dominance

leaders.episodeSummary: Maya Prohovnik shares how she built Anchor from employee #1 into the platform powering 75% of new podcasts, largely through obsessive friction reduction and a legendary growth hack of manually submitting podcasts via Apple accounts. She discusses dogfooding as a core practice, maintaining startup culture within Spotify, and her productivity systems for senior leadership.
leadershipPrinciples: Be obsessed with reducing friction — this should be your constant battle
Everyone on the product team should dogfood the product by creating their own podcast
Do things that don't scale to unlock massive distribution advantages

leaders.name: Mayur Kamat
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Mayur Kamat is CPO at N26, previously Global Head of Product at Binance and VP of Product at Agoda, with early career stints at Google (first PM on Hangouts) and Microsoft.

notableQuotes.quote: Strategy is a little bit overrated for product. For most product managers, your strategy should be, 'How fast can I go from hypothesis to data?'
notableQuotes.context: Challenging the common overemphasis on strategy vs execution speed

notableQuotes.quote: I was the first PM on Hangouts. We had thousands of people and the entire power of Google. We still didn't manage to build a great messaging product.
notableQuotes.context: Sharing his most spectacular product failure

notableQuotes.quote: The challenge with being a PM is everybody thinks they can do the job. The moment you build experimentation, you've made it scientific.
notableQuotes.context: On why experimentation legitimizes the PM discipline

leaders.episodeSummary: Mayur Kamat shares lessons from leading product at Binance, Agoda, and N26, including the spectacular failure of Google Hangouts despite unlimited resources. He argues that strategy is overrated for most PMs and that the real skill is speed from hypothesis to data through experimentation, offering career advice about optimizing for learning over compensation.
leadershipPrinciples: For most PMs, your strategy should be: how fast can I go from hypothesis to data?
Strategy is overrated for product — experimentation makes PM a real science
Don't take on projects that are six months or a year because you don't control the macro

leaders.name: Megan Cook
leaders.title: Head of Product
leaders.bio: Megan Cook is Head of Product for Jira at Atlassian, having spent 11 years at the company, previously working as an analyst, developer, and agile coach.

notableQuotes.quote: We call it Fight Club. It's 30 minutes every week for myself, my engineering, and my design leader; and we know we're going there to have a conflict.
notableQuotes.context: Describing her ritual for proactive conflict resolution among leadership

notableQuotes.quote: By having a specific slot of time in your week for something like that, you're in that mindset. You know you're going in there to solve a hard problem.
notableQuotes.context: On why scheduled conflict outperforms ad-hoc difficult conversations

leaders.episodeSummary: Megan Cook shares how she leads product for Jira, the world's most popular project management tool used by 75% of Fortune 500 companies. Her standout practice is 'Fight Club' — a weekly 30-minute meeting with her engineering and design leads dedicated specifically to having conflicts and solving hard problems early before they escalate.
leadershipPrinciples: Schedule regular 'Fight Club' sessions with your leadership triad to address conflicts early
When you have a specific time for hard conversations, you enter with the right mindset
Being conflict-averse makes problems bigger — get on top of disagreements early

leaders.name: Melanie Perkins
leaders.title: CEO & Co-founder
leaders.bio: Melanie Perkins is CEO and co-founder of Canva, valued at $42B+ with $3.3B in revenue, who was rejected by over 100 investors before building one of the most successful design platforms in the world.
keyThemes: pivot from yearbooks to design platform

notableQuotes.quote: The thing that I love about a crazy big goal is that you feel completely inadequate before it. You want to work really hard to will it into existence.
notableQuotes.context: On Canva's value of 'Crazy Big Goals'

notableQuotes.quote: It was really clear in my mind that it was the future and I thought the investors were wrong. But they also gave really helpful feedback, often in the form of rejection.
notableQuotes.context: On being rejected by over 100 investors and using each rejection to improve

notableQuotes.quote: I have a wall in my house in my office, which is my vision for what I'd like the world to look like in 2050.
notableQuotes.context: On her personal practice of long-term vision setting

leaders.episodeSummary: Melanie Perkins shares the extraordinary journey of building Canva from a yearbook platform rejected by 100+ investors into a $42B design powerhouse that's been profitable for eight years. She reveals her approach to 'crazy big goals,' how she used every investor rejection as fuel to improve her pitch, and why every project at Canva starts with a vision deck.
leadershipPrinciples: The thing about crazy big goals is that you feel completely inadequate before them — that's the point
Investor rejections are helpful feedback: each 'no' becomes a new slide in your pitch deck
Start by imagining the future you actually want, then work backwards to make it happen

leaders.name: Melissa Perri
leaders.title: CEO & Product Consultant
leaders.bio: Melissa Perri is CEO of Produx Labs, author of Escaping the Build Trap, Harvard Business School instructor, and has consulted with hundreds of product organizations on strategy and transformation.

notableQuotes.quote: 99% of the time I see that it's actually in the way they're setting their goals and deploying their strategy. Because once you train those people, they have no context on what to work towards.
notableQuotes.context: On why most orgs misdiagnose their product team problems

leaders.episodeSummary: Melissa Perri, who has seen more product orgs up close than perhaps anyone alive, reveals that the most common product team problems stem from strategy deployment rather than people skills. She covers when to hire your first PM, how to escape the build trap, and why product transformation requires fixing the system, not just training individuals.
leadershipPrinciples: 99% of product org issues are in goal-setting and strategy deployment, not in people training
Without context on what to work towards, even well-trained PMs will fail
Product transformation requires a holistic approach — training alone doesn't fix structural problems

leaders.name: Melissa Tan
leaders.title: Head of Growth
leaders.bio: Melissa Tan is a growth leader and advisor who was Dropbox's first growth PM and longtime head of B2B growth, and has advised Canva, Grammarly, Miro, and Ro on growth strategy.

notableQuotes.quote: We would hire a ton of really smart people that had never done sales and had them do sales. That's how we got our very innovative go-to-market motions.
notableQuotes.context: On how Dropbox's unconventional hiring drove growth innovation

leaders.episodeSummary: Melissa Tan shares how she built growth teams at Dropbox and Webflow, emphasizing the power of hiring smart generalists who approach problems from first principles rather than following playbooks. She covers building high-performing growth teams, aligning sales and product motions, and the transition from advising to operating roles.
leadershipPrinciples: Hire smart people who've never done the job before — they innovate because they don't know the rules
First principles thinking drives the best go-to-market innovation
People with deep user context from one role create breakthrough insights when they move to another

leaders.name: Meltem Kuran
leaders.title: Head of Growth
leaders.bio: Meltem Kuran is Head of Growth at Deel, arguably the fastest growing SaaS business of all time, going from $0 to $300M ARR in three years while staying EBITDA positive.

notableQuotes.quote: Build the skeleton before you put on the makeup. Do you have a website? Is it fast? Does the search engine know it exists?
notableQuotes.context: On the foundational growth steps most companies skip

leaders.episodeSummary: Meltem Kuran reveals the growth playbook behind Deel's extraordinary trajectory from $0 to $300M ARR in three years. She emphasizes getting fundamentals right before scaling — fast websites, SEO foundations, and content before paid acquisition — arguing that most companies skip the basics in their rush to scale.
leadershipPrinciples: Build the skeleton before you put on the makeup — get fundamentals right before scaling tactics
You can't run successful paid ads if your website loads in 4+ seconds
Go back to basics: does your website exist, is it fast, can search engines find it?

leaders.name: Merci Grace
leaders.title: Former Head of Growth
leaders.bio: Merci Grace is a founder, former Head of Growth at Slack, VC, and co-founder of Women in Product, with a background spanning game design, product management, and venture capital.

notableQuotes.quote: I got my first term sheet as a founder before I knew what venture capital was. Purely accidental.
notableQuotes.context: On her unconventional career journey from game designer to growth leader

leaders.episodeSummary: Merci Grace shares lessons from leading growth at Slack during its explosive PLG-driven expansion, covering the most common mistakes companies make when going product-led, signs your product is ready for PLG, and when to hire your first head of growth. Her career arc from game designer to VC to founder illustrates the power of following curiosity.
leadershipPrinciples: Follow your curiosity — the best career arcs come from genuine interest, not strategic planning
PLG requires the product to deliver enough value that users want to spread it organically
The most common PLG mistake is trying to bolt it on to a product that doesn't naturally spread

leaders.name: Michael Truell
leaders.title: Co-founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Michael Truell is co-founder and CEO of Anysphere, the company behind Cursor, the leading AI code editor that hit $300M ARR just two years after launch.

notableQuotes.quote: Our goal with Cursor is to invent a new type of programming. More and more being an engineer will feel like being a logic designer.
notableQuotes.context: On the vision for Cursor beyond just AI-assisted coding
