notableQuotes.quote: We definitely didn't expect to be doing any of our own model development. And at this point, every magic moment in Cursor involves a custom model.
notableQuotes.context: On the counterintuitive importance of custom models for product differentiation

notableQuotes.quote: Many people you hear hire too fast. I think we actually hired too slow to begin with.
notableQuotes.context: A contrarian hiring lesson from building a hypergrowth product

leaders.episodeSummary: Michael Truell shares the story of building Cursor into the leading AI code editor, hitting $300M ARR in two years. He reveals their vision of inventing a new type of programming where engineers become logic designers, the counterintuitive lesson that they needed to build custom models rather than just wrap APIs, and why they should have hired faster.
leadershipPrinciples: The goal is to invent a new type of programming where engineers become logic designers specifying intent
Every magic moment in the product should involve custom models — don't just wrap APIs
Many founders hire too fast, but we actually hired too slow and should have moved faster

leaders.name: Mihika Kapoor
leaders.title: Product Manager
leaders.bio: Mihika Kapoor is a design-engineering-PM hybrid at Figma known as the go-to person for leading zero-to-one products, including early work on FigJam, and was the most-mentioned PM when Lenny asked Twitter who the best PM people have worked with is.
keyThemes: design and prototype before green light

notableQuotes.quote: My take is that your scope is the world. Nothing should ever be perceived as being out of bounds.
notableQuotes.context: On the mindset she brings to product management at Figma

notableQuotes.quote: We lean heavily into designing and prototyping even before a project gets a green light.
notableQuotes.context: On Figma's approach to zero-to-one product development

leaders.episodeSummary: Mihika Kapoor, the most-mentioned PM when Lenny asked Twitter who the best PM is, shares her approach to zero-to-one product development at Figma. She emphasizes treating your scope as the entire world, prototyping heavily before getting project approval, and creating compelling visions that get cross-functional teams aligned around what the future should look like.
leadershipPrinciples: Your scope is the world — nothing should ever be perceived as out of bounds
Design and prototype heavily before a project gets the green light
If you and your team do your job correctly, imagine what the world looks like — start there

leaders.name: Mike Krieger
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Mike Krieger is CPO at Anthropic (makers of Claude) and co-founder of Instagram, leading product at one of the most important AI companies during a period when 90% of their code is written by AI.

notableQuotes.quote: Over half of our pull requests are Claude Code generated. Probably at this point it's over 70%. It completely blew out expectations.
notableQuotes.context: On the reality of AI-written code at Anthropic

notableQuotes.quote: We really rapidly became bottlenecked on our merge queue. We had to completely re-architect it because so much more code was being written.
notableQuotes.context: On the unexpected bottlenecks when AI dramatically increases code output

leaders.episodeSummary: Mike Krieger, Instagram co-founder turned Anthropic CPO, reveals that over 70% of Anthropic's pull requests are now AI-generated, creating entirely new bottlenecks around infrastructure rather than code writing. He discusses how product development fundamentally changes when AI writes most of the code, his thoughts on Anthropic vs OpenAI, and lessons from shutting down Artifact.
leadershipPrinciples: When 90% of code is AI-written, bottlenecks shift from writing to infrastructure like merge queues
The team using AI to build AI tools creates the most futuristic workflow
Custom models are essential for every magic moment in an AI product

leaders.name: Mike Maples Jr
leaders.title: Co-founder & Partner
leaders.bio: Mike Maples Jr is a legendary seed-stage investor at Floodgate, early backer of Twitter, Lyft, and Twitch, and eight-time Forbes Midas list member who has codified three elements of breakthrough startup ideas.

notableQuotes.quote: Business is never a fair fight. What inflections let the founder do is wage asymmetric warfare on the present.
notableQuotes.context: On why timing and inflection points matter more than execution alone

notableQuotes.quote: If you're living in the future and you notice what's missing, your intuition about what to build is far more likely to be right.
notableQuotes.context: On how breakthrough founders discover secrets

leaders.episodeSummary: Mike Maples Jr shares the three elements that separate breakthrough startups from the rest: inflections (technology shifts that create asymmetric opportunity), insights (secrets about the future), and founder-future fit. Drawing on 20 years of seed investing, he reveals that 80% of his biggest returns came from pivots and that living in the future is the best way to discover what to build.
leadershipPrinciples: Breakthrough startups require three elements: inflections, insights, and founder-future fit
Inflections let founders wage asymmetric warfare on the present
If you're living in the future and notice what's missing, your intuition about what to build is far more likely to be right

leaders.name: Molly Graham
leaders.title: Founder
leaders.bio: Molly Graham is an early Google and Facebook employee who worked closely with Zuck on CZI and with Brett Taylor at Quip, now leading Glue Club to help leaders grow as fast as their companies.

notableQuotes.quote: 80% of the culture of a company is literally defined by the personality of the founder.
notableQuotes.context: Comparing Google (PhD students' paradise) to Facebook (hacker's dorm room)

notableQuotes.quote: You have to grow as fast as your company is growing — both learning to give away what you've gotten good at and move on to the next shiny pile of Legos.
notableQuotes.context: On her famous 'give away your Legos' framework

leaders.episodeSummary: Molly Graham shares her most famous framework — 'give away your Legos' — along with other mindsets for leaders experiencing rapid scale. Drawing on her experience at Google, Facebook, and working with Zuck, she explains why 80% of company culture is the founder's personality, how to grow as fast as your company, and the difference between J-curve and staircase leadership growth.
leadershipPrinciples: Give away your Legos — learn to pass what you've gotten good at and move to the next challenge
80% of company culture is defined by the personality of the founder
You have to grow as fast as your company is growing to take advantage of the opportunity

leaders.name: Nabeel Qureshi
leaders.title: Researcher & Writer
leaders.bio: Nabeel Qureshi is a founder, writer, and researcher who was VP of Business Development at GoCardless, worked on the largest medical dataset at NIH, and recently researched AI policy at the Mercatus Center.

notableQuotes.quote: They were extremely careful about only making people PMs who had first proven themselves as forward deployed engineers.
notableQuotes.context: On Palantir's unique PM path that requires field experience first

notableQuotes.quote: They screened really hard for independent-minded people who weren't afraid to push back and people with broader intellectual interests.
notableQuotes.context: On what made Palantir's hiring so distinctive

leaders.episodeSummary: Nabeel Qureshi provides a rare inside look at Palantir's distinctive approach to product management, where PMs can only be promoted from forward-deployed engineers who work alongside customers. He explains why 30% of departing Palantir PMs start companies, the value of screening for intellectual curiosity and independent-mindedness, and his perspectives on AI policy.
leadershipPrinciples: Only make people PMs who have first proven themselves as forward-deployed engineers in the field
Screen hard for independent-mindedness and broad intellectual interests
The best PMs come from working alongside customers at their actual desks

leaders.name: Nan Yu
leaders.title: Head of Product
leaders.bio: Nan Yu is Head of Product at Linear, one of the most beloved and fastest-growing B2B SaaS products, known for its exceptional design quality and craft-focused product development.
keyThemes: speed and quality are not tradeoffs

notableQuotes.quote: People talk about speed and quality as a tradeoff because they over-index on rushing or being sloppy. What they should index on is being really competent.
notableQuotes.context: Challenging the common assumption that fast means low quality

notableQuotes.quote: If you look at people at the pinnacle of their craft, you can basically tell how good the output is going to be by how fast they're going.
notableQuotes.context: On why speed is actually a signal of quality, not its opposite

leaders.episodeSummary: Nan Yu reveals how Linear builds one of the most loved B2B products by rejecting the tradeoff between speed and quality, arguing that true craft mastery means both move together. He shares his system for creative problem-solving, how to discover the emotions customers want to avoid, and practical advice on landing dream PM roles.
leadershipPrinciples: Speed and quality are not a tradeoff — competence is what enables both simultaneously
At the pinnacle of craft, you can tell output quality by how fast someone is going
Talk to customers to discover the emotion they want to avoid, then solve for that

leaders.name: Nancy Duarte
leaders.title: CEO
leaders.bio: Nancy Duarte is a bestselling author, speaker, and CEO of Duarte Incorporated, which has helped create over 250,000 presentations for the world's most influential business leaders and institutions including Apple, TED, Google, the World Bank, and Al Gore's Inconvenient Truth.
keyThemes: what is vs what could be framework

notableQuotes.quote: A lot of people think that the only time you really need to present well is when you have a big stage talk. I can get my husband to do chores for me on the weekends with a real quick what is, what could be.
notableQuotes.context: On how the contrast framework works in any moment of influence, not just formal presentations

notableQuotes.quote: I have the whole history of the Silicon Valley in a way. Every little startup and then they grew to massive brands — you could actually look at the rise and fall of all these companies.
notableQuotes.context: On 35 years of crafting presentations for Silicon Valley companies

leaders.episodeSummary: Nancy Duarte shares tactical advice for improving presentations, telling better stories, and laying out convincing arguments, drawing on 35 years and over 250,000 presentations created for the world's top leaders. She reveals her 'what is vs what could be' contrast framework that works in any moment of influence, from board presentations to getting your spouse to do chores.
leadershipPrinciples: Every moment of influence benefits from contrast between what is and what could be
Great presentations work in any format — meetings, phone calls, not just big stage talks
Data storytelling requires standing in front of data and making it human

leaders.name: Naomi Gleit
leaders.title: Head of Product
leaders.bio: Naomi Gleit is Head of Product at Meta and the longest-serving executive after Mark Zuckerberg, having joined as employee number 29 and seen the company scale from 30 employees to a $1.5 trillion business over almost 20 years.

notableQuotes.quote: I really believe in frameworks for things that helps drive extreme clarity. There needs to be one canonical doc. Everyone should know exactly where the canonical doc is.
notableQuotes.context: On her approach to managing complexity across many projects at Meta

notableQuotes.quote: I ask five different people, get five different answers. That is unacceptable.
notableQuotes.context: On why canonical documentation is essential for organizational clarity

leaders.episodeSummary: Naomi Gleit, Meta's longest-serving executive after Zuckerberg (employee #29), shares lessons from Facebook's legendary growth team and her superpower of simplifying complex problems. She discusses why PMs are conductors, the importance of canonical docs for extreme clarity, leadership lessons learned from Zuck, and tactical tips for running meetings and writing effective documentation.
leadershipPrinciples: Every project needs one canonical doc — if you ask five people and get five answers, that's unacceptable
PMs are the conductor of the product team — they don't play every instrument but ensure harmony
The superpower is taking complex, gnarly problems and simplifying them to deliver results

leaders.name: Naomi Ionita
leaders.title: Investor
leaders.bio: Naomi Ionita is a VC at Menlo Ventures, formerly VP of Growth at Invoice2go and an early growth and monetization leader at Evernote, known for her expertise in pricing strategy and the Modern Growth Stack framework.

notableQuotes.quote: Do not set it and forget it. Think about your pricing just like you do your roadmap. Every 6 to 12 months, there's probably something meaningful that you're launching — treat that as an opportunity to revisit your monetization strategy.
notableQuotes.context: On the most common pricing mistake she sees companies make

notableQuotes.quote: Pricing's sort of plucked out of thin air, and then they don't revisit it. This was Evernote.
notableQuotes.context: On learning from Evernote's mistake of not revisiting pricing for years

leaders.episodeSummary: Naomi Ionita draws on her experience at Evernote and as a VC at Menlo Ventures to share when and how startups should start charging, how to evolve pricing strategy over time, and why pricing should be treated like a product roadmap. She also introduces her Modern Growth Stack framework mapping all the areas where products can leverage tools to grow.
leadershipPrinciples: Do not set pricing and forget it — revisit every 6 to 12 months as you launch meaningful features
Think about pricing just like you do your product roadmap
Treat every meaningful feature launch as an opportunity to revisit monetization strategy

leaders.name: Nick Turley
leaders.title: Head of ChatGPT
leaders.bio: Nick Turley is Head of ChatGPT at OpenAI, having helped conceive the product and scale it from zero to over 700 million weekly active users and billions in revenue, making it arguably the most successful consumer software product in history.

notableQuotes.quote: This is a pattern with AI — you won't know what to polish until after you ship. My dream is that we ship daily.
notableQuotes.context: On why speed of shipping matters more than perfection in AI products

notableQuotes.quote: I just really want to jump to the punchline: 'Why can't we do this now?' I always felt like part of my role here is to just set the pace and the resting heartbeat.
notableQuotes.context: On the 'maximally accelerated' principle that Kevin Weil credits to him

leaders.episodeSummary: Nick Turley shares the inside story of building ChatGPT from a hackathon codebase that was almost called 'Chat with GPT-3.5' into a product with 700 million weekly users. He reveals his 'maximally accelerated' philosophy of always asking 'why can't we do this now,' why AI products must ship before polishing, and how product development changes when your product is used by 10% of the world population.
leadershipPrinciples: With AI, you won't know what to polish until after you ship — so ship first
Always ask 'Why can't we do this now?' to maximize acceleration
Set the pace and the resting heartbeat of the organization

leaders.name: Nickey Skarstad
leaders.title: Director of Product Management
leaders.bio: Nickey Skarstad is a Director of Product Management at Duolingo, formerly at Airbnb and Etsy (where she rose from forum moderator to Director of PM), known for setting vision, executing strategy, and maintaining product quality.
keyThemes: career growth from IC to leader

notableQuotes.quote: Nickey Skarstad was the first name that I heard. She had a legendary reputation as a PM who everyone loved, but got shit done.
notableQuotes.context: Lenny describing Nickey's reputation among the newsletter Slack community

notableQuotes.quote: Making your strategy actionable and keeping your teams aligned and focused is the core challenge of product leadership.
notableQuotes.context: On the gap between having a strategy and actually executing on it

leaders.episodeSummary: Nickey Skarstad shares her approach to setting product vision, translating it into actionable goals, and maintaining quality through well-designed product review sessions. Drawing on her journey from Etsy forum moderator to Duolingo product director via Airbnb, she covers how to keep teams aligned, make strategy actionable, and which skills have most contributed to her career success.
leadershipPrinciples: Set a clear vision, translate it into goals, then execute — keeping teams aligned and focused throughout
Design your product review sessions to be the forcing function for quality
Making strategy actionable requires constant translation between vision and daily work

leaders.name: Nicole Forsgren
leaders.title: Researcher & Author
leaders.bio: Nicole Forsgren is the creator of the DORA and SPACE frameworks for measuring developer productivity, author of the award-winning book Accelerate and forthcoming Frictionless, and the foremost expert on developer experience measurement.

notableQuotes.quote: Starting with what is your problem or what is your goal — I would say this is a bigger challenge than most people recognize. 80% of the folks that I work with, this is their biggest problem.
notableQuotes.context: On the most common failure in developer productivity initiatives

notableQuotes.quote: If you're talking about culture, this is totally different than if you're talking about friction in toolchains. If you're on different pages, you're heading in completely different directions.
notableQuotes.context: On why precision in defining developer experience matters

leaders.episodeSummary: Nicole Forsgren dives deep into measuring and improving engineering team productivity using the DORA and SPACE frameworks she created. She reveals that 80% of organizations struggle because they don't clearly define what problem they're solving, and explains the critical difference between culture, toolchain friction, and inner vs outer loop developer experience.
leadershipPrinciples: Start with what is your problem or goal — 80% of teams fail because they skip this step
Developer experience means different things to different people — you must define it precisely
If you're talking about culture vs toolchain friction, you're heading in completely different directions

leaders.name: Nikhyl Singhal
leaders.title: VP of Product
leaders.bio: Nikhyl Singhal leads product teams for the Facebook app at Meta, overseeing groups, stories, messaging, and feed. Previously CPO at Credit Karma and a leader at Google on Hangouts and Photos, he has co-founded three startups and mentored hundreds of PMs.

notableQuotes.quote: The moment that the dogs, if they accidentally touched the rabbit, they would never run again because there was like, 'Well, what's next? I've achieved what I was looking for.'
notableQuotes.context: Using the greyhound track metaphor to explain why PMs need to plan beyond their first career goal

notableQuotes.quote: They'll keep working because they know nothing else to do, but they'll be sadder or they'll find ways to create war when peace is needed.
notableQuotes.context: On what happens when achievers reach their goal without a next chapter planned

leaders.episodeSummary: Nikhyl Singhal draws on his experience leading product at Meta, Credit Karma, and Google to share his passion for PM career coaching. Using his famous 'fake rabbit' metaphor from greyhound tracks, he explains why PMs must plan beyond their first big career goal, how to navigate career transitions, and what he's learned from mentoring hundreds of product managers through their most critical decision points.
leadershipPrinciples: Don't just plan for the first goal — plan what comes after, or you'll stop running like the dog that caught the rabbit
The most substantive time to help people is during moments of dilemma or forks in the road
Career coaching is about helping people through transitions, not giving ongoing advice

leaders.name: Nikita Bier
leaders.title: Founder & Consumer App Expert
leaders.company: tbh / Gas (acquired by Facebook and Discord)
leaders.bio: Nikita Bier has built, launched, and helped get more apps to the top of the App Store than almost anyone, selling tbh to Facebook for $30M+ and Gas to Discord, all with tiny teams and minimal funding.

notableQuotes.quote: The thing I didn't realize as a product manager in a large tech company is there is very little product management that you do. They're mainly just writing documents and being the team secretary. But products live and die in the pixels.
notableQuotes.context: On why he believes traditional PM roles miss the point of product building

notableQuotes.quote: I looked on the App Store and the number one app in the United States was an app called Surah, but the entire app was in Arabic — the strongest signal that people want something.
notableQuotes.context: On discovering the latent demand that led to building tbh

leaders.episodeSummary: Nikita Bier reveals how he repeatedly built apps that reached the top of the App Store with tiny teams, from tbh (sold to Facebook) to Gas (sold to Discord). He shares his approach to finding latent demand, why he believes products live and die in the pixels rather than in documents, and the absolute chaos of keeping viral consumer apps online during hypergrowth.
leadershipPrinciples: Look for latent demand — people going through distortive processes to obtain a particular value
Products live and die in the pixels — you should be designing the hierarchy, the flows, everything
Product management in large companies is mostly writing documents and being the team secretary

leaders.name: Nikita Miller
leaders.title: SVP & Head of Product
leaders.bio: Nikita Miller is SVP and Head of Product at The Knot Worldwide, previously VP of Product at Dooly and Head of Growth and Retention at Trello for over five years, known for balancing outcomes with output velocity.

notableQuotes.quote: Some folks, myself included at certain points, swung way too far on the outcomes train and forgot that output is an indicator of that. If you're not shipping a lot of things to market quickly enough, then it just doesn't matter that much.
notableQuotes.context: On the danger of over-indexing on outcomes while neglecting shipping velocity

notableQuotes.quote: Everyone was 'Outcomes, outcomes, outcomes,' which is right. But if you're also not shipping a lot of things to market quickly enough, then it just doesn't matter.
notableQuotes.context: On finding the balance between outcome-driven and output-driven product development

leaders.episodeSummary: Nikita Miller shares her framework for balancing outcome-driven thinking with shipping velocity, arguing that teams that over-index on outcomes while not shipping fast enough lose both. Drawing on her experience at Trello, Dooly, and The Knot Worldwide, she covers cross-functional role alignment, remote team effectiveness, and practical approaches to product development process.
leadershipPrinciples: Outcomes matter but output is an indicator — if you're not shipping quickly enough, ideation doesn't matter
Don't swing too far on the outcomes train and forget that shipping velocity is a leading indicator
Align roles and responsibilities within cross-functional teams using explicit frameworks

leaders.name: Nilan Peiris
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Nilan Peiris is CPO at Wise, where he has been for over 11 years. Wise moves $12 billion a month in cross-border payments, growing 30-40% year over year, with about 70% of growth coming through word of mouth.

notableQuotes.quote: Some people focus on conversion rate. That's cool, you get a bit more growth. But to get to recommendation, you're going to blow your user socks off. You have to give them an experience they didn't know was previously possible.
notableQuotes.context: On why Wise focuses on recommendation-worthy experiences over conversion optimization

notableQuotes.quote: When you are in that place of doing something that no one has ever done before, that's when you get it.
notableQuotes.context: On the secret to achieving 70% word-of-mouth growth

leaders.episodeSummary: Nilan Peiris breaks down exactly how Wise achieved 70% word-of-mouth growth by building experiences so good that users can't help but recommend them. He explains why optimizing for recommendation rather than conversion is the key to exponential growth, and shares the tactical playbook behind Wise's journey to moving $12 billion monthly in cross-border payments.
leadershipPrinciples: To get recommendation, you have to blow users' socks off — give them an experience they didn't know was possible
Optimizing conversion rate gives you a bit more growth, but recommendation-worthy products give you exponential growth
When you do something no one has ever done before, that's when word of mouth happens

leaders.name: Nir Eyal
leaders.title: Author & Speaker
leaders.bio: Nir Eyal is the author of two bestselling books — Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products and Indistractable: How to Control Your Attention and Choose Your Life — with over 1 million copies sold in 30+ languages.

notableQuotes.quote: The problem is not our technology. The problem is our inability to deal with discomfort. 90% of our distractions come from internal triggers — it's the feelings, not the pings, dings, and rings.
notableQuotes.context: On discovering that getting rid of all technology didn't solve his distraction problem

notableQuotes.quote: Once you realize it's just a feeling — it's all it is, just an emotion — then you can have tools ready to go, arrows in your quiver ready to take out as soon as you feel that discomfort.
notableQuotes.context: On why understanding internal triggers is empowering rather than discouraging

leaders.episodeSummary: Nir Eyal shares dozens of tactical tools for becoming less distractable, rooted in his insight that 90% of distractions come from internal triggers — the uncomfortable feelings we try to escape — not from technology itself. He explains how to identify your internal triggers, build systems to manage discomfort, and actually stay focused on the work that matters most.
leadershipPrinciples: 90% of distractions come from internal triggers — the feelings you're trying to escape, not pings and dings
The problem is not technology — it's our inability to deal with discomfort
Always identify the internal trigger, the itch you're looking to escape when distracted

leaders.name: Noah Weiss
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Noah Weiss is CPO at Slack, where he has spent seven years. Previously head of product at Foursquare and a PM at Google and Fog Creek Software, he led Slack through a self-service plateau and into AI product development.

notableQuotes.quote: We have this mental metaphor — 'Take bigger boulder bets.' Teams can often get lost crawling up that hill, not realizing that there's a huge, incredibly beautiful range behind it.
notableQuotes.context: On Slack's approach to ambitious product bets beyond incremental improvement

notableQuotes.quote: In the AI space, we're trying to hear from customers what they wish Slack could do with new superpowers. Incubate teams, give them space to run, then get something to launch that blows people away.
notableQuotes.context: On Slack's formula for building AI features

leaders.episodeSummary: Noah Weiss shares Slack's approach to ambitious product development through 'bigger boulder bets' and Complaint Storms, a process for systematically identifying product pain points. He covers the 10 traits of great PMs, how to work with opinionated founders, lessons from Slack's self-service business plateauing in 2019, and how they're incubating AI capabilities by listening to what customers wish was possible.
leadershipPrinciples: Take bigger boulder bets — teams can get lost crawling up a hill without realizing there's a beautiful range behind it
Incubate new teams from scratch in new areas before those areas mature
Use Complaint Storms to systematically identify product pain points

leaders.name: Noam Lovinsky
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Noam Lovinsky is CPO at Grammarly, previously an early PM at YouTube leading creator and consumer experience, CPO at Thumbtack where he reignited growth after a downturn, and creator of Facebook's New Product Experimentation team.
keyThemes: new product experimentation within big cos

notableQuotes.quote: There were many times where Google leadership reconsidered the acquisition and, 'Should we sell YouTube?' if you can believe it or not.
notableQuotes.context: On how close YouTube came to being abandoned by Google in its early days

notableQuotes.quote: The new model really started to show legs and one of the board members said it was the prettiest smile graph that he had ever seen.
notableQuotes.context: On the Thumbtack turnaround after rethinking their business model

leaders.episodeSummary: Noam Lovinsky shares lessons from rescuing YouTube's early financial struggles, reigniting Thumbtack's growth after a Google SEO-caused downturn with what a board member called 'the prettiest smile graph ever,' and creating Facebook's New Product Experimentation team to incubate big ideas protected from the larger org. Now as Grammarly CPO, he draws on this experience building and rebuilding products at scale.
leadershipPrinciples: At Thumbtack, going from 1 to -1 and back to 1 required fundamentally rethinking the model, not just optimizing
Creating a startup within a startup requires protecting the team from the larger org's processes
YouTube was nearly sold by Google — transformative products sometimes need patience before they work

leaders.name: Oji Udezue
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Oji Udezue is CPO at Typeform, with previous leadership roles at Twitter (head of product for creation and conversation), Calendly (CPO), Atlassian (head of product for communication tools), and Microsoft (Windows, Outlook, Hotmail, IE).

notableQuotes.quote: Products who try to be viral just for synthetic virality fail. Slack wasn't even viral — people at lunch were like, 'We got Slack and this is amazing.' This is the bedrock of virality. Build a great product that solves a sharp problem.
notableQuotes.context: On why organic virality from product quality beats engineered viral loops

notableQuotes.quote: Slack couldn't even connect to organizations for the longest time. You could be on the third floor and someone using Slack on the fourth floor and have no clue.
notableQuotes.context: On how Slack grew through genuine word of mouth despite lacking viral mechanics

leaders.episodeSummary: Oji Udezue draws on his experience across Microsoft, Atlassian, Calendly, Twitter, and Typeform to explain why organic virality from solving sharp problems beats synthetic viral mechanics, and why you should be careful applying product frameworks without considering your specific context. He shares tactical PLG lessons and how to get sharp with your ideal customer profile.
leadershipPrinciples: The bedrock of virality is building a great product that solves a sharp problem — synthetic virality fails
Be really careful applying frameworks at your company — context matters more than the framework itself
Getting sharp with your ICP is essential for product-led growth success

leaders.name: Paige Costello
leaders.title: Product Lead
leaders.bio: Paige Costello is a product lead at Asana overseeing the core product experience, previously Director of Product at Intercom and Group PM at Intuit for over five years, known for building trust as the youngest person in the room.

notableQuotes.quote: Bring the insight. Know thy customer. Know thy market. Know thy competitors. Know thy numbers. Know thy product.
notableQuotes.context: On how to build trust when you're the youngest person in the room

notableQuotes.quote: The moment I challenged myself and said, 'How might the opposite be true?' my shoulders dropped. I was like, 'Oh, yeah, I can do both.'
notableQuotes.context: On escaping the scarcity mindset that holds back new PMs

leaders.episodeSummary: Paige Costello shares strategies for building trust with more experienced stakeholders, coaching PMs through leading by example, and overcoming the scarcity mindset that holds new PMs back. She covers Asana's product development process, how it evolved as the company scaled, and the career missteps that taught her the most valuable lessons.
leadershipPrinciples: Bring the insight — know thy customer, market, competitors, numbers, and product to earn trust
Leading by example is often the most effective coaching strategy for PMs
Challenge yourself with 'How might the opposite be true?' to escape scarcity mindset thinking

leaders.name: Patrick Campbell
leaders.title: Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Patrick Campbell is the founder and CEO of ProfitWell, which he bootstrapped and sold for over $200 million without any funding. He is a leading expert on SaaS pricing, retention, and business building.

notableQuotes.quote: Real professionals ship, and they ship at a pretty high frequency. Your tempo framework is more important than your org design.
notableQuotes.context: On why shipping cadence matters more than organizational structure

notableQuotes.quote: If you've ever had a team that seems really smart but they're always planning or don't really ship a lot, you probably don't have enough alignment on what good looks like in terms of tempo.
notableQuotes.context: On diagnosing the root cause when smart teams underperform

leaders.episodeSummary: Patrick Campbell shares lessons from bootstrapping ProfitWell to a $200M+ exit, covering 10 rapid-fire topics including shipping tempo (which he argues matters more than org design), SaaS pricing, retention, competitive analysis, user research, and first principles thinking. He brings a contrarian, data-driven perspective to every topic based on his experience building and selling a pricing analytics company.
leadershipPrinciples: Your tempo framework is more important than your org design
Real professionals ship, and they ship at a high frequency — that's the defining signal
If a team seems smart but always planning and not shipping, you have a tempo alignment problem

leaders.name: Paul Adams
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Paul Adams is CPO at Intercom, a role he has held for over 10 years. Previously global head of brand design at Facebook, user researcher at Google, product designer at Dyson, and automotive interior designer.

notableQuotes.quote: This is a meteor coming towards you. This is going to radically transform society. If people don't explore AI properly, it will leave them behind.
notableQuotes.context: On why every product leader must take AI seriously as a strategic imperative

notableQuotes.quote: Go back to basics. What's the core premise behind your product? Why do people use it? Then ask, 'Can AI do that?' For a lot, the answer is going to be yes.
notableQuotes.context: On a simple framework for thinking about AI's impact on your product

leaders.episodeSummary: Paul Adams shares Intercom's experience going all-in on AI, offering a simple framework: start with what your product does, then ask whether AI can do that — leading to either replacement or augmentation strategies. He also shares vulnerable stories of public failure including freezing on stage, and what a decade as CPO at Intercom has taught him about product leadership.
leadershipPrinciples: AI is a meteor coming toward you — if you don't explore it properly, it will leave you behind
Go back to basics: What does your product do? Why do people use it? Then ask: Can AI do that?
For some things AI will replace, for others it will augment — you must figure out which applies to you

leaders.name: Paul Millerd
leaders.title: Author
leaders.bio: Paul Millerd is the author of The Pathless Path: Imagining a New Story for Work and Life, exploring how to break free of the default career path and find more meaningful work.

notableQuotes.quote: Take three hours during a workday. Block off your schedule, sneak out. Go for a walk without a destination or do something from your childhood. And just pay attention. What is emerging?
notableQuotes.context: On the first practical step to exploring a different path for your life and work

notableQuotes.quote: A lot of people have never really thought about, why do you work? People say money. Okay, that's fine. But what else? Are you trying to be a good person? Do you see a good person as somebody that works every day?
notableQuotes.context: On questioning the deeply embedded scripts about work that most people never examine

leaders.episodeSummary: Paul Millerd explores how to break free of the default career path, sharing practical exercises like taking three unstructured hours during a workday to reconnect with what brings you alive. He challenges the deeply embedded scripts about work that most people never question, offering a framework for reimagining what work and life could look like beyond the conventional path.
leadershipPrinciples: Take three hours during a workday to do something unstructured — pay attention to what emerges
Most people have never really thought about why they work beyond money
The scripts about being a good worker are deeply embedded and rarely questioned

leaders.name: Pete Kazanjy
leaders.title: CEO & Author
leaders.bio: Pete Kazanjy is the CEO and founder of Atrium (sales analytics SaaS), author of Founding Sales (Lenny's favorite sales book), and founder of the Modern Sales Pros community, who learned sales by doing rather than from a traditional background.

notableQuotes.quote: Don't be afraid of sales. There's a lot of people who would love to tell you it's magical or 'you've got to be a born seller.' Those people are just talking their book.
notableQuotes.context: On encouraging founders and PMs to embrace sales as a learnable skill

notableQuotes.quote: Getting good at those behaviors is going to benefit you in a myriad of ways.
notableQuotes.context: On why sales skills are valuable far beyond the sales function

leaders.episodeSummary: Pete Kazanjy makes the case that founders should do sales themselves for an extended period before hiring, sharing tactical tips for getting better at sales without a traditional sales background. He covers when to hire your first salesperson, what to look for in their profile, common hiring mistakes, and why sales is a learnable skill that benefits every aspect of building a company.
leadershipPrinciples: Founders should do sales themselves for a long time before hiring their first salesperson
Don't be afraid of sales — people who say you need to be a born seller are just talking their book
Getting good at sales behaviors benefits you in a myriad of ways beyond closing deals

leaders.name: Peter Deng
leaders.title: Former VP of Product
leaders.bio: Peter Deng is one of the most impactful under-the-radar product leaders in tech: VP of Product at OpenAI overseeing ChatGPT, first Head of Product at Instagram, Head of Rider product at Uber, and builder of Facebook News Feed and Messenger.

notableQuotes.quote: You have to plan your chess moves out in advance. You have to really think before you act and build systems that were going to let you go sustainably faster.
notableQuotes.context: On what it takes to build something from idea to billions of users

notableQuotes.quote: Sometimes your product actually doesn't matter. At Uber, the price and the ETA was the product. We humans consume the entirety of the product.
notableQuotes.context: On the counterintuitive lesson that the UI features may not be what matters most

leaders.episodeSummary: Peter Deng shares lessons from building products used by billions across Facebook News Feed, Instagram, Uber, and ChatGPT at OpenAI. He reveals the counterintuitive insight that sometimes your product doesn't matter (at Uber, price and ETA were the real product) and why planning chess moves in advance with sustainable systems beats rushing to ship.
leadershipPrinciples: Plan your chess moves in advance — think before you act and build systems that let you go sustainably faster
Sometimes your product doesn't matter — at Uber the price and ETA were the real product
Humans consume the entirety of the product, not just the feature you're building

leaders.name: Petra Wille
leaders.title: Product Leadership Coach & Author
leaders.bio: Petra Wille is an independent product leadership coach and author of Strong Product People, who has spent over 10 years helping product teams boost their skill sets through one-on-one coaching, events, and writing.

notableQuotes.quote: Getting promoted is way harder if you're not good at telling stories and rallying the team behind a shared goal. I would consider it a bit of a career staller if you don't get to a decent level of storytelling.
notableQuotes.context: On why storytelling is a non-negotiable skill for PM career advancement

notableQuotes.quote: In some teams, I've seen the product person not being really good at it, but then the whole team helped creating these stories. So you can compensate to some extent.
notableQuotes.context: On how teams can collaborate on storytelling even when the PM isn't a natural storyteller

leaders.episodeSummary: Petra Wille shares her approach to coaching product managers, emphasizing that storytelling is a critical career skill that can stall your advancement if not developed. She covers how to become a better PM manager, why finding a PM community is invaluable, and how teams can collaborate on storytelling even when individual skills vary.
leadershipPrinciples: Storytelling is a career staller if you don't reach a decent level — promotions require rallying teams behind shared goals
The whole team can help create stories if the PM isn't great at it, but the PM should still develop the skill
Finding a PM community is one of the most valuable things you can do for your career

leaders.name: Phyl Terry
leaders.title: Author
leaders.bio: Phyl Terry is the author of Never Search Alone, widely referenced as the most impactful resource for finding a job, applying product-market fit thinking to the job search through candidate-market fit.
keyThemes: playing to win not to lose

notableQuotes.quote: When you're looking for a job, you need a spear and not a net. Just like product market fit — we've learned that trying to be for everyone doesn't work. We need a narrow, clear focus.
notableQuotes.context: On applying product thinking to the job search process

notableQuotes.quote: Most people don't think about what they want and what they don't want. When they get laid off, they spray and pray.
notableQuotes.context: On the most common and costly mistake in job searching

leaders.episodeSummary: Phyl Terry applies product-market fit thinking to job searching, arguing that you need a spear not a net — narrow focus and clarity about what you want and don't want. He introduces the concept of candidate-market fit and explains why most people fail in their job search by spraying and praying instead of playing to win with clear intentionality.
leadershipPrinciples: When looking for a job, use a spear, not a net — narrow, clear focus beats spray and pray
Finding candidate-market fit is like finding product-market fit for your career
Know what you want AND what you don't want before starting your search

leaders.name: Raaz Herzberg
leaders.title: CMO & VP of Product Strategy
leaders.bio: Raaz Herzberg is CMO and VP of Product Strategy at Wiz, one of the fastest-growing startups in history. She was the first PM at Wiz and previously led security products at Microsoft including Azure Sentinel.

notableQuotes.quote: I was hired as the first product manager. I still did not exactly understand what we were going to build. At some point it was like, 'I have to ask, what exactly are we doing here?' And that ended up pivoting us to cloud security.
notableQuotes.context: On how asking a simple question as the first PM helped pivot Wiz to their winning product

notableQuotes.quote: Naturally, as human beings, you have a bias to look for affirmation, versus a bias for what you don't want to hear.
notableQuotes.context: On the danger of confirmation bias during customer discovery

leaders.episodeSummary: Raaz Herzberg shares the inside story of Wiz's early days — doing 10-15 customer meetings per day, pivoting six weeks in when she asked 'what exactly are we building,' and learning to detect real product-market fit signals when customers shift from explaining problems to asking about pricing. She also discusses her unusual journey from first PM to CMO at one of the fastest-growing startups ever.
leadershipPrinciples: When customers start asking about pricing and POVs instead of explaining their problems, you've found product-market fit
Do 10-15 customer meetings per day in the early days — volume of conversations accelerates discovery
As a PM, if you don't understand what you're building, ask directly — that question can pivot the company

leaders.name: Rachel Lockett
leaders.title: Executive Coach
leaders.company: Former HR Leader at Pinterest & Stripe
leaders.bio: Rachel Lockett is an executive coach and former longtime HR leader at Pinterest and Stripe, working with CEOs, founders, and tech leaders on emotional intelligence, resilience, vision-setting, and building trusted teams.
keyThemes: leaders don't need all the answers

notableQuotes.quote: Most leaders assume they have to have all the answers. But great leaders know that when you try to advise and have the answer all the time, you're training your team to come to you with all of the hard problems.
notableQuotes.context: On the biggest gap keeping technical leaders from being successful

notableQuotes.quote: People, when they want to have a conflict, come in ready to prove their point. Actually, the goal of any conflict is to create mutual understanding.
notableQuotes.context: On reframing the purpose of difficult conversations

leaders.episodeSummary: Rachel Lockett shares coaching frameworks for tech leaders, challenging the assumption that leaders need all the answers and that work is purely logical. She explains how having answers all the time actually disempowers teams, why the goal of conflict is mutual understanding rather than winning, and practical approaches to avoiding burnout and having difficult conversations.
leadershipPrinciples: When you try to have all the answers, you train your team to bring you all the hard problems instead of solving them
The goal of any conflict is to create mutual understanding, not to convince the other person they're wrong
Tech operates on a misguided belief that work is purely logical — professionals have feelings

leaders.name: Rahul Vohra
leaders.title: Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Rahul Vohra is the founder and CEO of Superhuman, known for being one of the most thoughtful and articulate founders in tech, famous for his product-market fit framework and craft-focused approach to product development.
keyThemes: building for specific users not all users

notableQuotes.quote: You have to deliberately not act on the feedback of many of your early users. We're here to make something that people want, but it can't be all people.
notableQuotes.context: On the counterintuitive approach to finding product-market fit

notableQuotes.quote: Your calendar says what you thought you were going to do, but it's really only your trail of work that describes what you actually did.
notableQuotes.context: On his 'switch lock' technique for CEO time management

leaders.episodeSummary: Rahul Vohra shares his counterintuitive approach to product-market fit: deliberately ignoring feedback from many early users to focus on the ones who matter most. He introduces the 'switch lock' technique for CEO time management and explains why he spends his time on product and design rather than the typical CEO activities of hiring and org building.
leadershipPrinciples: You have to deliberately not act on the feedback of many of your early users — it can't be all people
Your calendar says what you thought you'd do, but your trail of work describes what you actually did
CEOs should spend time on product and marketing design, not just hiring and org building

leaders.name: Ramesh Johari
leaders.title: Professor
leaders.bio: Ramesh Johari is a Stanford professor specializing in data science for online marketplaces, having advised Airbnb, Uber, Stripe, Bumble, Stitch Fix, Upwork, and many other major marketplace businesses.
keyThemes: winners and losers in marketplace changes

notableQuotes.quote: Marketplaces are a little bit like whac-a-mole. Many of the changes that are most consequential create winners and losers. Rolling with those changes is about recognizing whether the winners are more important to your business than the losers.
notableQuotes.context: On the fundamental challenge of marketplace optimization

notableQuotes.quote: You fix one side's experience and then you're like, 'Wait a second — now the other side is having a worse experience,' and your metrics keep moving around.
notableQuotes.context: On why marketplace changes always have second-order effects on the other side

leaders.episodeSummary: Ramesh Johari brings an academic and practical perspective to marketplace building, explaining why marketplace management is fundamentally a whac-a-mole game where every improvement creates winners and losers. Drawing on his work with Airbnb, Uber, Stripe, and others, he covers how to fuel marketplace flywheels, design better review systems, and why AI will transform experimentation in marketplaces.
leadershipPrinciples: Marketplace management is a game of whac-a-mole — moving attention and inventory creates winners and losers
Recognize whether the winners you've created are more important than the losers in the process
Don't think of yourself as a marketplace founder — think of yourself simply as a founder

leaders.name: Ravi Mehta
leaders.title: Product Leader & Coach
leaders.company: Former CPO at Tinder / Product at Facebook, Tripadvisor
leaders.bio: Ravi Mehta is a product leader and coach, former CPO at Tinder, and product leader at Facebook and Tripadvisor, known for his frameworks on PM competency assessment and leadership coaching.

notableQuotes.quote: Your ideal goal is to lead in a scalable way — you feel confident about direction and your team has autonomy. But there's another effective way: selective micromanagement.
notableQuotes.context: On the leadership matrix he uses when coaching product leaders

notableQuotes.quote: If you don't feel confident in the direction your team is moving, the right answer is not to be hands-off. The right answer is to micromanage, but do it in a very tactical and temporary way.
notableQuotes.context: On when micromanagement is actually the right leadership approach

leaders.episodeSummary: Ravi Mehta introduces his scalable leadership matrix, arguing that selective micromanagement is sometimes the right approach when you lack confidence in your team's direction — a contrarian view in a culture that demonizes micromanagement. He shares frameworks for PM competency assessment and explains how to lead differently based on your confidence level and team capability.
leadershipPrinciples: The ideal is scalable leadership — feeling confident about direction while your team has autonomy
Selective micromanagement is the right answer when you don't feel confident in your team's direction
Micromanage tactically and temporarily to help teams understand the right direction, then pull back

leaders.name: Ray Cao
leaders.title: Global Head of Monetization Product Strategy & Operations
leaders.bio: Ray Cao is the Global Head of Monetization Product Strategy and Operations at TikTok, where he has spent over four years. Previously he spent six years at Google helping scale Google Shopping globally.

notableQuotes.quote: The number one thing is context, no control. That's the reason why we're always encouraging people to see themselves as a business owner.
notableQuotes.context: On TikTok's core operating principle

notableQuotes.quote: If you don't really see the full picture, you won't be able to make the Lego as one thing at the end of the day. You have to see the other pieces.
notableQuotes.context: On why TikTok gives employees full context to make autonomous decisions

leaders.episodeSummary: Ray Cao provides a rare inside look at TikTok's operating culture, centered on 'context, no control' — giving people all the information they need and encouraging them to act as business owners. Drawing on his experience scaling monetization at both TikTok and Google Shopping, he explains how TikTok's unique approach to autonomy and context-sharing drives its rapid execution.
leadershipPrinciples: Context, no control — encourage people to see themselves as business owners
Give people all the information they need and let them act without specific instructions
You have to see the full picture to solve the puzzle — like building Legos without the picture on the box

leaders.name: Richard Rumelt
leaders.title: Professor & Author
leaders.company: UCLA / Author of Good Strategy Bad Strategy
leaders.bio: Richard Rumelt is a legendary strategy professor and author of Good Strategy Bad Strategy and The Crux, widely considered among the most important books on strategy ever written.

notableQuotes.quote: Don't call it strategy, call it an action agenda. Begin to try to identify the one or two key challenges that can actually be addressed and what are we going to do about it?
notableQuotes.context: On cutting through strategy theater to actual strategic thinking

notableQuotes.quote: There are huge numbers of people willing to sell you advice on mission and vision and values, all these things that have to be in place before strategy. That's not true.
notableQuotes.context: On why most strategy advice is backwards

leaders.episodeSummary: Richard Rumelt, author of Good Strategy Bad Strategy and The Crux, argues that most strategy is theater — focused on mission, vision, and values when it should be focused on identifying the crux (the one or two key challenges that can actually be addressed) and defining coherent actions to tackle them. He reframes strategy as an action agenda rather than aspirational planning.
leadershipPrinciples: Don't call it strategy — call it an action agenda focused on one or two key addressable challenges
Huge numbers of people sell advice on mission, vision, and values as prerequisites for strategy — that's not true
The essence of strategic thinking is identifying key challenges and defining coherent actions to address them

leaders.name: Robby Stein
leaders.title: VP of Product
leaders.bio: Robby Stein is VP of Product for Google Search, responsible for AI Overviews, AI Mode, Google Lens, and the ranking algorithm. Previously Head of Product at Instagram where he launched Stories, Reels, and Close Friends, growing it to 500M DAUs.

notableQuotes.quote: The core Google search isn't really changing. People want a specific phone number, a price, directions. The vastness of that is underappreciated. AI is expansionary — there's more curiosity being fulfilled now.
notableQuotes.context: On why AI enhances rather than threatens Google Search

notableQuotes.quote: What I'm feeling now is just an incredible sense of focus and urgency. Things have hit a tipping point where these models are now truly able to deliver for consumers.
notableQuotes.context: On the shift in energy at Google as AI models mature

leaders.episodeSummary: Robby Stein shares lessons from building products at massive scale — launching Instagram Stories and Reels to grow Instagram to 500M DAUs, and now leading Google Search through its AI transformation. He argues that AI is expansionary for search rather than threatening, and reveals his philosophy of relentless improvement that has driven success across both Instagram and Google.
leadershipPrinciples: AI is expansionary — there are more questions being asked and curiosity fulfilled, not less
Embody relentless improvement in everything you build
The vastness of what people use search for is underappreciated — AI expands it further

leaders.name: Roger Martin
leaders.title: Professor Emeritus & Strategy Advisor
leaders.company: Rotman School of Management / Author of Playing to Win
leaders.bio: Roger Martin is the world's #1 ranked management thinker (Thinkers50), professor emeritus at Rotman School of Management, and author of Playing to Win, considered one of the most important books on strategy.
keyThemes: playing to win vs playing not to lose
where to play and how to win

notableQuotes.quote: You have to have answers to five questions: What's your winning aspiration? Where to play? How can you win? What capabilities must you have? And what enabling management systems do you need?
notableQuotes.context: On the strategy choice cascade framework from Playing to Win

notableQuotes.quote: What's taught now in business schools generally sucks. People aren't prepared educationally, and they sure don't get prepared for it in companies. Strategy is intellectually challenging and emotionally intimidating.
notableQuotes.context: On why so many people are bad at strategy

leaders.episodeSummary: Roger Martin, ranked the world's #1 management thinker, shares his strategy choice cascade: five questions every company must answer to win. He explains why most strategy education fails, why strategy is both intellectually challenging and emotionally intimidating, and the critical difference between playing to win and playing not to lose.
leadershipPrinciples: Answer five questions: winning aspiration, where to play, how to win, required capabilities, and enabling management systems
What's taught in business schools about strategy generally sucks — people aren't prepared
Strategy is intellectually challenging and emotionally intimidating — that's why most people avoid it

leaders.name: Ronny Kohavi
leaders.title: World Expert on A/B Testing
leaders.company: Former VP at Airbnb / Microsoft / Amazon
leaders.bio: Ronny Kohavi is widely considered the world's foremost expert on A/B testing, having led experimentation at Airbnb, Microsoft (where he built the Experimentation Platform), and Amazon, now consulting and teaching experimentation.

notableQuotes.quote: Any code change that you make, any feature that you introduce has to be in some experiment. Even small bug fixes, even small changes can sometimes have surprising, unexpected impact.
notableQuotes.context: On his test-everything philosophy developed across Amazon, Microsoft, and Airbnb

notableQuotes.quote: If you go for something big, try it out, but be ready to fail 80% of the time.
notableQuotes.context: On why teams must embrace failure as the norm when running high-risk experiments

leaders.episodeSummary: Ronny Kohavi, the world's foremost A/B testing expert, makes the case for testing everything — including small bug fixes that can have surprising impact. Drawing on his experience building experimentation platforms at Amazon, Microsoft, and Airbnb, he explains why most experiments fail, how to allocate between safe and high-risk bets, and why it's impossible to experiment too much.
leadershipPrinciples: Test everything — any code change or feature must be in some experiment, because even small bug fixes can have surprising impact
It's not possible to experiment too much — the culture of testing should be pervasive
Allocate some experiments to high-risk, high-reward ideas that are most likely to fail but could be home runs

leaders.name: Ryan Hoover
leaders.title: Founder & Investor
leaders.bio: Ryan Hoover is the founder of Product Hunt, former product manager, and full-time investor at Weekend Fund, known for his writing on building products and communities.

notableQuotes.quote: That flutter in your stomach that you wake up with in the morning of just anxiety and stress and worry. Being a CEO or founder makes it slightly harder because you still have to put on this mask of confidence.
notableQuotes.context: On the emotional reality of being a founder that few people discuss openly

notableQuotes.quote: You don't want to subject them to the same anxiety that you're feeling and be 100% transparent.
notableQuotes.context: On calibrating transparency as a leader

leaders.episodeSummary: Ryan Hoover opens up about the emotional reality of building Product Hunt — the anxiety, the mask of confidence founders wear, and the tension between transparency and protecting your team. He shares lessons from building one of the most influential product-discovery communities and his transition from founder to investor at Weekend Fund.
leadershipPrinciples: Being a CEO means putting on a mask of confidence while feeling anxiety and stress internally
You don't want to subject your team to the same anxiety you're feeling as a founder
Being 100% transparent as a leader isn't always the right answer — calibrate what you share

leaders.name: Ryan J. Salva
leaders.title: VP of Product
leaders.bio: Ryan J. Salva is VP of Product at GitHub, where he incubated and launched GitHub Copilot — one of the most significant advances in developer productivity — using OpenAI's models trained on GitHub's public code repositories.

notableQuotes.quote: We took that same data snapshot and brought it to our friends at OpenAI to see what we can do with large language models built on public code. It turns out we can do some pretty cool things.
notableQuotes.context: On the origin story of GitHub Copilot emerging from the Arctic Code Vault project

notableQuotes.quote: We had put this snapshot of public repositories on silver film preserved for thousands of years in this Arctic Code Vault.
notableQuotes.context: On how preserving the world's open source code led to the idea for Copilot

leaders.episodeSummary: Ryan Salva tells the origin story of GitHub Copilot — born from an Arctic Code Vault project that preserved the world's public code, which was then fed to OpenAI's models. He shares lessons on incubating big product bets within a large company like Microsoft, navigating ethics and business model challenges, and taking a prototype from a small R&D team to massive scale.
leadershipPrinciples: Take a snapshot of existing assets and ask 'what can we do with this?' to discover breakthrough products
Incubating big bets at a large company requires protecting the team while navigating business model and ethics questions
Non-traditional backgrounds can be an advantage in product innovation

leaders.name: Ryan Singer
leaders.title: Author & Product Leader
leaders.bio: Ryan Singer was one of the first hires at 37signals (Basecamp), where he spent 17 years building product. He wrote Shape Up, which introduced a fundamentally different approach to building software using appetites, shaping, and fixed-time cycles.
keyThemes: see the end from the beginning

notableQuotes.quote: We are not going to start something unless we can see the end from the beginning. We're not going to take a big concept and say, 'What's the estimate for this thing?'
notableQuotes.context: On the core principle of Shape Up — shaping before building

notableQuotes.quote: If you're doing a home renovation and you haven't checked if there's electricity in that wall, it's going to drastically change the cost and the time.
notableQuotes.context: On why de-risking projects upfront through shaping is essential

leaders.episodeSummary: Ryan Singer introduces the Shape Up methodology from his 17 years at 37signals, which flips traditional product development: instead of estimating how long an idea takes, you set a maximum time appetite and shape an idea that fits. He explains why you should never start building unless you can see the end from the beginning, and why bringing design, engineering, and product together to shape before building avoids the most costly project risks.
leadershipPrinciples: Don't start building unless you can see the end from the beginning
Set the maximum time you're willing to spend, then shape an idea that fits — not the other way around
Bring design, engineering, and product together to shape the plan before writing any code

leaders.name: Sachin Monga
leaders.title: Head of Product
leaders.bio: Sachin Monga is Head of Product at Substack, previously a founder (Cocoon, acquired by Substack) and spent seven years at Facebook working on video, camera, developer platform, and ads growth.

notableQuotes.quote: We're just starting into this golden era of what it might mean to be a writer on the internet. The economic model for supporting great writing has been generally pretty terrible for the entirety of the internet's history.
notableQuotes.context: On Substack's mission to transform the economics of writing

notableQuotes.quote: People who are able to make a living, maybe even make a fortune just doing great work and not needing to have millions of viewers or play the attention games of other networks.
notableQuotes.context: On the new generation of Substack writers succeeding with quality over scale

leaders.episodeSummary: Sachin Monga discusses Substack's mission to create a golden era for writers on the internet, where quality work can generate a living without playing attention games. He reveals the story behind the Substack recommendations feature — potentially one of the most legendary growth features ever — and shares how building at a startup differs fundamentally from his seven years at Facebook.
leadershipPrinciples: The economic model for great writing on the internet has been terrible — Substack proves it doesn't have to be
You don't need millions of viewers — a small number of people who value your work highly is enough
Quality over attention: don't play attention games, just do really high quality work

leaders.name: Sahil Mansuri
leaders.title: CEO & Founder
leaders.bio: Sahil Mansuri is CEO and founder of Bravado, which has built the world's largest online sales community of 300,000+ salespeople, known for his unique perspective on sales strategy and founder-led selling.

notableQuotes.quote: When you have limited visibility, set up a really conservative plan and then have milestones — short-term milestones that unlock the ability to lean into growth based on hitting those targets.
notableQuotes.context: On how to plan sales strategy during a downturn

notableQuotes.quote: You don't want to be unreasonably conservative because you don't want to be floundering from 'we're screwed' to 'everything's better' and back.
notableQuotes.context: On finding the balance between caution and paralysis in uncertain markets

leaders.episodeSummary: Sahil Mansuri shares tactical advice for adapting sales strategy during market downturns, including setting conservative plans with milestone-based growth unlocks and refocusing on retention over acquisition. Drawing on experience building the world's largest sales community, he covers quotas, comp plans, forecasting, and founder-led selling techniques including cold emailing Sheryl Sandberg.
leadershipPrinciples: When you have limited visibility, set a conservative plan with short-term milestones that unlock growth spending
Don't flail between 'we're screwed' and 'everything's better' — have a stable plan with unlock triggers
In downturns, refocus on retention and existing customers rather than pure acquisition

leaders.name: Sam Lessin
leaders.title: Partner
leaders.bio: Sam Lessin is a partner at Slow Ventures, former VP of Product at Facebook, and two-time founder, known for his unconventional advice on professional etiquette and interpersonal dynamics in tech.
keyThemes: showing up with low heart rate

notableQuotes.quote: Etiquette is a skill for how to show up in a room with a low heart rate. Show up with the self-confidence and the calm of abundance.
notableQuotes.context: On why professional etiquette matters for founders and tech leaders

notableQuotes.quote: Young people have been holed up in a room coding and they show up encouraged by Silicon Valley to be abrasive on purpose. You want people to say, 'This is someone I can work with and trust.'
notableQuotes.context: On why tech culture's celebration of abrasiveness undermines founders

leaders.episodeSummary: Sam Lessin offers unconventional advice on professional etiquette for founders, arguing that showing up with a low heart rate and the calm of abundance is far more effective than the desperate transactional energy most young founders bring to networking. Drawing on experience as Facebook VP of Product and venture investor, he explains why nobody is teaching founders the basic social skills that build lasting trust.
leadershipPrinciples: Etiquette is a skill for showing up in a room with a low heart rate — calm and confident
Show up with the self-confidence and calm of abundance, not the desperation of scarcity
If you show up like an energizer bunny at networking events, you'll scare people off

leaders.name: Sam Schillace
leaders.title: Corporate VP & Deputy CTO
leaders.bio: Sam Schillace is Corporate VP and Deputy CTO at Microsoft leading consumer products, infrastructure, and AI. He is most known for inventing Google Docs through his company Writely, which became the foundation for Google Workspace (1B+ monthly users).
keyThemes: doing what you feel guilty getting paid for
work doesn't have to be hard

notableQuotes.quote: You should go do the thing that you feel guilty to get paid for. If you get pleasure from doing something that people want to pay you for, do it the best you can do it, as hard as you can do it.
notableQuotes.context: On career advice based on decades of experience from Google Docs to Microsoft AI

notableQuotes.quote: We tend to undervalue the things we're good at. We think work has to be unpleasant. So if something is easy and fun, we don't think it's valuable.
notableQuotes.context: On why people choose careers that don't match their strengths

leaders.episodeSummary: Sam Schillace shares the origin story of Google Docs — from three rented Windows servers in Texas to a billion monthly users — and his counterintuitive career advice: do the thing you feel guilty getting paid for. He argues that most people undervalue their natural strengths because they believe work must be unpleasant, and that following your pleasure leads to better outcomes than grinding through discomfort.
leadershipPrinciples: Do the thing you feel guilty getting paid for — if something is easy and fun, that's your strength
We undervalue things we're good at because we think work has to be unpleasant
If you get pleasure from doing something people want to pay you for, do the hell out of it

leaders.name: Sanchan Saxena
leaders.title: VP of Product
leaders.bio: Sanchan Saxena is VP of Product at Coinbase, previously Head of Product at Airbnb, Head of Product for Instagram Ads and Instagram Shopping, and a product leader at Yahoo and Microsoft. He has worked with Brian Chesky, Brian Armstrong, Zuck, and Kevin Systrom.
keyThemes: when to A/B test vs not

notableQuotes.quote: I don't think I've worked with a harder working PM, particularly someone who's incredibly kind and nice and generous.
notableQuotes.context: Lenny describing Sanchan's rare combination of hard work and kindness

notableQuotes.quote: We cover what he's learned from working with some of today's best CEOs, including Brian Chesky, Brian Armstrong, Zuck and Kevin Systrom.
notableQuotes.context: On the breadth of visionary leaders Sanchan has worked closely with

leaders.episodeSummary: Sanchan Saxena shares lessons from working with four of tech's most visionary CEOs — Brian Chesky, Brian Armstrong, Zuck, and Kevin Systrom — across Airbnb, Coinbase, Instagram, and Facebook. He covers navigating Airbnb through COVID when travel completely stopped, how to set up product development processes at startups, when to A/B test versus ship on conviction, and what to look for when hiring PMs.
leadershipPrinciples: Working with visionary CEOs like Chesky, Armstrong, Zuck, and Systrom teaches different leadership styles
COVID hitting Airbnb when travel stopped was the ultimate test of product leadership under crisis
Know when to A/B test and when to just ship based on conviction

leaders.name: Sander Schulhoff
leaders.title: AI Security Researcher
leaders.bio: Sander Schulhoff is a leading researcher in adversarial robustness who runs the biggest AI red teaming competition, works with frontier AI labs on model defenses, and teaches the leading course on AI security.
keyThemes: prompt engineering is real and matters
bad prompts vs good prompts impact

notableQuotes.quote: Studies have shown that using bad prompts can get you down to 0% on a problem, and good prompts can boost you up to 90%. People will always be saying 'it's dead' but then it comes out and it's not.
notableQuotes.context: On why prompt engineering continues to matter despite claims of its death

notableQuotes.quote: A set of techniques we call self-criticism: you ask the LLM to check its response, criticize itself, and then improve itself.
notableQuotes.context: On one of the most effective prompting techniques from analyzing 1,500 papers

leaders.episodeSummary: Sander Schulhoff, the OG prompt engineer, shares findings from The Prompt Report — the most comprehensive study of prompt engineering ever done, analyzing 1,500 papers and identifying 200 techniques. He demonstrates why prompt engineering matters enormously (bad prompts = 0%, good prompts = 90%), shares the most effective techniques like self-criticism, and explains prompt injection and red teaming.
leadershipPrinciples: Bad prompts can get 0% on a problem while good prompts can boost to 90% — prompt engineering matters
Self-criticism techniques — asking the LLM to check and improve its own response — are highly effective
Prompt engineering isn't dead and won't be with the next model — it keeps being important

leaders.name: Sarah Tavel
leaders.title: Partner
leaders.bio: Sarah Tavel is a partner at Benchmark, one of the most preeminent VC funds, focusing on consumer and marketplace startups. She was the first product manager at Pinterest and thinks like a product/growth leader despite her VC role.
keyThemes: markets as currents not bodies of water
dynamics of change over market size

notableQuotes.quote: A lot of people think about markets like bodies of water. I think the most interesting markets are like currents — there's something happening that's going to pull you forward. A plank of wood on the river will make progress.
notableQuotes.context: On her framework for evaluating market opportunity

notableQuotes.quote: We care less about market size because what you're looking for are the dynamics of change — the current and momentum that makes the founders' job easier.
notableQuotes.context: On why Benchmark focuses on market dynamics over TAM

leaders.episodeSummary: Sarah Tavel, partner at Benchmark and first PM at Pinterest, shares her framework for evaluating markets: think of them as currents rather than bodies of water, where the dynamics of change matter more than total size. She explains why market momentum pulls companies forward more effectively than building bigger boats in still water, drawing on experience investing in consumer and marketplace startups.
leadershipPrinciples: Think of markets like currents, not bodies of water — look for dynamics of change that pull you forward
Market size matters less than market momentum and the current driving the opportunity
A plank of wood on a fast current beats a big fancy boat in still water

leaders.name: Scott Belsky
leaders.title: Chief Strategy Officer & EVP
leaders.bio: Scott Belsky is CSO and EVP of Design and Emerging Products at Adobe, founder of Behance, author of The Messy Middle, and angel investor in Pinterest, Uber, Airtable, Flexport, and Warby Parker.

notableQuotes.quote: How much conviction do you have in the solution you're building? Knowing all you know now, do you have more or less conviction?
notableQuotes.context: On his go-to advice for founders deciding whether to continue or quit

notableQuotes.quote: If you've lost conviction, you should not be doing what you're doing. Quit. Your life is short. Pivot. Do something completely different.
notableQuotes.context: On when it's time to walk away from a startup

leaders.episodeSummary: Scott Belsky shares his conviction test for founders stuck in the messy middle: if you have more conviction now than when you started despite failures, persist — you're just in the messy middle. If you've lost conviction, quit immediately. Drawing on his journey from founding Behance to CPO at Adobe, he offers frameworks for enduring the hardest phase of building a company.
leadershipPrinciples: Ask yourself: knowing what I know now, do I have more or less conviction? That tells you whether to continue
If you have more conviction despite failures, you're in the messy middle — stick with it
If you've lost conviction, quit — your life is short, pivot and do something different

leaders.name: Scott Wu
leaders.title: Co-founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Scott Wu is co-founder and CEO of Cognition, which created Devin — the world's first autonomous AI software engineer. Their 15-person engineering team uses Devin to build Devin, with a quarter of their PRs committed by AI.

notableQuotes.quote: Our whole team is only 15 engineers. Most folks are working with up to five Devins at once. Devin merges several hundred pull requests into production every month.
notableQuotes.context: On how Cognition uses AI agents to dramatically multiply their small team's output

notableQuotes.quote: It's in the neighborhood of a quarter or so. We expect it to be a decent bit more than half by the end of the year.
notableQuotes.context: On the trajectory of AI-authored code at Cognition

leaders.episodeSummary: Scott Wu reveals how Cognition's 15-person engineering team uses Devin (their autonomous AI software engineer) to build Devin itself, with each engineer running up to five Devins simultaneously. Currently a quarter of their PRs are AI-authored, projected to exceed half by year's end, offering a glimpse into how AI agents will transform software development.
leadershipPrinciples: Use your own AI product to build your AI product — dogfooding at the deepest level
Each engineer working with up to five Devins simultaneously multiplies the team's output
AI PRs will go from 25% to over 50% within a year — plan for this acceleration

leaders.name: Sean Ellis
leaders.title: Growth Pioneer & Author
leaders.company: Author of Hacking Growth / Former Head of Growth at Dropbox & Eventbrite
leaders.bio: Sean Ellis coined the term 'growth hacking,' invented the ICE framework, developed the Sean Ellis test for product-market fit, was head of growth at Dropbox and Eventbrite, and co-founded LogMeIn (sold for $4B+).
keyThemes: when to grow vs when to fix PMF
