notableQuotes.quote: How would you feel if you could no longer use this product? Once you got a high enough percentage saying they'd be very disappointed, most of those products did pretty well.
notableQuotes.context: On the Sean Ellis test that transformed how startups measure product-market fit

notableQuotes.quote: Ignore the people who say they'd be somewhat disappointed. They're telling you it's a nice to have. If you start tweaking based on their feedback, you're going to dilute it for your must-have users.
notableQuotes.context: On the counterintuitive advice to focus only on 'very disappointed' users

leaders.episodeSummary: Sean Ellis shares the origin and application of his famous product-market fit test (how would you feel if you could no longer use this product?), the ICE prioritization framework, and why you should ignore 'somewhat disappointed' users who tell you your product is merely nice-to-have. He covers when to invest in growth versus when to fix product-market fit first.
leadershipPrinciples: Ask users 'how would you feel if you could no longer use this product?' — very disappointed = product-market fit
Ignore 'somewhat disappointed' users — they're telling you it's a nice-to-have that could dilute your must-have
Don't invest in growth until you've validated product-market fit through the disappointed user test

leaders.name: Seth Godin
leaders.title: Author & Entrepreneur
leaders.company: Author of 21 books including 18 international bestsellers
leaders.bio: Seth Godin is a legendary author (21 books, 18 bestsellers), daily blogger for almost 10,000 days, entrepreneur (Yoyodyne, Squidoo, altMBA), and former product manager whose work on how ideas spread has influenced millions.
keyThemes: AI will stop being a feature
tension as the heart of innovation

notableQuotes.quote: AI very soon is going to stop being a feature the same way electricity is not a feature. What AI companies need to do is say, what's in this for the user?
notableQuotes.context: On how AI companies should think about brand differentiation

notableQuotes.quote: Tension is at the heart of every art form and every innovation. When we launch a new product, the person imagines what their life might be like if it were true.
notableQuotes.context: On why tension drives both strategy and product adoption

leaders.episodeSummary: Seth Godin shares his perspective that AI will soon stop being a feature (like electricity) and companies must focus on the promise they make to users. He explores how tension is at the heart of every innovation and art form, how to develop taste, and how to build brands in an increasingly AI-saturated world — all grounded in his experience as a former PM turned legendary author and thinker.
leadershipPrinciples: AI will soon stop being a feature, just like electricity — focus on what's in it for the user
Tension is at the heart of every art form and every innovation
Make a difficult, remarkable promise to your users, then figure out how to keep it

leaders.name: Shaun Clowes
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Shaun Clowes is CPO at Confluent, previously CPO at MuleSoft (billion-dollar Salesforce business) and Metromile, with six years at Atlassian where he ran Jira Agile and built the first B2B growth team. He created popular Reforge courses on retention and data.

notableQuotes.quote: Product management is still such a relatively undeveloped discipline. We're 15 to 20 years into this. If we were doctors, you'd be like, 'That's totally unacceptable.'
notableQuotes.context: On why the state of PM craft is still immature

notableQuotes.quote: Always talk from the customer's perspective, the market's perspective, the competitor's perspective. The very small number of PMs do that. Most get dragged into internal politics.
notableQuotes.context: On what separates great PMs from the rest

leaders.episodeSummary: Shaun Clowes argues that most PMs are not good because the discipline is still underdeveloped, and the fix is simple: always talk from the customer's, market's, and competitor's perspective instead of getting dragged into internal politics. He shares his Bingo card approach to career development, lessons from building the first B2B growth team at Atlassian, and why AI's biggest PM impact will be data management.
leadershipPrinciples: Product management is still underdeveloped — if PMs were doctors, the state would be unacceptable
Always talk from the customer's, market's, and competitor's perspective — the very small number of PMs do this
Most PMs get dragged into internal politics and scrum management — you can't win that way

leaders.name: Shishir Mehrotra
leaders.title: Co-founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Shishir Mehrotra is co-founder and CEO of Coda, former leader of YouTube product, engineering, and design at Google (6+ years), former Microsoft (6 years), and board member at Spotify. Known as an incredibly deep first-principles thinker.

notableQuotes.quote: I generally value the reference check over interview signals. Those people worked with this person sometimes for years — what you get out of 30 minutes of artificial scenarios is never going to compare.
notableQuotes.context: On why reference checks are the most important hiring signal

notableQuotes.quote: Great teams are defined by their rituals, not just their strategies.
notableQuotes.context: On his ongoing collection of rituals from the best leaders in tech

leaders.episodeSummary: Shishir Mehrotra shares three powerful frameworks: Blue Loops vs Black Loops for growth strategy, Eigenquestions for finding the one question that determines all others, and Rituals of Great Teams as the secret behind high-performing organizations. He makes the case that reference checks are far more valuable than interviews, drawing on experience leading YouTube at Google and building Coda.
leadershipPrinciples: Reference checks are the best signal in hiring — years of working together beats 30 minutes of artificial scenarios
Great teams are defined by their rituals, not just their strategies
Eigenquestions help you find the one question whose answer determines all other answers

leaders.name: Shreya Shankar
leaders.title: AI Researcher and Educator
leaders.bio: AI researcher and co-creator of the definitive online course on evals (the number one course on Maven), who has taught over 2,000 PMs and engineers across 500 companies including OpenAI and Anthropic, known for making evals approachable and actionable for product teams.
keyThemes: evals as spectrum of quality measurement
actionable product improvement over perfect evals
new user cohort discovery through data
practical eval methodology for product builders

notableQuotes.quote: The goal is not to do evals perfectly, it's to actionably improve your product.
notableQuotes.context: On the practical philosophy behind building evals

notableQuotes.quote: People have been burned by evals in the past. People have done evals badly, so then they didn't trust it anymore, and then they're like, 'Oh, I'm anti evals.'
notableQuotes.context: On why there is so much controversy around evals in the AI community

notableQuotes.quote: Evals could also be a way of looking at your data regularly to find these new cohorts of people. You think, 'Oh, there's a different way you want to accommodate this new group of people.'
notableQuotes.context: On evals as a discovery mechanism for new user segments

leaders.episodeSummary: Shreya Shankar (alongside Hamel Husain) demystifies evals for AI product builders, explaining that evals are a broad spectrum of quality measurement far beyond simple unit tests. She emphasizes that the goal is actionable product improvement rather than perfect evaluation, explains how evals can discover new user cohorts you didn't know existed, and addresses the anti-eval sentiment that arises when teams have been burned by poorly implemented eval processes. The conversation provides a practical, accessible entry point for PMs and engineers new to building evals.
leadershipPrinciples: The goal is not to do evals perfectly, it's to actionably improve your product — perfection is the enemy of useful measurement
Evals are a big spectrum of ways to measure application quality — unit tests are a very small part of that very big puzzle
People have been burned by evals in the past and done them badly, which creates anti-eval sentiment — the solution is making the process approachable and practical

leaders.name: Shreyas Doshi
leaders.title: Product Leader & Advisor
leaders.company: Former PM at Stripe, Google, Twitter, Yahoo
leaders.bio: Shreyas Doshi is one of the most influential product management voices on the internet, known for sharing contrarian and memorable wisdom about PM craft. He held IC and management roles at Stripe, Google, Twitter, and Yahoo.

notableQuotes.quote: Most execution problems are really strategy problems.
notableQuotes.context: On why teams that think they have an execution issue often have a strategy issue

notableQuotes.quote: There's no one out there today who shares more wisdom, more consistently on the art of product management than Shreyas Doshi.
notableQuotes.context: Lenny's description of Shreyas's unique position in the PM community

leaders.episodeSummary: Shreyas Doshi goes deep on five of his most impactful ideas: the power of pre-mortems, how to best use PM time, the three levels of product work and how confusing them creates team tension, why most execution problems are really strategy problems, and a common prioritization pitfall. His contrarian, memorable frameworks have made him one of the most influential voices in product management.
leadershipPrinciples: Most execution problems are actually strategy problems in disguise
Understanding the three levels of product work prevents tension on your team
Pre-mortems are more powerful than post-mortems because you can still change the outcome

leaders.name: Shweta Shrivastava
leaders.title: Senior Director of Product Management
leaders.bio: Shweta Shrivastava is Senior Director of Product Management at Waymo (self-driving cars), previously CPO at Nauto, Head of Product at AWS for database and analytics services, and a product leader at Cisco.

notableQuotes.quote: Are you proactively trying to challenge your own assumptions? If there's no conflict, if there's no contention, then something is missing.
notableQuotes.context: On the mindset required for product leadership at safety-critical companies like Waymo

notableQuotes.quote: As a seasoned product leader, if you're not doing enough of that, then I think you might not be listening.
notableQuotes.context: On why constant assumption-challenging is the mark of a mature PM

leaders.episodeSummary: Shweta Shrivastava shares what it's like to do product management at Waymo, where the stakes of getting things wrong involve physical safety rather than just user experience. She explains how PM for self-driving cars differs from software-only products, why healthy contention is essential, and her principle that if there's no conflict in your product process, you're not challenging assumptions enough.
leadershipPrinciples: If there's no conflict and no contention, something is missing — proactively challenge your assumptions
Being a seasoned product leader means constantly questioning whether you're really listening
PM for physical products is both different from and similar to software-only products

leaders.name: Sri Batchu
leaders.title: Head of Growth
leaders.bio: Sri Batchu is Head of Growth at Ramp, the fastest growing SaaS and FinTech business in history ($100M ARR in 2 years, 4X growth). Previously VP of Ops at Opendoor and Head of Growth at Instacart.

notableQuotes.quote: There's a general path most B2B companies should take: founder-led sales, first salespeople, low-cost targeted marketing, PR, then paid and brand. The channels get more expensive as you go but more effective as you understand your customers.
notableQuotes.context: On the optimal progression of growth channels for B2B companies

notableQuotes.quote: They hit a hundred million dollar yearly run rate in two years, which is absurd, and in the last year grew 4X during a period where most companies barely grew at all.
notableQuotes.context: Lenny describing Ramp's unprecedented growth under Sri's leadership

leaders.episodeSummary: Sri Batchu reveals the growth playbook behind Ramp, the fastest growing SaaS and FinTech company in history. He shares the optimal B2B growth channel progression from founder-led sales to paid marketing, explaining why cheaper channels should come first to build customer understanding before investing in expensive ones, plus how Ramp structures its growth team and prioritization framework.
leadershipPrinciples: Start with founder-led sales, then first salespeople, then low-cost marketing, then PR, then paid — channels get more expensive but more effective as you learn
The progression works because cheaper channels teach you about customers before you invest in expensive ones
Content, community, and small events should come before paid marketing and brand

leaders.name: Sriram Krishnan & Aarthi Ramamurthy
leaders.title: Partner at a16z / Product Leaders
leaders.company: a16z / Former PMs at Netflix, Meta, Snap, Twitter, Microsoft
leaders.bio: Sriram Krishnan is a partner at a16z and Aarthi Ramamurthy is a product leader, both former PMs who between them worked at Netflix, Meta, Snap, Twitter, Microsoft, and Clubhouse. They host The Good Time Show.
keyThemes: People You May Know feature logic
making one user's experience worse for another's benefit

notableQuotes.quote: I hate Jobs-to-be-Done. No successful company has ever been built on top of JTBD. Facebook needed to get you to 10 friends in 14 days — they made your experience slightly worse to make new users' experience better.
notableQuotes.context: On why the JTBD framework falls apart when you consider growth mechanics

notableQuotes.quote: People You May Know was performing no job for you — it was trying to perform a job for the new user who needed friends.
notableQuotes.context: On Facebook's counterintuitive product decision that prioritized new user activation

leaders.episodeSummary: Sriram and Aarthi share contrarian product wisdom from working across every major tech company, including Sriram's provocative take that Jobs-to-be-Done is a terrible framework because successful products like Facebook often make one user's experience worse to benefit another (like People You May Know). They discuss Clubhouse's explosive growth from their Elon Musk interview and insights from Netflix, Meta, Snap, and Twitter.
leadershipPrinciples: JTBD is a terrible framework — no successful company was ever built purely on it
Facebook made your experience slightly worse to make new users' experience better (People You May Know)
Sometimes the right product decision is performing no job for the current user to help a different user

leaders.name: Stewart Butterfield
leaders.title: Founder
leaders.bio: Stewart Butterfield is the founder of Slack (sold to Salesforce in one of tech's largest acquisitions) and Flickr, known for his obsession with product craft, taste, and creating value for customers.
keyThemes: creating customer value as measure of success

notableQuotes.quote: What we have right now is just a giant piece of shit. If you can't see almost limitless opportunities to improve, then you shouldn't be designing the product.
notableQuotes.context: On his famous MIT Technology Review quote about Slack in 2014, reflecting his craft standards

notableQuotes.quote: In the long run, the measure of our success will be the amount of value that we create for customers. There's no substitute for actually having created it.
notableQuotes.context: On the mantra he made the entire company chant at all-hands meetings

leaders.episodeSummary: Stewart Butterfield, founder of Slack and Flickr, shares product wisdom he rarely discusses publicly, including utility curves, the owner's delusion, and his concept of 'hyperrealistic work-like activities' that make teams feel productive while accomplishing nothing. He explains the backstory of his legendary 'we don't sell saddles here' memo and why you should always see limitless opportunities to improve your product.
leadershipPrinciples: If you can't see almost limitless opportunities to improve your product, you shouldn't be designing it
The long-run measure of success is the amount of value created for customers — there's no substitute
Friction in a product can sometimes be a good thing

leaders.name: Tamar Yehoshua
leaders.title: President of Product & Technology
leaders.bio: Tamar Yehoshua is President of Product and Technology at Glean, previously CPO at Slack (through IPO and Salesforce acquisition), leader of Google Search product/engineering, and VP at Amazon A9.com. She serves on boards including ServiceNow.
keyThemes: companies don't have to be run well to win

notableQuotes.quote: Make sure you go somewhere where you have a good engineering partner. If you have great ideas but you can't get them built, then you go nowhere.
notableQuotes.context: On the most important criterion when evaluating a new PM role

notableQuotes.quote: You don't want people in the organization asking mom and dad and getting different opinions and playing one against the other. That doesn't work.
notableQuotes.context: On why PM-engineering alignment is essential for cross-functional teams

leaders.episodeSummary: Tamar Yehoshua draws on experience at Glean, Slack, Google Search, and Amazon to share why your engineering partnership is the most important factor in PM success and why companies don't have to be run well to win. She shares lessons from Jeff Bezos, Stewart Butterfield, and Marc Benioff, plus practical insights on building AI products where outputs are non-deterministic and unpredictable.
leadershipPrinciples: Make sure you have a good engineering partner — great ideas with no one to build them go nowhere
Align on roles and responsibilities so teams don't play mom against dad
Companies don't have to be run well to win — but they do have to be run well to endure

leaders.name: Tanguy Crusson
leaders.title: Product Leader
leaders.bio: Tanguy Crusson has been at Atlassian for over 10 years, working on HipChat, Stride, StatusPage, and most recently leading Jira Product Discovery from idea to launch as one of the fastest growing products in Atlassian history.
keyThemes: zero to one inside big companies

notableQuotes.quote: The company has a tendency to over-invest. Startups have the benefit of starving, and so you need to create scarcity.
notableQuotes.context: On the biggest challenge of zero-to-one innovation inside large companies

notableQuotes.quote: I needed the rest of the company to go away so we could get the autonomy to test the things that we needed.
notableQuotes.context: On why internal incubation requires separation from the parent organization

leaders.episodeSummary: Tanguy Crusson shares the real-talk challenges of zero-to-one innovation inside Atlassian, covering failures (HipChat, Stride) and successes (Jira Product Discovery, one of Atlassian's fastest-growing products). He explains why big companies over-invest in new bets, how to create startup-like scarcity through their Point A incubation program, and why autonomous teams need the rest of the company to go away.
leadershipPrinciples: Big companies tend to over-invest in new bets — startups have the benefit of starving, so create scarcity
You need the rest of the company to go away so you can get autonomy to test what you need to
Remind everyone things are going to fail — don't drag the rest of the company into it

leaders.name: Teresa Torres
leaders.title: Product Coach & Author
leaders.bio: Teresa Torres is a product coach, speaker, and author of Continuous Discovery Habits — the #1 most recommended book in Lenny's newsletter community. She is likely in the top five people globally for the number of PMs she has taught and impacted.
keyThemes: making the case for user research

notableQuotes.quote: Continuous Discovery Habits is the number one most recommended book in my newsletter Slack community.
notableQuotes.context: Lenny describing the outsized impact of Teresa's work on the PM community

notableQuotes.quote: Build a system within your team where you're talking to customers regularly — and automate this process so you don't spend all your time on it.
notableQuotes.context: On making continuous discovery sustainable rather than heroic

leaders.episodeSummary: Teresa Torres goes deep on her opportunity solution tree framework and how to build sustainable systems for continuous customer discovery. She covers the most common interviewing mistakes, how to automate the research process so it doesn't become a time burden, and how to make the case within your organization for spending more time talking to customers.
leadershipPrinciples: Build a system for talking to customers regularly — don't make it a one-time event
The opportunity solution tree is simple but incredibly powerful for organizing discovery work
Automate the customer conversation process so it doesn't become a time burden

leaders.name: Tim Holley
leaders.title: Product Leader
leaders.bio: Tim Holley is a product leader at Etsy who navigated the platform through the COVID face mask surge, one of the most dramatic demand spikes in marketplace history, and helped expand Etsy's category perception beyond masks.

notableQuotes.quote: We went to sleep one day with typical April traffic, and then it was Black Friday overnight. Nobody knew where to find face masks. Our sellers, if you knew how to sew and had material, making a mask is quite simple.
notableQuotes.context: On the unprecedented COVID demand surge that transformed Etsy

notableQuotes.quote: We did something we've never done in Etsy's past — we put out a call to sellers saying, 'Now's the time to make face masks if you can.'
notableQuotes.context: On Etsy's unprecedented direct call to sellers during the mask shortage

leaders.episodeSummary: Tim Holley shares the inside story of Etsy's COVID face mask surge — going from normal April traffic to Black Friday overnight — and how Etsy made the unprecedented decision to directly call on sellers to make masks. He explains how they then worked to expand category perception beyond masks, ensuring the surge became a lasting expansion rather than a one-time spike.
leadershipPrinciples: When crisis creates demand, call on your sellers directly — Etsy put out an unprecedented call to make masks
After the crisis surge, work hard to expand perception so the story isn't just about one category
Sellers are astute business people who can pivot quickly — wedding dress makers started sewing masks overnight

leaders.name: Timothy Davis
leaders.title: Performance Marketing Leader
leaders.company: Shopify / Consultant for Pinterest, LinkedIn, Redfin, Eventbrite
leaders.bio: Timothy Davis has led performance marketing for all of Shopify and consulted for Pinterest, LinkedIn, Redfin, and Eventbrite on kickstarting and scaling performance marketing teams.
keyThemes: signs of life tests on platforms

notableQuotes.quote: Hot take: paid is for everyone. If you look at Google, you have to scroll pretty far to get to organic. Meta is almost pay for play now.
notableQuotes.context: On why every company should invest in performance marketing

notableQuotes.quote: Instead of thinking about being on top of the page — that's ego marketing — it's about showing to the right person as often as possible.
notableQuotes.context: On the most common mistake agencies make in performance marketing

leaders.episodeSummary: Timothy Davis gets incredibly tactical on performance marketing, arguing that paid growth is for every company since organic reach has shrunk dramatically on Google and Meta. He shares how to run signs of life tests on each platform, what agencies consistently get wrong (ego marketing vs right-person targeting), when to invest pre vs post product-market fit, and what your first three performance marketing hires should look like.
leadershipPrinciples: Paid is for everyone — Google makes you scroll far for organic, Meta is pay-for-play
Show to the right person as often as possible, not just be number one on the page (that's ego marketing)
Run signs of life tests on each platform before investing big

leaders.name: Tobi Lutke
leaders.title: Founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Tobi Lutke is the founder and CEO of Shopify, operating with a 100-year vision and driven by dissatisfaction with the status quo to make entrepreneurship more common.
keyThemes: fun and delight as business power

notableQuotes.quote: My energy source is dissatisfaction with status quo. Today is the dystopia of the future. It behooves us to try to build the kinds of products that lead towards progress.
notableQuotes.context: On what drives him as a builder and why he stays energized

notableQuotes.quote: Pessimism sounds extremely sophisticated. Optimism always sounds dumb or at least naive. The most powerful unquantifiable things in business are fun and delight.
notableQuotes.context: On why the conventional business aesthetic misses what actually matters

leaders.episodeSummary: Tobi Lutke shares his 100-year vision for Shopify and the philosophy that drives it: dissatisfaction with the status quo as an energy source, working backwards from the future, and the contrarian belief that optimism and delight are more powerful than the sophisticated pessimism that dominates business thinking. He explains why Shopify exists to make entrepreneurship more common.
leadershipPrinciples: My energy source is dissatisfaction with the status quo — today is the dystopia of the future
Pessimism sounds sophisticated but optimism actually drives progress
The most powerful unquantifiable things in business are fun and delight

leaders.name: Todd Jackson
leaders.title: Partner
leaders.bio: Todd Jackson is a partner at First Round Capital, previously product lead for Gmail (4 years), PM for Facebook News Feed/Photos/Groups, Director of PM at Twitter, and VP of Product and Design at Dropbox.

notableQuotes.quote: Finding product-market fit is the single most important thing that your startup does in the first three years, and it's just underexplored and underexplained as a topic.
notableQuotes.context: On why he's been developing a comprehensive PMF framework at First Round

notableQuotes.quote: We've found a consistent set of patterns: demand, satisfaction, and efficiency. But you don't go for all three from the very beginning.
notableQuotes.context: On the three dimensions of product-market fit that emerge sequentially

leaders.episodeSummary: Todd Jackson, former PM lead for Gmail and Facebook News Feed turned First Round Capital partner, shares his comprehensive product-market fit framework with four levels (nascent, developing, strong, extreme) and three dimensions (demand, satisfaction, efficiency). He reveals that roughly 60% of startups never get past level 2, and explains why PMF remains the most important and underexplored topic in startups.
leadershipPrinciples: Finding product-market fit is the single most important thing a startup does in the first three years
PMF has three components: demand, satisfaction, and efficiency — but you don't go for all three from the start
There are four levels of PMF: nascent, developing, strong, extreme — roughly 60% never pass L2

leaders.name: Tom Conrad
leaders.title: CEO
leaders.company: Zero Longevity Science / Former CTO Pandora, VP Product Snap
leaders.bio: Tom Conrad is CEO of Zero Longevity Science, former CTO of Pandora (0 to 80M users), VP of Product at Snap alongside Evan Spiegel, CPO at Quibi, and board member at Sonos. He was also at Apple and Pets.com.
keyThemes: not everyone should be a founder

notableQuotes.quote: Our industry would be much better off if there were fewer founders. An entire category of smart, creative people would be so much better off finding a team that needs their skillset.
notableQuotes.context: On why the pressure to become a founder leads many talented people astray

notableQuotes.quote: You don't have to be the person that raises the seed round. You can achieve acclaim, financial reward, cultural impact through collaboration with others.
notableQuotes.context: On why joining a great team can be better than founding a company

leaders.episodeSummary: Tom Conrad shares hard-won wisdom from both famous successes (Pandora, Snap) and infamous failures (Quibi, Pets.com), arguing controversially that our industry would be better with fewer founders. He explains why many talented people would be better off joining great teams rather than founding doomed startups, plus lessons on business model math, burnout, and picking where to work.
leadershipPrinciples: Our industry would be better if there were fewer founders — many would be better off joining great teams
Smart, creative people who raise $2M seed and build a company that goes nowhere should have joined existing teams
Understanding the math formula of the business model is essential before committing

leaders.name: Tomer Cohen
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Tomer Cohen is longtime CPO at LinkedIn, piloting the Full Stack Builder Program — a new model where anyone from any function can take products from idea to launch using human-plus-AI teams.

notableQuotes.quote: I start backwards. What is the potential here? LinkedIn ultimately is a platform for economic opportunity that sits on top of a very strong social graph.
notableQuotes.context: On the strategic vision behind LinkedIn's product transformation

notableQuotes.quote: This is not a springboard for other products. It's not a traffic jumpstart, it's not an upsell feed. It's about people that matter, talking about things that I care about professionally.
notableQuotes.context: On how redefining the feed's purpose drove LinkedIn's turnaround

leaders.episodeSummary: Tomer Cohen reveals the strategy behind LinkedIn's feed transformation from a place nobody checked to one people visit 10+ times daily. The key insight was redefining the feed's purpose: not a traffic jumpstart or upsell feed, but people who matter talking about things you care about professionally. He also explains how LinkedIn adopted an AI-first mindset well before AI became mainstream.
leadershipPrinciples: Start backwards from potential — LinkedIn is a platform for economic opportunity sitting on a strong social graph
The feed's purpose is people who matter talking about things you care about professionally — not an upsell feed
Shift to AI-first by redefining the feed's purpose, not just adding AI features

leaders.name: Tristan de Montebello
leaders.title: Co-Creator
leaders.bio: Tristan de Montebello is the co-creator of Ultraspeaking and the fastest competitor to reach the finals of the World Championship of Public Speaking in 2017, now teaching others to speak more naturally and confidently.
keyThemes: public speaking voice vs real voice

notableQuotes.quote: People get into a public speaking voice. They'll be chatting normally and then we say 'give a speech' and suddenly they enter a different, professional version of themselves. It's so much more effective to speak conversationally.
notableQuotes.context: On the most common speaking mistake that Ultraspeaking helps people overcome

notableQuotes.quote: Becoming a better speaker is such an accelerant of your professional life.
notableQuotes.context: On why public speaking skills deserve more investment from product leaders

leaders.episodeSummary: Tristan de Montebello, fastest finalist in the World Championship of Public Speaking, shares tactics for speaking more naturally and confidently. He explains why people adopt an artificial 'public speaking voice' that's less effective than their conversational voice, and demonstrates live exercises that help build comfort with speaking on the spot.
leadershipPrinciples: People enter a 'public speaking voice' that's less effective than their natural conversational voice
It's more freeing, powerful, connecting, and effective to speak conversationally
Becoming a better speaker is one of the biggest accelerants of professional life

leaders.name: Upasna Gautam
leaders.title: Product Manager
leaders.bio: Upasna Gautam is a PM at CNN leading the content management system used by journalists, a leader in the News Product Alliance elevating PM discipline in newsrooms, and a longtime meditation and mindfulness teacher.

notableQuotes.quote: Breaking news breaks, and it takes so much effort to gather editors across the globe. When breaking news happens, they have to prioritize that over everything. So we always have to have backup and buffers.
notableQuotes.context: On the unique challenges of doing PM work at a breaking news organization

notableQuotes.quote: Mindfulness as a meditation teacher ends up being pretty damn handy working at a place like CNN.
notableQuotes.context: On how mindfulness practice directly applies to high-stress product work

leaders.episodeSummary: Upasna Gautam provides a rare look at product management outside Silicon Valley at CNN, where breaking news can disrupt any plan at any moment. She shares how the product team collaborates with journalists, why building buffers into plans is essential when disruption is the norm, and how her background as a mindfulness teacher is surprisingly practical for high-stress product work.
leadershipPrinciples: When breaking news breaks, always have backup and buffers — you must be ready to pivot at the drop of a hat
Mindfulness is a practical PM skill, especially in high-stress environments like newsrooms
You can be frustrated when plans get disrupted, but having buffers built in makes pivoting sustainable

leaders.name: Uri Levine
leaders.title: Co-founder
leaders.bio: Uri Levine is co-founder of Waze and nine other companies, having sold two for over $1 billion each. He has served on 20 startup boards and advised over 50 startups.
keyThemes: fall in love with the problem

notableQuotes.quote: Fall in love, fall in love, fall in love with the problem. Then engage everyone else to fall in love with the same problem, to go into this journey and follow your leadership.
notableQuotes.context: On the single biggest lesson from co-founding 10 companies and building two unicorns

notableQuotes.quote: Every time you hire someone new, mark your calendar for 30 days. Ask: knowing what I know today, would I hire this person? If no, fire them immediately.
notableQuotes.context: On his ruthlessly practical approach to hiring and firing

leaders.episodeSummary: Uri Levine, co-founder of Waze and nine other companies with two billion-dollar exits, shares his core philosophy: fall in love with the problem, not the solution. He covers his 30-day hiring test (would you hire them again?), fundraising tactics, and why engaging others in the problem you're solving is the essence of startup leadership.
leadershipPrinciples: Fall in love with the problem, not the solution — and engage everyone else to fall in love with the same problem
Mark your calendar 30 days after every hire and ask: knowing what I know today, would I hire them? If no, fire immediately
Leadership is getting everyone to follow you on the journey of solving a problem they all care about

leaders.name: Varun Mohan
leaders.title: Co-founder & CEO
leaders.bio: Varun Mohan is co-founder and CEO of Windsurf, one of the most popular AI coding tools with over 1 million users in four months, and the main competitor to Cursor. They pivoted from GPU infrastructure to AI coding tools.
keyThemes: pivot from GPU to AI coding
AI makes ROI of tech higher

notableQuotes.quote: We should be cannibalizing the existing state of our product every six to 12 months. It should make our existing product look silly.
notableQuotes.context: On the pace of self-disruption required in AI products

notableQuotes.quote: I want the company to be like a dehydrated entity. Every hire is a little bit of water, and we only hire when we're back to being dehydrated.
notableQuotes.context: On his hiring philosophy that keeps the team lean and hungry

leaders.episodeSummary: Varun Mohan shares how Windsurf reached 1 million users in four months through two pivots from GPU infrastructure to AI coding tools, and why they invest in self-cannibalization every 6-12 months. He explains his 'dehydrated company' hiring philosophy, why agency will be the most critical skill in the AI era, and why AI actually increases the ROI of hiring engineers rather than reducing it.
leadershipPrinciples: You should cannibalize your existing product every 6-12 months — it should make the current version look silly
Keep the company like a dehydrated entity — only hire when you're back to being dehydrated
AI means engineers produce more, so the ROI of building technology goes up — hire more, not fewer

leaders.name: Varun Parmar
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Varun Parmar is CPO at Miro, previously SVP and CPO at Box, known for building product culture in an incredibly competitive market where Miro continues to grow.
keyThemes: every release makes product better or worse

notableQuotes.quote: Every single time you push code to production, you are making the product better or worse. The product never remains the same. You are either making chess points against competitors or going negative.
notableQuotes.context: On the framework that drives clarity about the impact of every release

notableQuotes.quote: Everyone I've ever met from Miro has been super interesting and super smart.
notableQuotes.context: Lenny describing the distinctive product culture at Miro

leaders.episodeSummary: Varun Parmar reveals the product culture that has made Miro successful in an incredibly competitive market, centered on the principle that every code push either makes the product better or worse — like chess points against competitors. This framework drives clarity about impact and prevents the complacency of thinking the product is 'good enough.'
leadershipPrinciples: Every code push either makes your product better or worse — it never stays the same
With every release you and your competitor make, you're either gaining or losing chess points
This framework drives insane clarity about what you're doing and the impact it will have

leaders.name: Vijay Iyengar
leaders.title: Head of Product
leaders.bio: Vijay Iyengar is Head of Product at Mixpanel, who made the unusual transition from engineering manager to director of product. He navigated Mixpanel's journey from multi-product complexity back to focused core analytics.
keyThemes: invest profits not people in new ventures
don't take people from core product

notableQuotes.quote: Don't take people away from the core to go to these other things because then you end up distracted. Invest profits, not people, into the next venture.
notableQuotes.context: On the key lesson from Mixpanel's journey of expanding then refocusing

notableQuotes.quote: As an engineer, you build up scar tissue and an immune response to say no to new ideas. I had to unlearn that moving into product because ideas are fragile.
notableQuotes.context: On the biggest mindset shift from engineering leader to product leader

leaders.episodeSummary: Vijay Iyengar shares lessons from Mixpanel's journey of expanding to multiple products and then making the hard decision to refocus on core analytics. His key insight: invest profits, not people, in new ventures — taking people from your core product leaves you open to disruption. He also discusses the unusual transition from engineering manager to product leader and unlearning the engineer's default 'no.'
leadershipPrinciples: Don't take people away from your core product for new ventures — invest profits, not people
If you're the leader in a core product, out-invest everyone else in that core
The trap is leaving yourself open to disruption while chasing new things

leaders.name: Vikrama Dhiman
leaders.title: Head of Product
leaders.bio: Vikrama Dhiman heads all product at Gojek (PM, design, program management, research) across India, Singapore, and Indonesia. He is among the most well-known product leaders in Asia.
keyThemes: what you produce vs what you bring

notableQuotes.quote: I created a career growth framework for PMs comprising three things: what you produce, what you bring to the table, and what's your operating model.
notableQuotes.context: On his PM career development framework used across Asia

notableQuotes.quote: Can you show me your last PRD? Can you show me your product strategy doc? You must have impact through the artifacts that you work on.
notableQuotes.context: On why tangible outputs matter more than theoretical knowledge for PM career growth

leaders.episodeSummary: Vikrama Dhiman, one of Asia's most respected product leaders, shares his PM career growth framework based on three dimensions: what you produce, what you bring to the table, and your operating model. He argues that early-career PMs should focus on getting things done and having artifacts to show, not just thinking strategically, and discusses how PMs often shoot themselves in the foot.
leadershipPrinciples: PM career growth has three dimensions: what you produce, what you bring to the table, and your operating model
Early in your career, focus on getting stuff out and done — show your artifacts
Can you show me your last PRD, product note, or strategy doc? You must have impact through artifacts

leaders.name: Wes Kao
leaders.title: Executive Communication Coach & Entrepreneur
leaders.company: Co-founder of Maven / Co-creator of altMBA with Seth Godin
leaders.bio: Wes Kao co-created the altMBA with Seth Godin, co-founded Maven, and now teaches Executive Communication and Influence. She is widely regarded as one of the best teachers of communication in tech.

notableQuotes.quote: Most people assume that their boss has to manage them. But if you embrace managing up, your boss will appreciate you more, you'll get more opportunities, more trust — there's all these great things that happen.
notableQuotes.context: On why managing up is a skill most people resist but all should embrace

notableQuotes.quote: You can continue to think your boss should manage you and your career might be fine. But embracing managing up opens doors that waiting never will.
notableQuotes.context: On the career impact of proactive upward management

leaders.episodeSummary: Wes Kao shares tactical advice for managing up, the super specific who framework, and the state change method for running better meetings. She explains why most people resist managing their boss out of resentment but those who embrace it get dramatically more opportunities, trust, and career advancement.
leadershipPrinciples: If you manage up, your boss will appreciate you more, give you more opportunities, and trust you more
Most people feel resentful about managing up — embracing it is a career accelerator
The super specific who forces you to define exactly who your message or product is for

leaders.name: Will Larson
leaders.title: CTO
leaders.bio: Will Larson is CTO at Carta, former engineering leader at Stripe, Uber, and Calm, and author of An Elegant Puzzle, Staff Engineer, and The Engineering Executive's Primer — essential reading for all engineers.

notableQuotes.quote: We often treat engineers like children instead of giving them the responsibilities to thrive as adults. 'The engineers won't want to do that work' — it's not good to shelter them from what's important.
notableQuotes.context: On the biggest cultural shift needed in how companies treat engineering talent

notableQuotes.quote: We're coming to this moment where we can treat engineers like our peers and put them into really senior leadership roles without assuming we have to coddle them.
notableQuotes.context: On the evolution of the engineering leadership role

leaders.episodeSummary: Will Larson, one of the most requested podcast guests, argues that the tech industry needs to stop treating engineers like children who need to be sheltered from real business problems. Drawing on experience at Carta, Stripe, Uber, and as author of three essential engineering books, he explains how putting engineers in senior leadership roles and exposing them to real problems is how they and the company grow.
leadershipPrinciples: We often treat engineers like children instead of giving them responsibilities to thrive as adults
It's not good for engineers to be sheltered from what's important — they need to see the real problems
Engineers should be put into senior leadership roles without the assumption that we need to coddle them

leaders.name: Yuhki Yamashita
leaders.title: Chief Product Officer
leaders.bio: Yuhki Yamashita is CPO at Figma, previously a product leader and Head of Design at Uber, with experience at Google and Microsoft. He also taught introductory CS at Harvard.
keyThemes: championing a new way of working

notableQuotes.quote: One of the first responses we saw to Figma was 'if this is the future of design, I'm quitting.' That narrative tension is signal that you're part of a revolution.
notableQuotes.context: On why controversial reactions to multiplayer design meant Figma was onto something

notableQuotes.quote: Users aren't just championing a tool — they're also championing a new way of working. How do you equip your customers to want to talk about that?
notableQuotes.context: On how Figma turned product advocacy into a movement

leaders.episodeSummary: Yuhki Yamashita reveals how Figma turned controversy into advocacy: when early users said 'if this is the future of design, I'm quitting,' that narrative tension was a signal they were part of a revolution. He explains how to build products that equip users to champion not just a tool but a new way of working, and how Figma's multiplayer design fundamentally changed the design industry.
leadershipPrinciples: Controversy about your product is signal that you're part of a revolution and trying to change something
When your product equips customers with a narrative to champion, they'll advocate for you
Users aren't just championing a tool — they're championing a new way of working

leaders.name: Yuriy Timen
leaders.title: Growth Advisor
leaders.company: Former VP Growth at Grammarly / Advisor to Canva, Airtable, Otter
leaders.bio: Yuriy Timen is a full-time growth advisor who spent nine years at Grammarly leading growth and marketing. He has advised Canva, Airtable, Otter, Whimsical, Hims, and dozens of other companies on growth strategy.

notableQuotes.quote: The only thing worse than a channel not working is when you didn't give it an appropriate shot and prematurely concluded it doesn't work. It's remarkable how often that's the case.
notableQuotes.context: On the most common growth failure mode he sees across companies

notableQuotes.quote: 'Oh, YouTube, we tried it. It doesn't work.' I look at what they tried and it was not designed to even have a shot at working from the get-go.
notableQuotes.context: On why companies wrongly dismiss growth channels

leaders.episodeSummary: Yuriy Timen provides the most tactical and actionable conversation on product growth, especially for subscription products, drawing on nine years leading Grammarly's growth and advising Canva, Airtable, and dozens of others. His key insight: the biggest growth failure mode is prematurely dismissing channels that were never properly tested to begin with.
leadershipPrinciples: The worst thing is prematurely concluding a channel doesn't work because you didn't give it an appropriate shot
When companies say 'YouTube doesn't work for us,' it's remarkably often because they never set it up to succeed
Growth channels should be evaluated on whether they were properly tested, not just whether they worked

leaders.name: Zevi Arnovitz
leaders.title: Product Manager
leaders.bio: Zevi Arnovitz is a PM at Meta with zero technical background who has learned to use Cursor and Claude Code to build significant products entirely on his own, creating a clever workflow that any non-technical person can copy.

notableQuotes.quote: I have zero technical background, did music in high school. When Sonnet 3.5 came out, it basically felt like someone came up to me and said, 'You have superpowers now.'
notableQuotes.context: On the moment AI changed what was possible for non-technical PMs

notableQuotes.quote: In the next coming years, I think everyone's going to become a builder. Titles are going to collapse and responsibilities are going to collapse.
notableQuotes.context: On how AI is fundamentally changing who can build products

leaders.episodeSummary: Zevi Arnovitz demonstrates that non-technical PMs can build significant products using AI tools like Cursor and Claude Code, sharing his clever workflow that anyone can copy. With zero technical background, he shows how AI has given him superpowers to ship real products, arguing that in the coming years everyone will become a builder as titles and traditional role boundaries collapse.
leadershipPrinciples: In the coming years, everyone is going to become a builder — titles and responsibilities will collapse
AI gives non-technical people superpowers to ship real products without writing code
Code is terrifying for non-technical people but AI makes so much more possible

leaders.name: Zoelle Egner
leaders.title: Head of Marketing & Growth
leaders.bio: Zoelle Egner was one of the earliest employees at Airtable, leading early marketing and customer success. She also worked at Box, advised dozens of startups, and is now head of marketing and growth at Block Party.
keyThemes: getting people to root for you

notableQuotes.quote: Have your sample content be references to your industry so people are like 'Oh, that's a joke about Steve Jobs. This person is thinking about me.' It's small stuff but it builds brand trust.
notableQuotes.context: On how Airtable used sample content details to make customers feel seen

notableQuotes.quote: When you are small, you need everyone rooting for you that you can possibly get. Personality and details in your product make people want to root for you.
notableQuotes.context: On why early-stage startups should invest in small quality details

leaders.episodeSummary: Zoelle Egner shares how Airtable grew into a legendary business through attention to small details that made customers feel seen — like using industry-relevant sample content instead of generic placeholders. She explains why moving fast doesn't mean skipping quality in writing, illustration, and content, and how these small investments build the brand trust that makes people root for you when you're small.
leadershipPrinciples: Small details like thoughtful sample content tell customers you built the product with them in mind
When you're small, you need everyone rooting for you — personality and details create that
Move fast but have someone reread your email, invest in decent illustrations, make sample content relevant
